teile.einleitung: Winter tyres are car tyres built specially for cold, snow and ice. Their soft rubber compound and their tread with many fine grooves give the car better grip in winter. This makes braking and steering on wintry roads much safer.
wichtigste: Thanks to a special rubber compound, winter tyres stay soft even in the cold.
Fine cuts in the tread, called sipes, interlock with the snow.
Real winter tyres carry the symbol of a snowflake in front of a mountain.
According to a rule of thumb, winter tyres have advantages below about 7 degrees Celsius.
A well known German rule of thumb is: winter tyres “von O bis O”, that is, from October (Oktober) to Easter (Ostern).
In Switzerland there is no general obligation to fit winter tyres, but the car must be equipped to suit the conditions (as of 2025).
The legal minimum tread depth is 1.6 mm; for winter tyres, experts recommend at least about 4 mm.

abschnitte.text: A tyre has the important job of connecting the car to the road. Only the contact patches of the four tyres, each about the size of a postcard, hold the whole car. Normal **summer tyres** become hard and slippery in the cold, like a cold rubber. Winter tyres have a **rubber compound** that stays soft even when it is below freezing. This lets them grip the road better.

The tread of winter tyres has deep grooves and many fine cuts, the **sipes**. These sipes open slightly as the tyre rolls and interlock with the snow. Snow also sticks well to snow, so some snow stays caught in the tread and improves grip. The wide grooves carry away water and slush. The less **tread depth** a tyre has, the worse this works.

You can recognise real winter tyres by a symbol with a **snowflake in front of a mountain**. It shows that the tyre has reached a certain performance in a test on snow. The letters **M+S** stand for mud and snow, but on their own they do not guarantee tested winter performance. All season tyres try to combine summer and winter properties. They are a compromise and in the mountains are often less good than proper winter tyres.

In Switzerland there is no general **obligation to fit winter tyres** (as of 2025). But the law requires a vehicle to be equipped to suit the road conditions. Anyone who causes an accident or blocks traffic with summer tyres can be fined and may have problems with their insurance. The legal minimum tread depth is 1.6 mm. For winter tyres, experts recommend about 4 mm, because below that they grip much less well on snow.

The German rule of thumb “von O bis O” means: fit winter tyres from **October (Oktober) to Easter (Ostern)**. Another rule says that winter tyres have the advantage below about 7 degrees Celsius. In mountain regions such as the Grisons or Valais you often need them earlier. On some pass roads, **snow chains** are also compulsory when a sign says so. Many garages store the tyres for the other season for their customers.

begriffe.erklaerung: The pattern of grooves and blocks on the running surface of a tyre.
Fine cuts in the tyre tread that interlock with snow and ice.
How deep the grooves in the tyre still are, measured in millimetres.
Chains that are put round the tyres to give better grip on snow and ice.

gewusst: The first winter tyres were developed in Finland in the 1930s.
On a snowy road, the braking distance with good winter tyres can be much shorter than with summer tyres.
Studded tyres with small metal pins are allowed in Switzerland only in the winter half of the year and with a speed limit.

teile.einleitung: Cones are sensory cells in the retina of the eye with which we see colours. They work mainly in bright light and give a sharp image. Together with the rods, they turn light into signals that the brain processes into pictures.
wichtigste: Cones are light sensitive sensory cells in the retina.
They are mainly responsible for seeing colours.
People with normal colour vision have three kinds of cone.
A human eye has about 6 million cones.
In the macula, the spot of sharpest vision, there are particularly many cones.
The rods are responsible for seeing in twilight.
At night you can hardly make out colours, because the cones need a lot of light.

abschnitte.text: At the back of the eye lies the **retina**, a thin layer full of sensory cells. Light falls through the pupil and the lens and forms a picture there. In the retina there are two kinds of light sensitive cell: **cones** and **rods**. Their names come from their shape under the microscope. They turn light into electrical signals that travel to the brain through the optic nerve.

There are three kinds of cone, which react particularly strongly to different light. One kind is sensitive mainly to short wave, bluish light, one to medium, greenish light and one to long wave, reddish light. The brain compares how strongly each kind is stimulated and works out the colour from this. In this way millions of shades arise from only three signals. Screens make use of this by mixing all colours from **red, green and blue**.

The cones are not spread evenly. They are packed particularly densely in the **macula**, the spot of sharpest vision in the middle of the retina. At its centre, the fovea, there are almost only cones. When we look at something closely, for example a letter when reading, we point the eye so that the image lands exactly there. At the edge of the retina there are far fewer cones, which is why you see blurred out of the corner of your eye.

An eye has about 6 million cones but around 120 million **rods**. Rods are much more sensitive to light and help us see in twilight. But they cannot tell colours apart. That is why at night we see almost only shades of grey, because the cones need a lot of light and then hardly work. A German saying puts it like this: at night all cats are grey.

In some people one type of cone is missing or works differently. The most common is **red green colour blindness**, in which red and green shades are hard to tell apart. It is usually inherited and affects men much more often than women. The English scientist John Dalton described it in himself at the end of the 18th century, which is why it is also called **Daltonism**. With test charts full of coloured dots, an eye doctor can detect such a deficiency.

begriffe.erklaerung: The light sensitive layer at the back of the eye.
Sensory cells of the retina for colour vision and sharp vision in bright light.
Sensory cells of the retina for seeing in low light.
The spot on the retina where we see most sharply.
The nerve that carries the signals from the eye to the brain.

gewusst: Many birds have four kinds of cone and can even see ultraviolet light.
Dogs have only two kinds of cone and therefore see fewer colours than people.
When you go from the sun into a dark room, it takes a while until the rods are working fully.

teile.einleitung: The wave equation is an important formula in physics that describes how waves spread out. It applies to water waves, sound waves, vibrating strings and even to light. If you understand it, you can predict where a wave will be at what moment.
wichtigste: A wave is a vibration that spreads through space and carries energy as it does so.
The function y(x, t) gives the displacement of a wave at position x at time t.
The classical wave equation is a linear partial differential equation of second order.
Because it is linear, solutions can simply be added together; this is called superposition.
The speed of propagation is calculated with c = ω / k.
In the 18th century, Jean-Baptiste le Rond d'Alembert found the general solution for one dimension.
Points half a wavelength apart vibrate in antiphase.

abschnitte.text: If you throw a stone into water, rings spread out, even though the water itself hardly flows onwards. Each water particle only moves up and down, but the **wave** travels on. It is the same with sound, a plucked guitar string or a shaken rope. The amount by which a point moves away from its resting position is called the **displacement**. The function y(x, t) tells you how big this displacement is at position x at time t.

The classical wave equation links how fast the displacement changes with time to its curvature in space. In one dimension it is written as ∂²y/∂t² = c² · ∂²y/∂x². Here c is the **speed of propagation** of the wave. Because it contains second derivatives with respect to position and time, it is a second order **partial differential equation**. For children the idea is enough: the equation is a rule that every wave must obey.

The simplest solution is a sine wave of the form y = A · sin(ωt − kx). Here A is the **amplitude**, that is, the greatest displacement. The angular frequency ω tells you how fast a point vibrates, and the angular wavenumber k how closely the crests are packed. Such a wave travels in the positive x direction, and its speed is c = ω / k. Example: for y = 0.02 m · sin(2π · (5 s⁻¹ · t − 0.5 m⁻¹ · x)) the speed works out at 10 m/s.

The wave equation is **linear**. This means: if two waves are solutions, then their sum is a solution too. That is why waves can pass through each other undisturbed and strengthen or cancel each other as they do so. This interplay is called **interference**. If two points are half a wavelength apart, they have a phase difference of π and vibrate exactly against each other.

Around 1747 the French mathematician **Jean-Baptiste le Rond d'Alembert** studied the vibrating string. He showed that every solution in one dimension is made up of two waves travelling in opposite directions. This solution bears his name today. In the 19th century **James Clerk Maxwell** concluded from his equations that light is also a wave that obeys a wave equation.

Engineers use the wave equation to calculate how bridges vibrate during earthquakes. Instrument makers use it to understand why a shorter string sounds higher. In seismology it helps to explore the inside of the Earth from earthquake waves. Radio, mobile phones and wifi are also based on electromagnetic waves that follow this equation.

begriffe.erklaerung: The greatest displacement of a wave from its resting position.
The distance from one crest of a wave to the next.
The speed at which a crest moves on, calculated as c = ω / k.
An equation in which an unknown function appears together with its rates of change.
The overlapping of waves, in which they strengthen or weaken each other.

gewusst: With a Mexican wave in a football stadium, the wave travels through the rows, although every person stays in their seat.
Noise cancelling headphones use superposition: they create an opposite wave that partly cancels the noise.
The same kind of equation describes water waves in a pond and the light of distant stars.

teile.einleitung: A weather vane is a turning piece of metal on top of a roof or tower that shows the wind direction. The weathercock on church towers is particularly well known. It is one of humanity's oldest weather instruments.
wichtigste: A weather vane shows the direction the wind is blowing from.
It turns because the wind presses against its broad surface.
The point shows where the wind is coming from.
Below the vane there are often the letters N, E, S and W for the points of the compass.
On church towers there is often a cockerel as a weather vane.
Weather vanes are usually made of metal and stand right at the top, where the wind blows freely.
A weather vane cannot show the temperature or wind speed.

abschnitte.text: A weather vane consists of an upright rod with a turning figure on top. The figure has a narrow **point** at the front and a broad **tail** at the back. Below it there is often a cross with the letters N, E, S and W. These show the four **points of the compass**: north, east, south and west. So you can read from below which direction the wind is coming from.

The wind pushes harder against the large rear surface than against the narrow point. That is why the vane turns until the surface is in the shelter of the wind and the point faces straight into it. So if the point faces west, there is a **westerly wind**. When there is no wind, the vane simply stays still. So that it turns easily, it sits on a well greased **bearing**.

On many church towers in Switzerland and Europe there is a **weathercock**. The cockerel is a symbol of watchfulness, because it announces the day with its crowing in the morning. In Christianity it also recalls the story of the apostle Peter, which is told in the Bible. Other weather vanes show arrows, fish, ships, dragons or heraldic animals. The year it was built is often worked into it too.

Weather vanes are usually made of **metal** such as copper, iron or sheet metal, so that they can stand up to rain, snow and storms. Some are gilded and shine in the sun for a long way. They stand right at the top of roofs and towers, because the wind blows freely there. Further down, houses and trees would deflect the wind and give a false reading. That is why fitting them is often a job for brave roofers.

In ancient Athens, a turning figure on the **Tower of the Winds** already showed the wind. In the Middle Ages, weather vanes became common on churches, castles and town halls. Farmers and sailors used them to tell whether the weather was changing, because a change of wind can announce rain or a storm. Today weather stations measure the wind with precise instruments, but the old weather vanes have remained popular decorations.

At airfields, a fabric **windsock** shows the wind direction and roughly the wind strength too. The stronger the wind, the more horizontal the sock hangs. Wind speed is measured with an **anemometer**, which often has small spinning cups. Modern weather stations combine both with an electronic wind vane that records the direction automatically.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point of the compass the wind is coming from.
North, east, south and west, which are used to give directions on Earth.
A fabric tube that shows the wind direction and strength at airfields.
An instrument for measuring wind speed.

gewusst: The wind is always named after the direction it comes from: the föhn in the Alpine valleys is usually a southerly wind.
The English word “weathercock” means the same as the German “Wetterhahn”, a weather cockerel.
Because it turns with every wind, a person who keeps changing their mind is sometimes called a weather vane in German.

teile.einleitung: Eddy currents are electric currents that flow in circles in a piece of metal when a magnetic field changes inside it. You cannot see them, but they can heat metal or slow it down. Induction hobs, metal detectors and some train brakes use them on purpose.
wichtigste: Eddy currents arise in metal when the magnetic field in it changes or the metal moves in a magnetic field.
Their energy is mainly turned into heat.
An induction hob heats the bottom of the pan with eddy currents.
Eddy current brakes slow trains without friction and therefore without wear.
When a vehicle is standing still, an eddy current brake does not work, because without movement no eddy currents arise.
Transformer cores are made of thin, insulated sheets to reduce eddy currents.
Metal detectors find hidden metal objects with the help of eddy currents.

abschnitte.text: If a **magnetic field** changes in a metal, an electric voltage is produced in it. This process is called **induction**. In a solid piece of metal, currents then flow in closed circles, rather like eddies in a stream. This also happens when a metal moves through a stationary magnetic field. According to **Lenz's law**, these currents always act against their cause, which is why they slow the movement down.

Eddy currents meet resistance in the metal, which makes it warm. An **induction hob** uses this: under the glass plate there is a coil through which a rapidly alternating current flows. Its changing magnetic field produces eddy currents directly in the bottom of the pan, which then gets hot. The glass plate itself stays cooler; it is only warmed a little by the hot pan. That is why you need pans with a magnetic base.

In an **eddy current brake**, electromagnets produce eddy currents in the rail or in a metal disc. These slow the vehicle down without anything rubbing together. That is why the brake hardly wears out. High speed trains such as the German ICE 3 and many roller coasters use such brakes. Because eddy currents arise only with movement, an ordinary brake is also needed to keep the vehicle still.

abschnitte.titel: When they get in the way
abschnitte.text: In transformers and electric motors, eddy currents are unwanted because they waste energy as heat. That is why the iron cores are built from many thin **sheets** that are insulated from one another. The currents then cannot flow in large circles. **Waltenhofen's pendulum** shows this too: a solid metal plate is strongly braked between the poles of a magnet. A slotted plate, by contrast, swings through almost without being slowed.

**Metal detectors** produce a changing magnetic field that sets off eddy currents in hidden metal and so creates a signal. In recycling, an **eddy current separator** separates aluminium cans from the rest of the waste: a fast rotating magnetic field flings the aluminium pieces away. In industry, eddy currents are used to check parts for fine cracks without damaging them. Eddy currents were discovered in the 19th century; after the French physicist Léon Foucault they are also called Foucault currents.

begriffe.erklaerung: Producing an electric voltage through a changing magnetic field.
Induced currents always act against their cause.
A brake that uses magnets and eddy currents to brake without friction.
A coil with current flowing through it that acts like a magnet and can be switched on and off.

gewusst: If you drop a strong magnet down a copper pipe, it sinks very slowly because of the eddy currents.
Copper is not magnetic, yet it slows a moving magnet down through eddy currents.
At airport security, the metal detector arches work with changing magnetic fields.

teile.einleitung: The orbital period is the time a body needs for one whole round on a circle or an orbit. This can be a wheel, a Ferris wheel, a satellite or a planet. The Earth needs one year to go round the Sun once.
wichtigste: The orbital period T is the time taken for one full turn or one orbit.
Period and frequency are linked: T = 1 / f.
A wheel turning at 50 Hz has a period of 0.02 seconds.
Measured against the fixed stars, the Moon needs about 27.3 days to orbit the Earth.
A geostationary satellite goes round the Earth in about 24 hours.
According to Kepler's third law, planets further away have much longer orbital periods.

abschnitte.text: With every circular motion the movement repeats itself after a certain time. This time is called the **orbital period** or period and is written as T. It is measured in seconds, and for heavenly bodies also in days or years. How many rounds take place per second is given by the **frequency** f, measured in hertz.

The rule is T = 1 / f: if a wheel turns 50 times a second, one turn lasts 0.02 seconds. If a Ferris wheel makes 12 turns in 6 minutes, the period is 30 seconds. A record at 33⅓ revolutions per minute needs 1.8 seconds per turn. If you know the speed along the path and the radius, T = 2πr / v, and with the **angular velocity** ω, T = 2π / ω.

The Earth needs about 365.25 days to go round the Sun once, which is why there is a leap year every four years. Measured against the fixed stars, the Moon goes round the Earth in about 27.3 days. From full moon to full moon, however, it takes about 29.5 days, because in the meantime the Earth has moved further round the Sun. The outermost planet, Neptune, needs about 165 years for one round.

At the beginning of the 17th century the astronomer **Johannes Kepler** found out how orbital period and the size of the orbit are linked. The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the **semi-major axis**. If a planet has a semi-major axis four times as big as the Earth's, its orbit takes 8 years, because 8² = 4³ = 64. So the further away a planet is, the longer its year lasts.

The International Space Station flies only about 400 kilometres high and goes round the Earth in about an hour and a half. A **geostationary satellite**, on the other hand, flies about 36,000 kilometres above the equator. Its orbital period is about 24 hours, exactly as long as the Earth takes to turn once. That is why it seems to stand still in the sky, and satellite dishes do not need to follow it.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number of turns or vibrations per second, measured in hertz.
How fast the angle of rotation changes, measured in rad/s.
Half of the greatest diameter of an elliptical orbit.
The name for a satellite that seems to stand above one point on the Earth.

gewusst: The astronauts on the ISS see about 16 sunrises every day.
Since its discovery in 1846, Neptune has only gone round the Sun about once.
The Moon turns on its own axis in the same time it takes to orbit the Earth, which is why we always see the same side.

teile.einleitung: A kettle is an electric kitchen appliance that brings water to the boil quickly. It has a heater in its base and switches itself off as soon as the water boils. It is useful for tea, instant soups or for heating water in advance for pasta.
wichtigste: A kettle needs electricity to heat.
In many kettles the heater is in the base.
Water usually boils faster in a kettle than in a saucepan on the cooker.
Over time a white layer of limescale forms, which you can remove with vinegar.
You fill it with only as much water as you need, to save electricity.
You must never dip a kettle into the sink and never switch it on empty.

abschnitte.text: A **kettle** is a jug with a built in electric heater. It stands on a base with a cable, from which you can lift it off to pour. On the outside, a scale with marks shows how much water is in it. Most kettles hold between one and two litres.

In the base there is a **heating element**, through which electric current flows and makes it very hot. The heat goes straight into the water, so it gets hot faster than in a saucepan on the cooker. When the water boils, steam rises to a switch with a **bimetallic strip**. This bends in the heat and switches the kettle off automatically.

Tap water contains dissolved **lime**, especially in areas with a lot of limestone, such as the Jura. When the water is heated, the lime settles as a white layer on the bottom. This layer makes the water take longer to boil and uses more electricity. With vinegar or citric acid you can dissolve the limescale and then rinse well.

You fill in only as much water as you really need, because every extra decilitre has to be heated as well. For pasta, you can heat the water in the kettle first and then pour it into the pan. This saves time and often energy too. A descaled kettle also works more economically.

A kettle is an **electrical appliance** and must never be dipped into the sink. Water in the base or on the plug can cause a dangerous electric shock. You never switch it on without water, because it could get too hot; many kettles have **boil dry protection** for this. The cable should not hang over the edge of the table, so that nobody pulls the hot kettle down.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part that turns electric current into heat.
A strip made of two metals that bends when warm and so works as a switch.
A white coating of minerals that were dissolved in the water.
A safety device that switches the appliance off if there is no water in it.

gewusst: A typical kettle has a power of about 2000 watts, much more than a television.
In Great Britain, so many kettles are switched on at the same time during the advert breaks of popular TV programmes that the power stations have to supply more electricity.
The rushing noise just before boiling comes from small steam bubbles collapsing again in the colder water.

teile.einleitung: The washing machine is a household appliance that cleans clothes with water, detergent and movement. In the past, doing the washing was hard manual work that could take a whole day. There is a lot of physics inside a washing machine.
wichtigste: Inside the washing machine a drum with lots of holes turns round.
Water, detergent, heat and movement loosen the dirt from the washing.
At the end the machine spins, turning very fast.
In many Swiss blocks of flats, the washing machine is in the shared laundry room.
Light and dark washing are washed separately, because dark colours can run.
The little pictures on the label show how a garment should be washed.
Before washing, you check the trouser pockets.

abschnitte.text: Inside the machine is a **drum** with many small holes. It fills with water, which a heater warms to the chosen temperature. The drum turns first one way and then the other, so the washing is lifted up and falls back into the water. The **detergent** loosens grease and dirt from the fibres.

At the end the drum turns very fast, often more than 1000 times a minute. The washing is pressed against the drum wall by **centrifugal force**. The water cannot follow and sprays out through the holes. That is why the washing is only damp after the **spin** and dries faster.

In many Swiss blocks of flats, all the families share a **laundry room** in the cellar. A **laundry rota** sets out who may do their washing on which day. There is often a tumble dryer there too, or a drying room with lines. In Switzerland, the rules of the laundry room are sometimes even a topic of conversation between neighbours.

The little pictures on the **care label** show, for example, at how many degrees a garment may be washed. Light and dark washing are kept apart so that no colour runs. A wool jumper can **shrink**, that is, get smaller, if the water is too hot. Before washing, you empty the pockets, because tissues, coins or pens can damage the washing and the machine.

In the past, people washed clothes in a stream or in big tubs and rubbed them on a **washboard**. Then they had to wring them out by hand. Electric washing machines have existed since the beginning of the 20th century. In Swiss households they gradually became common after the Second World War and saved a lot of time.

abschnitte.titel: Washing in an environmentally friendly way
abschnitte.text: The machine uses most of its energy to heat the water. Washing at 30 or 40 degrees instead of 60 degrees saves a lot of electricity. It is worth filling the drum well and not using too much detergent. Modern machines have an **energy label** that shows how economical they are.

begriffe.erklaerung: The rotating container in which the washing lies.
The force that pushes outwards when something spins fast.
A shared room for doing the washing in many Swiss buildings.
A sewn in label with washing instructions shown as little pictures.

gewusst: During the spin, a washing machine drum can turn faster than a car engine when idling.
A sock that disappears sometimes slips between the drum and the rubber seal.
Before there were washing machines, washing day was often the most tiring day of the week.

teile.einleitung: In combined heat and power, CHP for short, a plant produces electricity and usable heat at the same time. The heat that would otherwise be lost unused heats houses or provides hot water. In this way the fuel is used much better than in a normal power station.
wichtigste: Combined heat and power produces electricity and heat at the same time.
Such plants reach an overall efficiency of up to about 90 per cent.
A small, compact CHP plant is called a block-type heat and power plant.
Fuel cells can also supply electricity and heat without a flame.
The power-to-heat ratio is the ratio of electricity to heat.
Heat-led plants adjust their output to the demand for heat.
CHP suits Switzerland well, because it supplies electricity mainly in winter, when heating is also needed.

abschnitte.titel: What is combined heat and power?
abschnitte.text: An ordinary fuel-burning **power station** turns heat into electricity, but a large part of the energy is lost as waste heat. Often it uses only about 40 per cent of the energy for electricity. In **combined heat and power** this waste heat is captured. It is fed through water pipes into heating systems and hot water tanks. In this way the same fuel is put to use twice over.

The **overall efficiency** says how much of the energy put in is used as electricity and heat. If a plant produces 35 kilowatt hours of electricity and 50 kilowatt hours of heat from 100 kilowatt hours of fuel, it is 85 per cent. Good plants manage up to about 90 per cent. The **power-to-heat ratio** divides the electricity by the heat. With 35 kilowatts of electricity and 50 kilowatts of heat, this gives 0.7.

A **block-type heat and power plant** is a compact plant, for example for a housing estate, a school or a hospital. Usually an engine running on natural gas, biogas or wood gas drives a generator. The heat from the engine and the exhaust gas is used for heating. A **fuel cell** even manages CHP without a flame, because it turns hydrogen chemically into electricity and heat. Large heat and power stations also supply whole districts of a city through district heating.

A plant can be run in a **heat-led** way. Then it adjusts its output to the demand for heat in the houses. In winter it runs a lot, in summer only a little. An electricity-led plant, on the other hand, follows the demand for electricity. Surplus heat can be stored in large water tanks.

In Switzerland a lot of electricity comes from hydropower, which supplies most in summer. In winter electricity tends to be scarce, and at the same time heating is needed. That is why **CHP** suits Switzerland well, because it produces electricity precisely in winter. Many **waste incineration plants** use the heat from rubbish for electricity and district heating. If biogas or wood is burned, the energy is even renewable.

begriffe.erklaerung: Heat that is produced in a process and is often lost unused.
A small plant that produces electricity and heat for buildings nearby.
Hot water that flows through pipes from a power station to many houses.
The share of the energy put in that is actually used.

gewusst: Some detached houses have a mini CHP plant in the cellar that is hardly bigger than a fridge.
The heat from a waste incineration plant can heat thousands of flats.

teile.einleitung: The range of a throw tells you how far a thrown object flies before it lands on the ground. It depends mainly on how fast and at what angle you throw. It can be calculated with a simple formula, and athletes in the javelin or shot put use this knowledge to get as far as possible.
wichtigste: Without air resistance, on level ground: R = v0² · sin(2α) / g.
Without air resistance, the greatest range is reached at a release angle of 45 degrees.
If you double the release speed, the range becomes four times as great.
A ball thrown at 20 m/s at 45 degrees flies about 40 metres.
On the Moon the same throw would fly about six times as far.
In the shot put the best angle is below 45 degrees, because the shot is released above the ground.
In reality, air resistance shortens the range.

abschnitte.text: If you throw a ball upwards at a slant, it flies along a curved path, a **trajectory parabola**. It first rises, slowing down as it does so, and then falls back down. The horizontal distance from release to impact is the **range**. Physicists call such a throw an **angled throw**.

Without air resistance on level ground: R = v0² · sin(2α) / g. Here v0 is the release speed, α the release angle and g the **acceleration due to gravity**, about 10 metres per second squared. A ball thrown at 20 metres per second at 45 degrees flies 400 divided by 10, that is 40 metres. At 60 degrees it is about 34.6 metres, and a stone thrown at 30 metres per second at 15 degrees goes 45 metres.

The sine of 2α is greatest when 2α is exactly 90 degrees, that is, at a **release angle** of 45 degrees. If you throw flatter or steeper, the range becomes smaller. At 30 degrees instead of 45 it falls to about 87 per cent. What is exciting is that 30 degrees and 60 degrees give the same range, but at 60 degrees the ball flies much higher.

In the formula the speed is **squared**. So if you throw twice as fast, the ball flies four times as far. To get 90 metres at 45 degrees, you need a release speed of 30 metres per second. On the Moon, where gravity is only about a sixth as strong, the same throw would fly about six times as far.

In the **shot put**, the shot leaves the hand at about shoulder height, that is, above the landing point. That is why the best angle there is below 45 degrees, often around 37 to 40 degrees. In the **javelin** and discus the air also plays a part, because these implements glide a little like wings. But the most important thing is always a high release speed.

The simple formula applies only without **air resistance**. In reality, the air strongly slows down light objects such as shuttlecocks or paper aeroplanes, so that they fly much shorter distances. For heavy, small bodies such as an iron ball, on the other hand, the formula fits quite well. With air resistance, the best angle is usually a little below 45 degrees.

begriffe.erklaerung: The curved flight path of a thrown object.
The angle between the ground and the direction of flight at the moment of release.
How strongly the Earth pulls things downwards, about 9.81 metres per second squared.
The braking force of the air on a moving body.

gewusst: Without air resistance, two throws at 20 and 70 degrees land equally far away, because their angles add up to 90 degrees.
Galileo Galilei was one of the first to realise that the paths of throws are parabolas.
Thanks to its dimples, a golf ball flies further than a smooth ball, because the air then slows it down less.

teile.einleitung: Long sightedness is a vision defect in which you find it hard to see things close up sharply. The eye then has to work hard, which can lead to headaches. Long sightedness can easily be corrected with glasses or contact lenses.
wichtigste: Long sighted people see things close up particularly badly.
Usually the eyeball is a little too short.
Without effort, the sharp image of a nearby object would lie behind the retina.
Lenses for long sightedness have dioptre values with a plus.
Children often do not notice slight long sightedness, because their flexible lens makes up for it.
Uncorrected long sightedness can cause headaches when reading.
The technical term for long sightedness is hyperopia.

abschnitte.text: Light enters the eye through the cornea and the **lens**. Together they focus the light like a magnifying glass. In a healthy eye, the sharp image forms exactly on the **retina** at the back of the eye. The retina turns the light into signals that travel to the brain through the optic nerve. So that we can see nearby things sharply, a small muscle makes the lens rounder.

With long sightedness the eyeball is usually a little too short, or the focusing power is too weak. The sharp image of a nearby object would then lie behind the retina without any effort. The eye has to keep curving the lens more strongly; this is called **accommodation**. In the long run this is tiring, and it leads to burning eyes or headaches, especially when reading. With strong long sightedness you also see blurred in the distance.

Many babies and small children are slightly long sighted, because their eyes are still small. As they grow, the eyeball gets longer, and the long sightedness often decreases. Children have a very flexible lens and can therefore make up for slight long sightedness themselves. That is why they often notice nothing at all. But stronger long sightedness can lead to a squint or to learning problems with reading, so eye tests at the **eye doctor** are important.

Lenses that are thicker in the middle than at the edge help with long sightedness. Such lenses are called **converging lenses**, because they focus the light even more. Their strength is given in **dioptres** and has a plus sign, for example plus 2. With short sightedness it is the other way round; there you need lenses with a minus. Contact lenses or, for adults, eye surgery can also help.

Long sightedness is not the same as **age related long sightedness**. With this, from about the age of 45 the lens becomes less flexible and can no longer curve well. That is why older people often hold newspapers far away and need reading glasses. Converging lenses with plus dioptres help here too. But the cause is different from real long sightedness.

begriffe.erklaerung: The light sensitive layer at the back of the eye on which the image forms.
The unit that shows how strongly a lens bends light.
A lens that is thicker in the middle and focuses rays of light.
The eye's ability to focus near and far by changing the shape of the lens.

gewusst: Most babies are born slightly long sighted.
With a magnifying glass made from a converging lens, you can focus sunlight so much that paper starts to smoulder.
Many long sighted people see sharply when young and notice the problem only later.

teile.einleitung: A water pump moves water from one place to another, often upwards too. Without pumps there would be no water from the tap on the top floor, no heating and no cooled car engine. More than 2000 years ago, people already invented clever devices for lifting water.
wichtigste: A water pump moves water.
The old hand pump with a long lever at a well is called a lever pump.
The Archimedes screw lifts water upwards with a turning screw.
A submersible pump is sunk completely in the water.
Most pumps today are driven by an electric motor.
In a car, a water pump pumps cooling water through the engine.
After a storm, pumps pump water out of flooded cellars.

abschnitte.text: A **pump** is a machine that sets liquids in motion. It can push water through pipes or carry it upwards. For this it needs energy, in the past from people, animals or waterwheels, today mostly from an **electric motor**. Pumps are found in washing machines, dishwashers, heating systems and wells. Your heart is a pump too, driving blood round your body.

In a **piston pump**, a piston moves back and forth in a cylinder. When it is pulled back it sucks water in, and when it is pushed forward it presses it out; valves let the water flow in one direction only. In a **centrifugal pump**, an impeller spins very fast and flings the water outwards. Centrifugal pumps are the most common today. A suction pump can suck water up only about 10 metres at most, because the air pressure cannot manage more.

The **Archimedes screw** is a very old invention and is credited to the Greek scientist Archimedes. A sloping screw inside a tube lifts water upwards step by step as it turns. It was used to water fields. Later, **lever pumps** with a long handle were built at village wells. By moving the handle up and down, people brought water up from the depths.

If there is water in the cellar after a storm, the fire brigade pumps it out with pumps. A **submersible pump** is sunk completely in the water for this. In deep wells too, submersible pumps bring up the groundwater. In an aquarium, a small pump moves the water through a filter and adds oxygen to it. The circulation pump of a heating system sends warm water through the radiators.

A car with a petrol engine has a **water pump** that pumps cooling water through the engine. This stops the engine getting too hot. In Switzerland there are also **pumped storage power stations**. They pump water into a higher reservoir when there is plenty of electricity. When electricity is needed, the water flows back down and drives turbines.

begriffe.erklaerung: A moving cylinder in a pump that sucks water in and pushes it out.
A flap that lets the water flow in one direction only.
A pump that works completely under water.
A power station that pumps water up and so stores energy.

gewusst: At rest, a human heart pumps about five litres of blood a minute.
Today Archimedes screws are also used the other way round as small hydroelectric power stations; they are considered fish friendly.

teile.einleitung: A throw is a movement in which an object is let go with momentum and then flies freely through the air. In physics, people study what path it takes. In sport there are many throwing events and ball games in which a good throw matters.
wichtigste: A thrown object flies along a curved path.
Gravity pulls it downwards throughout its flight.
With more force and momentum, a ball flies further.
When throwing, you swing your arm far back to get more momentum.
In athletics you throw the javelin, the discus and the hammer.
Thanks to its shape, a boomerang can fly back to the thrower.
In games such as basketball or boccia you have to aim precisely.

abschnitte.text: When you throw, an object gets momentum from your hand and arm. As soon as you let go, it flies on freely, and only **gravity** and air resistance act on it. Physics distinguishes the **vertical throw** upwards, the **horizontal throw** and the angled throw upwards at a slant. In a vertical throw, a ball flies straight up and falls back down. In the other throws it flies in a curve.

A ball thrown at a slant first flies upwards, gets slower and slower, reaches its highest point and then falls again. Its path is a **curve** that mathematicians call a parabola. Without air, a ball would fly furthest if you threw it at an angle of 45 degrees. How far it goes depends above all on the **release speed**. That is why you swing your arm far back: a longer path for your hand gives more momentum.

In athletics there are four throwing and putting events. In the **javelin**, you throw a long, pointed spear after a run up. In the **discus**, you spin round and hurl a flat, round disc. In the hammer throw you throw a metal ball on a wire, and in the shot put you push a heavy ball. In Switzerland there is also stone putting, for example with the famous Unspunnen stone.

Many ball games are all about throwing. In **basketball** you throw the ball into a basket hanging just over three metres high. Handball, water polo and dodgeball are other throwing games. In **boccia** you throw balls as close as possible to a small target ball. In skittles and bowling, on the other hand, you roll the ball along the ground.

A **boomerang** is a curved throwing stick that was used by the Aboriginal peoples in Australia. Its arms are shaped like little wings. If you throw it correctly, it spins fast and flies a curve that brings it back to the thrower. Not all boomerangs come back; some were made as straight flying hunting weapons. Today boomerang throwing is a sport with its own competitions.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which the Earth pulls everything downwards.
The path a thrown object takes through the air.
The angle at which an object is let go.
The braking force of the air on a moving object.

gewusst: In competitions, the men's javelin weighs 800 grams and the men's discus 2 kilograms.
The Unspunnen stone, which is put at the Unspunnen festival, weighs more than 80 kilograms.
A good boomerang thrower can catch their boomerang again after a long flight.

teile.einleitung: An inflatable beach ball is a popular toy at the swimming pool and by the lake. With it you can watch beautifully how buoyancy works in water. But the German word “Wasserball” also means an exciting team sport played in a swimming pool, which in English is called water polo.
wichtigste: An inflated beach ball floats on top and sinks in only a little way.
It is filled with air and is therefore much lighter than the water it could push aside.
If you push it under water, it is pushed strongly upwards.
If you let go of it under water, it leaps out of the water.
On a lake, the wind easily blows a beach ball away.
A beach ball is not a life saving aid.
Water polo is also a sport in which two teams throw goals in a pool.

abschnitte.text: A **beach ball** for playing with is usually made of thin, colourful plastic. You blow it up with your mouth or with a pump. Almost its whole volume is air, so it is very light. If you let the air out, it goes floppy and can be folded up small. That way it fits in any swimming bag.

Every body in water feels **buoyancy**. It is as big as the weight of the water that the body pushes aside; the Greek **Archimedes** already realised this. A beach ball weighs very little, so it only has to push aside a tiny amount of water to float. That is why it sinks in only a little way. A stone, on the other hand, is heavier than the water it pushes aside and sinks.

If you want to push a big beach ball under water, you need a lot of strength. Under water it pushes aside a great deal of water and is pushed upwards just as strongly. A ball 50 centimetres across displaces about 65 litres, which corresponds to a force like the weight of 65 kilograms. If you let go, it shoots upwards and leaps out of the water. The force of buoyancy turns into movement.

Because a beach ball is so light and sticks up high out of the water, even a gentle **wind** can push it away. On a lake it can quickly be a long way out. You should not swim far out after it, because the ball is not a **life saving aid**. It can roll away or burst and does not carry a person safely. It is better to let the ball go or to get help.

**Water polo** is a team sport played in a swimming pool. Two teams of seven players each, including a goalkeeper, try to throw the ball into the other team's goal. The water is so deep that nobody can stand, so the players have to swim and tread water all the time. Usually you may hold the ball with one hand only. Water polo has been part of the Olympic Games since 1900 and is one of the oldest Olympic team sports.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which water pushes a body upwards.
A body pushes water aside and takes its place.
A Greek scientist who discovered the law of buoyancy.
A swimming movement that keeps you in one place above the water.

gewusst: During a match, water polo players may not support themselves on the bottom or on the edge of the pool.
A beach ball also floats in the salty sea, where it sinks in even a little less.

teile.einleitung: The Venturi effect describes what happens in a narrowing of a pipe: the liquid or gas flows faster there, and the static pressure falls. This low pressure can suck in air, petrol or perfume. The effect is named after the Italian physicist Giovanni Battista Venturi.
wichtigste: In a narrowing of a pipe a fluid flows faster and the static pressure falls.
The effect is named after Giovanni Battista Venturi.
It follows from the continuity equation and the Bernoulli equation.
A Venturi tube is used mainly to measure flow rate.
Carburettors, Bunsen burners, water jet pumps and perfume atomisers use the effect.
If you blow between two hanging sheets of paper, they move towards each other.

abschnitte.text: When water or air flows through a pipe with a narrow point, the same amount has to get through less space. That is why the flow becomes faster at the narrow point. At the same time the **static pressure** there falls, that is, the pressure on the wall of the pipe. The Italian physicist **Giovanni Battista Venturi** studied this more closely around 1800.

The **continuity equation** says: if the cross-section is four times smaller, the water flows four times faster. The **Bernoulli equation**, named after Daniel Bernoulli from Basel, shows that higher speed means less pressure. If water flows into the inlet at 2 m/s, it is 8 m/s in the narrow point that is four times smaller. The difference in pressure is then ½ · 1000 kg/m³ · (64 minus 4) m²/s², that is 30 kPa.

A **Venturi tube** first narrows and then slowly widens again. If you measure the pressure before and in the narrow point, you can work out how much flows through the tube. That is why in technology it is used mainly to measure flow rate. Behind the narrow point it widens only gradually, so that the flow does not break away and the pressure is recovered.

In the **carburettor** of older petrol engines the low pressure sucked in petrol and mixed it with air. In a Bunsen burner the jet of gas produces low pressure and sucks in air through openings at the side. The water jet pump in the laboratory uses running tap water to produce low pressure, for example for suction. In a perfume atomiser fast air flows over a small tube and draws the liquid up.

Hold two sheets of paper parallel next to each other, a few centimetres apart, and blow hard between them. Instead of flying apart, they move towards each other. The fast air between the sheets has a lower pressure than the still air outside. In a similar way a shower curtain is sometimes pulled inwards while you shower.

begriffe.erklaerung: The pressure that a flow exerts sideways on the walls.
A general term for liquids and gases that can flow.
The amount of liquid or gas that flows through a pipe per second.
A part of older engines that mixes petrol and air.

gewusst: In narrow gaps between tower blocks or in mountain valleys the wind also whistles especially strongly because of the Venturi effect.
Daniel Bernoulli, whose equation explains the effect, came from a famous family of scholars in Basel.
When two ships sail close alongside each other, they can be pulled towards each other by the low pressure between them.

teile.einleitung: A sonic boom is a loud bang that happens when an aeroplane or another object flies faster than sound. The sound waves can then no longer run away ahead of the object and pile up into a shock wave. The crack of a whip is also a small sonic boom.
wichtigste: A sonic boom happens when an object flies faster than sound.
It is produced not only when breaking the sound barrier, but throughout the whole supersonic flight.
The Mach number shows how many times faster than sound something is flying.
An aeroplane flying at 1029 m/s with a speed of sound of 343 m/s is flying at Mach 3.
At Mach 2 the half-angle of the Mach cone is 30°.
Often you hear a double bang, because the bow and tail shocks form an N-wave.
The tip of a cracking whip is faster than sound.
In 1947 Chuck Yeager became the first person proven to fly faster than sound.

abschnitte.text: A flying aeroplane pushes the air in front of it away and produces sound waves, which spread out at the **speed of sound**. In air at 20 °C this is about 343 metres per second, roughly 1235 km/h. If the aeroplane flies more slowly, the waves run ahead of it. If it flies faster, they can no longer get ahead of it and overlap to form a strong **shock wave**, which we hear as a bang.

The **Mach number** is named after the Austrian physicist Ernst Mach. It says how many times faster than sound something is flying: 1029 m/s divided by 343 m/s gives Mach 3. Behind the aeroplane the shock wave forms a cone, the **Mach cone**. The faster the aeroplane, the more pointed the cone; at Mach 2 its half-angle is 30°.

Many people think the bang only happens once, when the sound barrier is broken. In reality the aeroplane drags the cone along with it throughout the whole supersonic flight. Wherever the cone touches the ground, you hear the bang, like a carpet unrolling under the aeroplane. Because one shock forms at the front at the nose and one at the back at the tail, they form an **N-wave**, which is often heard as a double bang.

On 14 October 1947 the American **Chuck Yeager** became the first person proven to fly faster than sound, in the rocket plane Bell X-1. From 1976 to 2003 **Concorde** carried passengers across the Atlantic at about Mach 2. From Paris or London to New York it needed only about three and a half hours. Because of the noise it was not allowed to fly at supersonic speed over populated land.

abschnitte.titel: A bang on a small scale
abschnitte.text: A **whip** also cracks, because its thin tip becomes faster than sound when it is swung. In Switzerland this is known from Geisslechlöpfe, an old custom of whip cracking in country areas. Bullets also often fly at supersonic speed and make a bang. Thunder in a thunderstorm, on the other hand, is created differently, namely by the suddenly heated air of a lightning bolt.

begriffe.erklaerung: How fast sound travels; in air about 343 m/s.
The ratio of speed to the speed of sound.
A sudden, strong pressure wave.
The limit at which an object becomes as fast as sound.
A pressure wave with two shocks that looks like the letter N.

gewusst: The whip was probably the first human-made thing that was faster than sound.
You only hear the sonic boom after the aeroplane has already flown over you.
In flight Concorde got so hot from friction that it became several centimetres longer.

teile.einleitung: Kilo, mega, milli and nano: prefixes like these stand in front of many units. They tell you by which power of ten a unit is multiplied. In this way very large and very small values can be written briefly and clearly.
wichtigste: Prefixes are syllables in front of units such as metre, gram or watt.
Kilo means a thousand, mega a million, giga 10 to the power of 9.
Milli means a thousandth, micro a millionth, femto 10 to the power of minus 15.
One micrometre is 1000 nanometres.
Capital and small letters matter: Mm is a megametre, mm a millimetre.
In 2022 the new prefixes ronna and quetta were introduced for huge numbers.
For computer memory there are binary prefixes such as kibi, which means exactly 1024.

abschnitte.text: With **prefixes** you do not have to write long numbers with lots of zeros. Instead of 3500 metres you say 3.5 kilometres. Each prefix stands for a **power of ten**, that is, a number such as 10, 100 or 1000. The prefixes are part of the International System of Units, the SI. They work with almost all units, such as metre, gram, litre, watt or volt.

Kilo, with the symbol k, stands for a thousand. Mega, with the symbol M, means a million, and **giga**, with G, a billion, that is 10 to the power of 9. Then come tera, peta, exa, zetta and yotta. In 2022 **ronna** for 10 to the power of 27 and **quetta** for 10 to the power of 30 were added. With them you can, for example, give the mass of the Earth in ronnagrams.

For small values there are deci, centi and **milli**, a thousandth. Micro, with the Greek letter µ, means a millionth. After that come nano, pico, **femto** with 10 to the power of minus 15, and atto. So a micrometre is 1000 nanometres, and a hair is about 50 to 100 micrometres thick. 47 picofarads is 4.7 times 10 to the power of minus 11 farads; electronic components are often this small.

You have to be careful with the symbols. **Mm** stands for megametre, that is a thousand kilometres, and **mm** for millimetre. So a capital M is a billion times more than a small m. Most prefixes for large numbers are written with a capital letter, but kilo is written with a small k. When converting, it helps to count the powers of ten: 3.5 kilometres is 3.5 times 10 to the power of 6 millimetres.

Computers calculate in the **binary system**. That is why memory sizes are often powers of 2. For exactly 1024, that is 2 to the power of 10, there is the binary prefix **kibi** with the symbol Ki. In the same way there are mebi and gibi for 2 to the power of 20 and 2 to the power of 30. Anyone who mixes up kilobytes and kibibytes is sometimes surprised that a memory seems smaller than it says on the packet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number such as 10, 100 or 1000, written as 10 to the power of a number.
The International System of Units, with units such as the metre, the kilogram and the second.
A syllable in front of a unit that gives a factor.
Calculating with only two digits, namely 0 and 1.

gewusst: The kilogram is the only SI base unit that already has a prefix in its name.
The prefixes ronna and quetta were introduced partly because the amount of data in the world is growing so fast.

teile.einleitung: The watt is the unit of power. It tells you how much energy a device or a power station converts each second. It is named after the Scottish inventor James Watt, who improved the steam engine.
wichtigste: One watt equals one joule per second.
The unit is named after James Watt.
A kilowatt is 1000 watts, a megawatt a million watts.
0.75 kilowatts is 750 watts, and 2.4 kilowatts is 2400 watts.
The label “2000 W” on a kettle is its electrical power.
An LED lamp typically has a much lower power than a hairdryer or a kettle.
The watt measures power, whereas the kilowatt hour measures the energy used.

abschnitte.text: The **watt**, with the symbol W, is the unit of **power**. Power means how much energy is converted in a certain time. One watt equals one **joule** per second. For electrical devices: power equals voltage times current. So a device on 230 volts with 1 ampere flowing through it has 230 watts.

**James Watt** lived from 1736 to 1819 and came from Scotland. He greatly improved the steam engine so that it needed much less coal. His engines powered factories and helped to drive industrialisation forward. To describe the power of his engines, he compared them with horses and so coined the term **horsepower**. Later the new unit of power was named after him.

A **kilowatt** is 1000 watts, and a megawatt is 1000 kilowatts or a million watts. So a hairdryer with 2.4 kilowatts has 2400 watts, and 0.75 kilowatts is 750 watts. One metric horsepower is about 735 watts. Large power stations are given in megawatts. The Gösgen nuclear power station has an electrical output of about 1000 megawatts.

Every electrical appliance says how many watts it needs. A kettle marked “2000 W” has an electrical power of 2000 watts, which is why it heats water very quickly. An **LED lamp** often needs only 5 to 10 watts, while an old light bulb of the same brightness needs about ten times as much. A laptop needs roughly 30 to 60 watts. A person cycling over a longer time produces about 100 to 200 watts.

Watts and **kilowatt hours** are often mixed up. Watts tell you how strongly a device is converting energy right now. The kilowatt hour measures how much energy has been used in total. If a device with 1000 watts runs for one hour, it uses one kilowatt hour. That is why on the electricity bill you pay for kilowatt hours and not for watts.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much energy is converted each second.
The unit of energy.
The energy that a device with 1000 watts uses in one hour.
An old unit of power, about 735 watts.

gewusst: A professional racing cyclist can produce well over 1000 watts in a short sprint.
At rest, your body gives off roughly as much heat as an old 100 watt light bulb.

teile.einleitung: The Wheatstone bridge is an electrical circuit with which an unknown resistance can be determined very precisely. It consists of four resistors connected like a square, with a meter in the middle. To this day it is found in many sensors, for example in electronic scales.
wichtigste: The bridge consists of two voltage dividers connected between their midpoints by a bridge branch.
It is balanced when no current flows in the bridge branch.
When balanced, R₁/R₂ = R₃/Rₓ, from which the unknown resistance is calculated.
The result then does not depend on the supply voltage.
Samuel Hunter Christie was the first to describe the circuit, in 1833.
Charles Wheatstone made it well known from 1843, which is why it bears his name.
Today it is used above all to read strain gauges and other sensors.

abschnitte.text: The bridge consists of four **resistors** R₁, R₂, R₃ and Rₓ connected to form a square. A voltage, the **supply voltage**, is applied to two opposite corners. Between the other two corners lies the **bridge branch** with a sensitive ammeter. You can think of the circuit as two voltage dividers side by side. The ammeter compares whether the voltage in the middle of both dividers is the same.

You change one of the known resistors until the meter shows zero. Then the bridge is **balanced**, and R₁/R₂ = R₃/Rₓ. Example: with R₁ = 100 Ω, R₂ = 200 Ω and R₃ = 150 Ω, you get Rₓ = 300 Ω. With R₁ = 470 Ω, R₂ = 1000 Ω and R₃ = 2350 Ω, you get Rₓ = 5000 Ω. Because you only balance to zero, the size of the supply voltage does not matter, which makes the method very precise.

At school a **slide wire bridge** is often used. Instead of two resistors there is an even wire, usually 1 m long, along which a contact is moved. The two pieces of wire l₁ and l₂ behave like two resistors. If the comparison resistor is 30 Ω and the balance point is at l₁ = 40 cm, then l₂ = 60 cm and Rₓ = 20 Ω. In this way you can measure resistances with a ruler.

The British mathematician **Samuel Hunter Christie** described the circuit in 1833. But it became well known only through the English physicist **Charles Wheatstone**, who presented it in 1843 and mentioned Christie in doing so. Wheatstone was a many sided inventor; he also worked on the electric telegraph. The bridge quickly became a standard instrument in laboratories, for example for testing telegraph cables.

Today, bridge circuits are often used to measure tiny changes in the resistance of **sensors**. A **strain gauge** changes its resistance a tiny bit when it is stretched. In electronic scales, force meters and pressure sensors it sits in a bridge. An example: at 10 V with three resistors of 1000 Ω and a sensor of 1100 Ω, the diagonal of the bridge shows about 0.24 V. This small voltage is amplified and evaluated electronically.

begriffe.erklaerung: A quantity that shows how strongly a component slows down electric current, measured in ohms (Ω).
The connection in the middle of the bridge in which the meter sits.
The state in which no current flows in the bridge branch.
A thin sensor whose resistance changes when it is stretched or squashed.

gewusst: Although it is called the Wheatstone bridge, Charles Wheatstone did not invent it but made it well known.
Charles Wheatstone also invented the concertina, a small instrument like an accordion.
Many bathroom scales contain strain gauges in a bridge circuit.

teile.einleitung: The greenhouse effect describes how certain gases in the atmosphere keep heat on the Earth, similar to the glass of a greenhouse. Without this natural effect the Earth would be an icy planet. But because people are releasing more and more of these gases, the Earth is getting warmer.
wichtigste: In the greenhouse effect gases in the atmosphere keep heat on the Earth.
Important greenhouse gases are water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane.
Without the natural greenhouse effect the average temperature would be about minus 18 °C instead of about plus 15 °C.
By burning coal, oil and natural gas, people are strengthening the greenhouse effect.
The strengthened greenhouse effect is the main cause of today's climate change.
In Switzerland it has become much warmer since measurements began than the world average.
The Paris climate agreement of 2015 aims to limit warming.

abschnitte.text: The Sun sends light to the Earth, which warms the ground and the seas. The warm Earth gives off the energy again as invisible **heat radiation**. **Greenhouse gases** in the air swallow part of this radiation and send some of it back to the Earth. In this way more heat stays in the lower atmosphere, as in a greenhouse with a glass roof.

The most important natural greenhouse gas is **water vapour**. Then there are carbon dioxide, CO2 for short, methane and nitrous oxide. CO2 is produced mainly by burning coal, oil and natural gas. Methane comes, among other things, from cows' stomachs, rice fields and rubbish tips.

Without the natural greenhouse effect the Earth would be about minus 18 °C on average. Thanks to it, the average temperature is a pleasant plus 15 °C or so. Only this makes liquid water, and so life as we know it, possible all over the Earth. So the greenhouse effect in itself is not a bad thing.

Since **industrialisation** in the 19th century, people have been burning large amounts of fossil fuels. As a result the CO2 content of the air has risen sharply, partly also because many forests have been cut down. The greenhouse effect is strengthened, and it is getting warmer all over the world. Experts call this **human-made climate change**.

Since measurements began around 1864, Switzerland has warmed about twice as much as the world average. The **glaciers** are melting, for example the Great Aletsch Glacier, which gets shorter every year. There are more hot days, less snow at low altitudes and more frequent heavy rain. Permafrost in the mountains is also thawing, which can make rock falls more likely.

In the **Paris climate agreement** of 2015 almost all countries committed themselves to keeping warming well below 2 °C. Switzerland wants to release no more greenhouse gases overall by 2050; this is called net zero. Renewable energies such as hydro, solar and wind power are to replace oil and gas. Everyone can help, for example by using the bike and public transport instead of the car or by wasting less energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The layer of air that surrounds the Earth.
A gas that holds back heat radiation, for example CO2 or methane.
Coal, oil and natural gas, which formed from ancient plants and animals.
The long-term change in the climate, today mainly warming.
No more greenhouse gas is released than is removed from the air again.

gewusst: As early as 1896 the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius calculated that more CO2 would warm the Earth.
On Venus there is an extreme greenhouse effect, and it is over 400 °C hot there.
The air bubbles in the ice of Antarctica tell scientists how much CO2 the air contained hundreds of thousands of years ago.

teile.einleitung: When a liquid evaporates, its surroundings get cooler. This effect is called evaporative cooling. You can feel it when you come out of the swimming pool wet and shiver in the wind.
wichtigste: A liquid needs energy to evaporate.
It takes this energy as heat from its surroundings.
People sweat because the evaporating water cools the skin.
In humid, muggy air sweat evaporates less well and cools less.
Alcohol evaporates especially quickly and therefore feels cold.
A fridge uses a refrigerant that vaporises and takes heat away as it does so.
A psychrometer measures humidity with a dry and a wet thermometer.

abschnitte.text: A liquid consists of tiny particles that are always moving. The fastest particles can escape from the surface and turn into vapour; this is **evaporation**. The slower particles are left behind, and slower particles mean a lower **temperature**. The liquid takes the missing energy as **heat** from its surroundings, for example from your skin.

When you are hot, **sweat glands** make water on your skin. As it evaporates, the sweat takes heat from the body and cools it. This works very well in dry air. In humid, muggy air, however, the air is already almost full of water vapour, so the sweat evaporates badly and you feel sticky and hot.

Disinfectant with **alcohol** feels cold on the skin because alcohol evaporates very quickly. Wet clothes in the wind make you feel cold. Water in an unglazed **clay jug** stays cool because it slowly seeps through the wall and evaporates on the outside. Dogs also cool themselves by panting, because water evaporates on their tongue.

In a **fridge** a refrigerant flows through pipes inside and vaporises there. As it does so, it takes in heat from the inside. At the back of the appliance it gives this heat off again, which is why the back is warm. Air conditioners and heat pumps also work on this principle.

A **psychrometer** has two thermometers, one of which is wrapped in a wet cloth. Water evaporates at the wet thermometer, and it shows a lower temperature. The drier the air, the bigger the difference between the two. From this you can work out the **humidity**.

begriffe.erklaerung: When a liquid turns into vapour below its boiling point.
How much water vapour there is in the air.
A liquid in a fridge that vaporises easily and so cools.
A device for measuring humidity with two thermometers.

gewusst: In hot countries people have cooled their water in porous clay jugs for thousands of years.
If you hold a wet finger up in the air, the cold side tells you where the wind is coming from.
On a hot day a person can sweat out several litres of water.

teile.einleitung: Volume tells you how much space a body takes up or how much fits into a container. Whether a milk carton, a swimming pool or a balloon: everything has a volume. It is measured, for example, in litres or in cubic metres.
wichtigste: Volume is the amount of space a body takes up.
The base unit of volume in the International System of Units is the cubic metre.
One litre is 1000 cubic centimetres.
One millilitre is exactly one cubic centimetre.
A cube with edges 3 centimetres long has a volume of 27 cubic centimetres.
Liquids are measured with a measuring jug or a measuring cylinder.
The water level is read at eye level at the lowest point of the curved surface.

abschnitte.text: **Volume** says how much space an object needs. A surface only has length and width; a body also has height. That is why volume has three dimensions. A big balloon has more volume than a small one, even if it is lighter than a stone. So volume and weight are two different things.

The base unit is the **cubic metre**, that is, a cube one metre long, wide and high. Smaller units are the cubic decimetre and the cubic centimetre. A cubic decimetre is exactly one **litre**, and a litre is 1000 cubic centimetres. A millilitre is one cubic centimetre, about the size of a dice. 1000 litres fit into a cubic metre.

For a **cuboid** you multiply length times width times height. In a cube all the edges are the same length, so you multiply edge times edge times edge. A cube with edges of 3 centimetres therefore has 3 times 3 times 3, that is 27 cubic centimetres. For cylinders, spheres and cones there are separate formulas. It is important that all the lengths are given in the same unit.

In the kitchen liquids are measured with a measuring jug and in the laboratory with a **measuring cylinder**. At the edge, water forms a surface that curves slightly downwards, called the **meniscus**. You read the value at eye level at the lowest point of this curve. You find the volume of an irregular stone by putting it into water and measuring how much the water level rises. This principle of displacement is often linked with the Greek scientist Archimedes.

A milk carton usually holds one litre, a drinking bottle often half a litre. A full bath holds about 150 litres of water. When buying a house or heating it, people talk about cubic metres of enclosed space. The size of reservoirs in the Swiss Alps is given in millions of cubic metres. The engine capacity of a motor is also a volume and is measured in cubic centimetres.

begriffe.erklaerung: The volume of a cube with edges one metre long.
A unit of volume for liquids, the same as a cubic decimetre.
A narrow glass with a scale for measuring liquids exactly.
The curved surface of a liquid in a narrow container.

gewusst: Water expands when it freezes, which is why ice has a bigger volume than the same water.
A cubic metre of water weighs about a tonne, as much as a small car.
Exactly one litre fits into a cube with edges of 10 centimetres.

teile.einleitung: In a race, several competitors want to be the first to reach the finish. Whether in the playground, on sports day or at the Olympic Games: only the one who covers the course in the shortest time can win. There is physics behind every race too, because it is about distance, time and speed.
wichtigste: A race is won by whoever reaches the finish first.
A well known starting call is: On your marks, get set, go!
Anyone who runs off before the starting signal makes a false start.
The finishing line marks the end of the course.
In a relay race the runners pass on a baton; in a hurdles race they jump over obstacles.
Fun races include the sack race and the egg and spoon race.
Speed is calculated as distance divided by time.

abschnitte.text: Every race has a start and a **finishing line**. At the start someone calls “On your marks, get set, go!”, or a starting pistol goes bang. If someone runs off before the signal, that is a **false start**. In athletics today you are disqualified after just one false start.

The winner needed the least time for the same distance and was therefore the fastest on average. **Speed** is calculated by dividing the distance by the time. In Berlin in 2009, Usain Bolt ran the 100 metres in 9.58 seconds, which is more than 10 metres per second on average. At the beginning, all runners first have to **accelerate**, which is why the start is so important.

In a **relay race**, several runners run one after the other and pass on a baton. In a **hurdles race** you jump over obstacles that look like small fences. There are short sprints, long runs such as the marathon over just over 42 kilometres, and races on bikes, skis, in cars or boats. In Switzerland, ski races such as the Lauberhorn downhill in Wengen are particularly well known.

Not every race is serious. In the **sack race**, children stand in a sack and hop to see who is fastest. In the egg and spoon race you carry an egg on a spoon and must not drop it. In the three legged race, two children are tied together by one leg and have to run in step.

In the fairy tale “The Hare and the Hedgehog”, written down by the Brothers Grimm, the hedgehog challenges the proud hare to a race. The hedgehog is clever: at the other end of the field his **wife** is waiting, and she looks exactly the same. Every time the hare arrives, she calls out “I'm already here!”. The hare runs back and forth again and again until he gives up exhausted.

At big competitions, electronic clocks measure to the hundredth of a second. A **photo finish** taken with a special camera shows who crossed the finishing line first with their upper body. Swiss watch companies have been involved in timing at the Olympic Games for decades. Light barriers and chips on shoes also help to record times precisely.

begriffe.erklaerung: When someone runs off before the starting signal.
A race in which several runners take turns and hand over a baton.
A special photo that shows who reached the finish first.
To get faster.

gewusst: In a photo finish, what counts is not the tip of the nose or the foot but the upper body.
Starting shots in athletics today often come from electronic pistols, whose signal can be heard through loudspeakers behind each runner.
The hedgehog in the fairy tale wins not by speed but by a trick.

teile.einleitung: Thermal conductivity tells you how well a substance passes on heat. Metals conduct heat very well, whereas wood, plastic and air conduct it poorly. That is why a metal handle feels colder than a wooden one, even though both are equally warm.
wichtigste: Thermal conductivity describes how fast heat travels through a substance.
Metals such as copper, silver and aluminium are very good conductors of heat.
Wood, plastic, wool and air are poor conductors of heat.
Metal feels cold because it carries heat away from the hand faster.
Poor conductors of heat are used for insulation.
Good conductors of heat are used for pans and heat sinks.
The unit is watts per metre and kelvin.

abschnitte.text: Heat can travel through a substance by the particles passing on their movement to their neighbours. **Thermal conductivity** says how well this works for a particular substance. The higher it is, the faster the temperature evens out. It is measured in watts per metre and kelvin.

**Metals** are the best conductors of heat, because they have free-moving electrons that carry energy quickly. Silver and copper conduct heat especially well, and so does aluminium. That is why good pans often have a base made of copper or aluminium. A diamond conducts heat even better than copper, although it is not a metal.

Wood, cork, plastic, wool and above all **air** conduct heat poorly. Materials with lots of small air bubbles are therefore good **insulators**, for example polystyrene, glass wool or down. Snow also insulates well, which is why an igloo is much warmer inside than the air outside. A vacuum conducts heat hardly at all.

If you touch a metal railing and a wooden bench on a cool morning, the metal feels much colder. Yet both have the same temperature. But the metal carries the heat away from your hand much faster than the wood. So our skin does not feel the **temperature**, but how fast it is losing heat.

Houses in Switzerland are insulated with **insulating materials** so that little heating is lost in winter. Double and triple glazed windows have a layer of air or noble gas between the panes. In computers, heat sinks made of aluminium or copper make sure the processor does not overheat. Pan handles made of plastic or wood protect hands from burns.

Many animals use poor conductors of heat to keep warm. Polar bears have thick fur and a thick **layer of fat**. Birds fluff up their feathers so that more air is trapped in them. The marmot also survives the Alpine winter in a burrow lined with hay.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that passes on heat well, for example copper.
A substance that passes on heat poorly, for example polystyrene.
A material built into walls and roofs to keep heat in.
A metal part with fins that carries heat away from electronic components.

gewusst: Copper conducts heat more than 10,000 times better than air.
With bare feet, tiles feel colder than a carpet, even though both are equally warm.
An igloo can be warmer than zero degrees inside while it is bitterly cold outside.

teile.einleitung: The Very Large Telescope, VLT for short, is one of the most powerful observatories in the world. It stands on the mountain Cerro Paranal in the Atacama Desert in Chile. With its four huge telescopes, scientists look deep into space, as far as distant galaxies and black holes.
wichtigste: The VLT is run by the European Southern Observatory, ESO.
It stands on Cerro Paranal in Chile, at a height of about 2600 metres.
It consists of four large main telescopes, each with a mirror 8.2 metres across.
The four telescopes have names from the Mapudungun language: Antu, Kueyen, Melipal and Yepun.
In the VLT Interferometer the light of several telescopes is combined to see the finest details.
Observations at the VLT contributed to the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for Reinhard Genzel.
Nearby, ESO is building the Extremely Large Telescope with a mirror of about 39 metres.
Switzerland is a member of ESO and uses the VLT for its research.

abschnitte.text: The **Very Large Telescope** really lives up to its name. It consists of four main telescopes of the same size and four smaller, movable auxiliary telescopes. Each main telescope has a **primary mirror** 8.2 metres in diameter, which is about as wide as a classroom. The mirror is only about 18 centimetres thick and is constantly pushed into the right shape by many small pistons. The first main telescope saw its first light in 1998.

The VLT stands on **Cerro Paranal** in the **Atacama Desert** in the north of Chile. This desert is one of the driest places on Earth. Almost every night the sky there is clear, and there is hardly any light from towns. In the southern hemisphere you can also see the centre of the Milky Way especially well. The scientists live in a residence that is partly underground.

The names of the four main telescopes come from **Mapudungun**, the language of the Mapuche people in Chile. Antu means Sun and Kueyen means Moon. The telescopes can work on their own or together as the **VLT Interferometer**. For this, their light is brought together through tunnels.
