In this way they reach a sharpness as if they had a mirror more than 100 metres across.

At the VLT a team led by **Reinhard Genzel** observed stars near the centre of the Milky Way for many years. There the stars race around an invisible, very heavy body. This shows that a **supermassive black hole** sits there, about four million times as heavy as the Sun. For this, Genzel received a share of the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2020. In 2004 the VLT also took the first photo of a planet orbiting another star.

The **European Southern Observatory**, ESO, is an organisation of many European countries; its headquarters are in Garching near Munich. Switzerland has been a member since 1982, and Swiss universities build measuring instruments for the telescopes. On the nearby mountain Cerro Armazones the **Extremely Large Telescope** is being built. Its primary mirror is to measure about 39 metres and consist of almost 800 separate segments. It will be the largest telescope for visible light in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that collects light from distant objects so that you can see them better.
The large curved mirror in a telescope that catches the light.
Several telescopes are linked together so that they give sharper images.
A place in space whose gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.

gewusst: Parts of the James Bond film “Quantum of Solace” were filmed in the residence of the Paranal Observatory.
At the VLT scientists sometimes shoot laser beams into the sky to create artificial guide stars for sharp images.

teile.einleitung: The electric eel is a fish from South America that can produce strong electric shocks. With its bursts of electricity it stuns prey and fights off enemies. For physics it is fascinating, because its body works like a living battery.
wichtigste: The electric eel lives in fresh water in South America, mainly in the Amazon and Orinoco regions.
It can grow more than 2 metres long.
Despite its name, it is not an eel but a knifefish.
It uses its electric shocks for hunting and for defence.
An electric shock can have more volts than a mains socket.
With weak electrical signals it finds its way in murky water.
It comes up to the surface of the water to breathe air.

abschnitte.text: The electric eel has a long, round body without a dorsal fin and is usually dark grey to brownish. It grows more than 2 metres long and can weigh around 20 kilograms. It swims with a long **anal fin** on its underside that moves in waves, which lets it swim forwards and backwards. About four fifths of its body consists of **electric organs**; its vital organs are right at the front.

The electric eel lives in rivers, streams and swamps in northern South America, especially in the basins of the **Amazon** and the Orinoco. The water there is often murky, warm and low in oxygen. That is why the electric eel breathes air: it regularly comes to the surface and gulps air, taking in most of its oxygen through its mouth in this way. If it stays under water too long, it can even suffocate.

The electric organs consist of thousands of flat cells, the **electrocytes**. Each cell produces only a small voltage of about 0.15 volts. But because thousands are connected one after the other like batteries, the voltages add up. In this way a shock reaches several hundred volts; in a species described in 2019, about 860 volts were even measured, almost four times as much as a Swiss mains socket at 230 volts.

The electric eel eats mainly fish; young animals also hunt crayfish and insects. With strong bursts of electricity it paralyses its prey for a moment and then sucks it in. In addition, it constantly sends out **weak electrical signals** and senses how objects and animals change the electric field around it. In this way it finds its way even in complete darkness and in muddy water.

In 1800, the scientist **Alexander von Humboldt** watched electric eels attacking horses with electric shocks in Venezuela and described this in detail. Even before that, electric fish had inspired researchers such as Alessandro Volta, who built the first battery around 1800. Today experts study electrocytes in order to develop new, soft batteries for medical devices. Since 2019, three species of electric eel have been distinguished instead of just one.

For people a shock is very painful and can become dangerous, for example if it makes you fall in the water. But the electric eel attacks mainly when it feels threatened. In some large zoos and aquariums you can watch electric eels; sometimes a meter there shows its bursts of electricity. In the wild it is not currently considered seriously endangered.

begriffe.erklaerung: A special cell in the electric eel that produces electric voltage.
The unit of electric voltage.
A group of South American fish with a long anal fin, to which the electric eel belongs.
An invisible area around an electric charge in which forces act.

gewusst: The electric eel can leap out of the water to hit an attacker directly with its electric shock.
With short bursts of electricity, an electric eel can make hidden prey fish twitch and so track them down.
Its German name “Zitteraal”, trembling eel, comes from the trembling that its electric shocks cause in other animals.

teile.einleitung: A water rocket is a home made rocket made from a PET bottle that flies using water and air pressure. It shows in an exciting way how real rockets work. If it is well built, it flies many metres high.
wichtigste: A water rocket is usually made from a PET bottle.
You fill it about one third full with water.
When you pump, high air pressure builds up in the bottle.
At launch the water squirts downwards and the rocket flies upwards.
Cardboard fins make sure it flies straight.
You launch it outdoors in an open field.
At launch you keep your distance, because it shoots off suddenly and fast.

abschnitte.text: A water rocket usually consists of a **PET bottle** standing upside down on a launch pad. It is partly filled with water and pumped up with an air pump. As soon as the stopper opens, the water shoots out and the bottle takes off. With a bicycle pump and some craft materials you can easily build one yourself.

The water rocket works by the **principle of recoil**. When water is pushed downwards with great force, the bottle is pushed upwards with an equally great force. Isaac Newton described this rule as his third **law of motion**: every force has an opposing force. Real rockets work in exactly the same way, except that they push out hot gases instead of water.

When you pump, the air in the bottle is squeezed together, which raises the **air pressure**. The compressed air wants to expand and pushes the water out powerfully. About one third water has proved to be a good filling. With too little water there is hardly any thrust; with too much water there is too little room for the compressed air.

So that the rocket does not wobble, you stick cardboard **fins** onto the bottom. A nose cone made of cardboard or half a bottle makes it more streamlined. A little weight in the nose helps it fly steadily. In schools and competitions, rockets are even fitted with parachutes.

Water rockets are launched only outdoors in an open **field**, far away from roads, windows and people. You pump only up to the pressure the bottle can stand, and you use only undamaged bottles. At launch everyone keeps their distance, because the rocket shoots off suddenly. You never look straight down over the rocket, and you still get wet now and then.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force produced when something is pushed out backwards.
How hard the air presses on a surface.
The stand on which the rocket rests before launch.
A steering surface that keeps the rocket steady in flight.

gewusst: Well built water rockets made of several bottles can fly more than 100 metres high.
After landing, you can simply refill the same rocket and launch it again.
Squid also use the principle of recoil by pushing water out powerfully.

teile.einleitung: Heat is a form of energy that flows from a warmer body to a colder one. We feel it in the sun, by the stove or in a hot cup of tea. Heat makes chocolate melt, water boil and keeps us alive.
wichtigste: Heat is energy that flows from the warmer to the colder.
How warm something is, is measured with a thermometer.
Metal conducts heat very well, which is why a metal spoon in hot tea quickly gets warm.
Wool holds in body heat, which is why people wear a woolly jumper in winter.
If you rub your hands together quickly, friction produces heat.
Black surfaces get hottest in the sun.
Heat makes substances melt, like chocolate in the hot sun.

abschnitte.text: Heat is a form of **energy**. By itself it always flows from the warmer body to the colder one, never the other way round. If you hold a cold hand against a warm cup, heat moves from the cup into your hand. The amount of heat is measured in the unit **joule**, and in the past also in calories.

Heat and temperature are not the same thing. **Temperature** shows how warm something is and is measured with a thermometer. Heat is the amount of energy that is transferred. A full bath at 40 °C contains much more heat than a cup of tea at 80 °C, even though the tea is hotter.

Heat can travel by **conduction**, for example through a metal spoon that quickly gets warm in hot tea. Metals are good conductors of heat, wood and plastic are poor ones. In water and air heat is spread by currents; warm air rises above the radiator, for example. The Sun warms us by **radiation**, which even travels through empty space.

A woolly jumper keeps you warm because a lot of **air** is trapped between the fibres. Air conducts heat poorly and so holds in body heat. Down jackets, double glazing and house insulation also work on this principle. Animals such as marmots or ptarmigans protect themselves from the cold in the Alps with thick fur or feathers.

Heat is produced in many ways. When you **rub** your hands, kinetic energy turns into heat. When wood or gas is burned, chemical energy is released. Dark surfaces absorb a lot of sunlight and turn it into heat, which is why a black T-shirt gets much hotter in the sun than a white one.

Heat can change substances. Chocolate **melts** in the hot sun, because it already goes soft at about 30 to 35 °C. Water evaporates when it boils, and most substances expand when heated. Our body needs heat to live and keeps itself at about 37 °C.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ability to move something, heat it up or make it glow.
A substance through which heat travels quickly, for example metal.
A layer that lets heat through poorly and so keeps things warm or cool.
The unit used to measure energy and heat.

gewusst: Chocolate melts in your mouth because its cocoa butter becomes liquid just below body temperature.
At rest a person gives off about as much heat as a 100 watt light bulb.
Emperor penguins stand close together in the cold to lose as little heat as possible.

teile.einleitung: Deformation is a change in the shape of an object when a force acts on it. Some things spring back into their old shape afterwards, others stay bent or even break. Whether modelling clay, a rubber ball or a glass bottle, every material reacts differently.
wichtigste: When a force acts on an object, it can change shape.
A rubber ball becomes round again after being squeezed; it is elastic.
Modelling clay stays pressed in; this is called permanent deformation.
An empty drinks can is crushed if you stand on it.
A glass bottle can break on a stone floor.
Loose snow becomes a hard snowball when it is pressed together.
You can see footprints in wet sand because the foot presses the sand down.
A thin branch bends a little when a bird sits on it.

abschnitte.text: If you squeeze a rubber ball and let it go, it becomes round again. A deformation like this, which disappears by itself, is called **elastic**. A thin branch that a bird sits on also only bends a little and then springs back. Springs, trampolines and rubber bands work on this principle.

Modelling clay stays pressed in if you press it hard; it can be deformed **plastically**. If an object does not return to its old shape after being pressed, this is called **permanent deformation**. A crushed drinks can and a footprint in wet sand are good examples. Loose snow also turns into a hard snowball when it is pressed, because the air between the flakes is squeezed out.

Some materials hardly change shape and then suddenly break; they are called **brittle**. That is why a glass bottle that falls onto a stone floor can break. Porcelain and thin ice are also brittle. Metals such as copper or aluminium, on the other hand, bend for a long time before they tear.

In the 17th century the English scientist Robert Hooke discovered an important rule. With a spring, the extension is twice as big if you pull twice as hard. But this **Hooke's law** only applies as long as the deformation stays elastic. Spring balances, used in physics lessons to measure forces, work on this principle.

Engineers use deformation deliberately for safety. The **crumple zone** at the front of a car is crushed in an accident and absorbs kinetic energy as it does so. This means much smaller forces act on the people inside. Bike helmets also deform in an impact and so protect the head.

Even large structures deform a little. A bridge sags slightly when a heavy lorry drives over it and then springs back. Tall towers sway by a few centimetres in strong wind. Engineers calculate exactly how much deformation a structure can take without being damaged.

begriffe.erklaerung: Returns to its old shape after being pressed or pulled.
Stays in its new shape after being pressed.
Breaks easily without bending much first.
A part of a car that deforms on purpose in an accident.

gewusst: Even a steel girder bends a tiny bit under a load; you just cannot see it.
A tennis ball is squashed very flat for a brief moment when it hits the racket.
Hooke first published his law as a letter puzzle so that nobody could steal the idea.

teile.einleitung: White light is not a single colour but a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow. With a glass prism you can split it into a colourful band. Sunlight is the best known example of white light.
wichtigste: White light is made of many different colours that together look white.
A prism or raindrops split white light into a band of colours, the spectrum.
Isaac Newton used prisms to show that sunlight is made up of colours.
Red, green and blue light together also make white light.
Seen from space, the Sun is white and not yellow.
Beyond violet lies invisible ultraviolet, and beyond red lies infrared.
An object shows only the colours that are present in the light falling on it.

abschnitte.text: Our eyes see light as white when all the colours of the **spectrum** are present in it roughly equally strongly. The spectrum runs from red through orange, yellow, green and blue to violet. Each colour corresponds to a different **wavelength** of light. Red light has long waves, violet light short waves. Only the mixture of all colours gives the impression of white.

When white light passes at a slant through a glass prism, it is refracted, that is, bent. Violet light is bent more than red. This makes the light fan out, and a colourful band appears on a wall. This fanning out is called **dispersion**. A rainbow forms in just the same way, only there millions of raindrops take the role of the prism.

In the 1660s the English scientist **Isaac Newton** studied sunlight with prisms. He split the light into colours and joined the colours back into white with a second prism. In this way he proved that the colours are already in white light and are not created by the glass. Before that, many people believed that white light was especially pure and unmixed. Newton later described his experiments in detail in his book “Opticks”.

If a red, a green and a blue lamp shine on the same spot, white light appears. This is called **additive colour mixing**. The screens of mobile phones and televisions use exactly this: each pixel consists of tiny red, green and blue points of light. Many white **LED lamps** also mix their light: a blue light emitting diode excites a yellow glowing layer, and together this looks white. If, on the other hand, only red light falls on a white sheet of paper, the sheet looks red, because it can reflect only that light.

Not all white light looks the same. Candlelight and old light bulbs look yellowish, because they give off more red and yellow light. The light on a cloudy day, by contrast, looks rather bluish. Experts describe this difference with the **colour temperature**, which is given in kelvin. Our brain balances a lot of this out, which is why a white sheet of paper almost always looks white to us.

As well as the visible colours, there is light our eyes cannot perceive. After violet comes **ultraviolet**, UV light, which can cause sunburn. After red comes **infrared**, which we feel as warmth on our skin. Under black light, that is UV light, white T-shirts often glow bluish, because washing powder contains special brighteners. These substances turn invisible UV light into visible blue light.

begriffe.erklaerung: The band of all colours into which white light can be split.
A triangular glass body that bends light and splits it into colours.
The fanning out of light into its colours, because each colour is bent by a different amount.
Mixing coloured light, in which red, green and blue together make white.
A measure of whether white light looks warm and yellowish or cold and bluish.

gewusst: The Sun is actually white; it only looks yellowish because the Earth's atmosphere scatters some of the blue light to the side.
Snow and clouds are white because they reflect all the colours of light roughly equally strongly.
The 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for the invention of the blue light emitting diode, without which there would be no bright white LED lamps.

teile.einleitung: Magnification means that something looks bigger than it really is. With a magnifying glass, a microscope, binoculars or a telescope we can look closely at tiny cells or at chamois and craters on the Moon far away. The object itself does not get bigger, only our image of it.
wichtigste: A “10x magnification” means that something looks ten times as big.
Optical instruments actually enlarge the visual angle at which we see an object.
A magnifying glass magnifies roughly 25 cm divided by its focal length.
With microscopes you can see tiny things such as cells, with telescopes distant things such as the Moon.
Binoculars make distant animals look much closer.
Magnification that shows no new details is called empty magnification.

abschnitte.text: Magnification tells you how many times bigger something looks through an instrument. If a beetle 2 cm long looks 6 cm long through a magnifying glass that magnifies 3 times, the magnification is 3. The beetle itself stays the same size, though. Optical instruments enlarge the **visual angle**, that is, the angle at which the image enters the eye. The bigger this angle, the bigger an object seems to us.

A magnifying glass is a curved **converging lens**. You calculate with a near viewing distance of 25 cm, because that is how far away you hold something to look at it comfortably. If a magnifying glass has a **focal length** of 5 cm, it magnifies about 25 divided by 5, so 5 times. The more strongly the lens is curved, the shorter the focal length and the more it magnifies. A make-up mirror in the bathroom also magnifies, because it is curved inwards.

A light microscope has two lens systems: the **objective** close to the object and the **eyepiece** at the eye. You get the total magnification by multiplying the two values, for example 40 times 10 equals 400. A cell of 0.01 mm looks 4 mm big at 400 times magnification. Light microscopes can usefully manage up to about 1000 times; beyond that the image only gets bigger and blurrier. Electron microscopes reach much greater magnifications and even show viruses.

A **telescope** makes distant things look closer. If a chamois is 1000 m away, through a telescope that magnifies 20 times it looks as if it were only 50 m away. Binoculars consist of two small telescopes side by side, one for each eye. The label “8x42” means 8 times magnification and objective lenses 42 mm in diameter. Stargazers use telescopes to look at craters on the Moon, the rings of Saturn or distant galaxies.

As early as the Middle Ages people ground reading stones out of glass, from which glasses later developed. Around 1600 spectacle makers in the Netherlands built the first telescopes and microscopes. In 1609 **Galileo Galilei** pointed a telescope he had built himself at the sky. In the 17th century Antoni van Leeuwenhoek used simple microscopes to discover tiny living things in a drop of water. Today instruments such as the Hubble Space Telescope take pictures of star systems billions of light years away.

begriffe.erklaerung: A curved glass that makes small things look bigger.
The distance between the lens and the point where the light rays meet.
The angle at which an object enters the eye; it decides how big we see something.
The lens of an instrument that faces the object being looked at.
Magnification that only makes the image bigger, but not sharper or more detailed.

gewusst: A drop of water on a leaf works like a little magnifying glass itself.
With good binoculars you can watch chamois in the Glarus Alps from the Uetliberg.
Antoni van Leeuwenhoek's first microscopes had only a single tiny lens.

teile.einleitung: Evaporation is the quiet change of a liquid into a gas without it boiling. Washing dries on the line, puddles disappear and perfume can be smelt all over the room, all thanks to evaporation. It is also an important part of the Earth's water cycle.
wichtigste: A blackboard that has been wiped wet becomes dry again because the water evaporates.
You can smell perfume all over the room because it evaporates and spreads out.
A lid stops water in a glass from evaporating.
Water evaporates much faster than cooking oil.
Felt-tip pens and glue sticks dry out if the lid is left off.
In summer water evaporates from the paddling pool, which is why you have to top it up.
Wet shoes dry fastest in a warm, airy place.

abschnitte.text: In a liquid the particles move at different speeds. Some especially fast particles at the surface can break free and escape into the air as a gas. This is called **evaporation**. It also happens at temperatures far below the boiling point; even snow and ice can slowly turn into gas.

Warmth makes water evaporate faster, which is why wet footprints on warm tiles at the swimming pool soon disappear. **Wind** also helps, because it carries away the damp air above the surface. The bigger the **surface**, the more particles can escape, which is why washing is hung up spread out. If the air is already very damp, on the other hand, less evaporates, which is why washing dries badly on foggy days.

Perfume evaporates quickly, and its scent particles spread throughout the room. Felt-tip pens and glue sticks dry out if you do not put the lid back on. A lid on a glass stops the water vapour from escaping. Cooking oil, on the other hand, hardly evaporates, which is why an oil stain stays visible for a long time.

For particles to escape, they need energy, which they take from their surroundings. That is why it gets cool when something evaporates; this is called **evaporative cooling**. When we sweat, the evaporating sweat cools our skin. That is also why someone climbing wet out of the swimming pool often feels cold as soon as a wind blows.

Every day the Sun makes huge amounts of water evaporate from seas, lakes and soil. Plants also give off water through their leaves. The water vapour rises, cools down and forms clouds. Later the water falls back as rain or snow, and so the **water cycle** is complete.

begriffe.erklaerung: The cooling that happens during evaporation.
Water in the form of a gas, which is invisible.
How much water vapour there is in the air.
The constant journey of water between sea, air and land.

gewusst: On a hot summer's day a large tree can evaporate hundreds of litres of water through its leaves.
In hot countries water is cooled in clay jugs, because water evaporates through the wall and cools what is inside.
Without evaporation there would be no clouds and no rain.

teile.einleitung: Thermal conduction is one of the ways heat travels from a warm place to a cold one. The particles of a substance pass their energy of motion on to their neighbours, without the substance itself flowing. That is why the handle of a metal spoon in hot soup quickly gets warm.
wichtigste: In thermal conduction, energy is passed from particle to particle without any material being carried along.
Heat always flows from the warmer to the colder body.
Metals such as copper are very good conductors of heat.
Materials that conduct heat poorly are called insulators, for example wood, plastic and air.
How much heat flows through a wall depends on the material, thickness, area and temperature difference.
Water conducts heat much better than air.

abschnitte.text: All substances are made of tiny particles that are constantly moving. The warmer a substance is, the more strongly its particles jiggle. In **thermal conduction**, fast particles bump into their slower neighbours and so pass on energy. The substance itself stays where it is, unlike in **convection** in water or air.

Metals conduct heat particularly well, because their freely moving electrons carry the energy quickly. **Copper** and silver are among the best conductors of heat, which is why good pans often have a copper base. If a metal spoon stands in hot soup, its handle soon gets warm. A metal railing feels colder in winter than a wooden one, because the metal carries heat away from your hand faster.

Materials that conduct heat poorly are called **insulators**. They include wood, plastic, wool, polystyrene and, above all, still air. That is why wooden spoons and pan handles often have parts made of wood or plastic. Down jackets and wool jumpers keep you warm because they trap a lot of air between their fibres.

How much heat is conducted through a wall each second depends on the material, thickness, area and **temperature difference**. The French mathematician Joseph Fourier described this relationship in the 19th century. Well insulated houses lose less heat in winter and need less energy for heating. In Switzerland there are building standards for this, such as Minergie.

When camping in winter, you put a thick mat under your sleeping bag so that less body heat flows into the cold ground. In water at 15 °C you cool down much faster than in air at 15 °C, because water conducts heat about twenty times better. That is why it is dangerous to swim for a long time in cold lakes or rivers. For the same reason, wet clothes keep you much less warm than dry ones.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material that passes heat on quickly, for example copper.
A material that conducts heat only poorly, for example wood or air.
A layer that stops heat escaping from a house.
How much warmer one side is than the other; it drives the flow of heat.

gewusst: Diamond conducts heat even better than copper, which is why a real diamond feels cool.
Under their fur, polar bears have a thick layer of fat that protects them from the cold like an insulator.
A tiled floor and a carpet in the same room are at the same temperature, yet the tiled floor feels much colder.

teile.einleitung: The centimetre is a unit of length. One centimetre is a hundredth of a metre, about as wide as a child's fingernail. Centimetres are used to measure things that are not very big, for example a rubber, an exercise book or your own height.
wichtigste: A centimetre is a hundredth of a metre.
The abbreviation for centimetre is cm.
100 centimetres make a metre, and 1 centimetre has 10 millimetres.
Centimetres are good for measuring small things such as a rubber.
The word comes from the Latin “centum”, which means hundred.
The centimetre belongs to the metric system, which has been in force in Switzerland since 1877.

abschnitte.text: The **centimetre** is a unit used to measure lengths. It is abbreviated to **cm**. The prefix “centi” comes from the Latin word centum, which means hundred. So a centimetre is a hundredth of a **metre**. On a ruler, the centimetres are marked with long lines and numbers.

Centimetres are easy to convert into other units. 1 centimetre has 10 **millimetres**, and 100 centimetres make 1 metre. So 120 centimetres is longer than 1 metre, namely 1 metre and 20 centimetres. You can add centimetres like ordinary numbers: 3 centimetres and 4 centimetres make 7 centimetres. The only important thing is always to use the same unit when calculating.

A rubber is about 4 to 6 centimetres long, a pencil about 17 centimetres. An A4 exercise book is roughly 21 centimetres wide and just under 30 centimetres high. At the paediatrician, your height is measured in centimetres; a ten year old child is often about 140 centimetres tall. Children's clothing sizes are also often based on height in centimetres, for example size 140. If you want to estimate quickly, you can use your hand to help.

In the past almost every town had its own measures, such as the ell, the foot or the inch. This often led to arguments in trade. That is why the **metric system**, in which everything is built up in steps of ten, was invented in France at the end of the 18th century. In Switzerland it has been compulsory since 1877. Today the metre is defined by the speed of light, and the centimetre is derived from it.

Centimetres help us to compare and build things precisely. Joiners, dressmakers and architects work with measurements in centimetres every day. In craft lessons you measure with a **ruler** or a folding rule. For very small things you use millimetres, for long distances metres or kilometres. That way you always choose the unit that is easiest to calculate with.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed quantity used to measure something, for example the metre or the kilogram.
A tenth of a centimetre, abbreviated to mm.
The basic unit of length; it has 100 centimetres.
A straight measuring tool with marks for centimetres and millimetres.

gewusst: The metre was originally defined as one ten millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator.
In the USA, lengths are often still measured in inches; one inch is 2.54 centimetres.

teile.einleitung: Pond skaters are insects that dart across the surface of ponds and streams on their long, thin legs without sinking. This is made possible by the surface tension of water. They are skilful hunters that catch small animals on the water.
wichtigste: Pond skaters walk on the surface of ponds, lakes and slow streams.
They belong to the true bugs, a group of insects.
Fine, water repellent hairs on their legs stop them from sinking in.
The surface tension of the water carries their low weight.
Pond skaters feed on insects that have fallen into the water.
They detect their prey through the small ripples on the water.
In Switzerland the common pond skater can be seen on many waters.

abschnitte.text: Pond skaters have a narrow, elongated body, which in the common pond skater is about 1 centimetre long. They have six legs: the front ones are short and are used for holding prey. The middle pair of legs is very long and is used like oars, and the back pair is used for **steering**. The animals belong to the **true bugs** and have a piercing beak instead of jaws for chewing.

The surface of water behaves like a very thin, stretchy skin. This **surface tension** comes about because the water particles attract each other. On the pond skater's legs there are thousands of tiny hairs that are **water repellent**. So the legs only press small dents into the water without breaking through it. With powerful strokes of their middle legs they glide forward at lightning speed.

Pond skaters live on calm **fresh waters** such as ponds, small lakes, pools and slow flowing streams. There are several hundred species worldwide. A few species, the **sea skaters**, even live on the open ocean, far from land. Several species are found in Switzerland; the one seen most often is the common pond skater.

Pond skaters are **predators**. They mainly eat insects that have fallen into the water and are struggling, for example flies or midges. The movements of the prey create small ripples, which the pond skater feels with its legs. It grabs the animal with its front legs and sucks it out with its **piercing beak**.

Many pond skaters can fly and so find new waters when a pool dries up. The females lay their eggs on water plants. The adults usually spend the winter on land, hidden in leaves or moss on the bank. In spring they return to the water.

Scientists study pond skaters closely in order to learn from them. They have already built small **robots** that run across water like pond skaters or can even jump. Water repellent surfaces for clothing are also being developed on the model of animals and plants. This kind of research is called **biomimetics**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The property of water that makes it hold together at the surface like a thin skin.
A group of insects with a piercing beak with which they suck up food.
Made in such a way that water rolls off and does not soak in.
A science that develops inventions modelled on nature.

gewusst: If you put washing up liquid in the water, the surface tension becomes weaker and a pond skater would sink.
Some pond skaters live on the open sea, hundreds of kilometres from the coast.
Pond skaters notice prey that has fallen into the water by tiny ripples.

teile.einleitung: A transverse wave is a wave in which the particles vibrate at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels. You know it from skipping ropes, from a plucked guitar string or from the Mexican wave in the stadium. Light is also such a transverse wave.
wichtigste: In a transverse wave the particles vibrate across, that is at right angles to the direction of travel.
The highest point is called the crest, the lowest the trough.
Transverse waves travel along a plucked guitar string.
Inside liquids and gases there are no transverse waves, because they cannot pass on shear forces.
Only transverse waves can be polarised.
In solids their speed depends on the shear modulus and the density.
A crest that is reflected at a fixed end of a rope comes back as a trough.

abschnitte.text: With every wave, energy is passed on without the material travelling along with it. In a **transverse wave** each particle only moves up and down, while the wave travels on sideways. The counterpart is the **longitudinal wave**, in which the particles swing back and forth in the direction of travel, as with sound in air. The word transverse comes from Latin and means across.

In the stadium the Mexican wave is a nice model. Each person only stands up briefly and sits down again, so they move up and down. Even so, the wave travels right round the stadium. A transverse wave works in exactly this way: the movement is passed on from neighbour to neighbour.

The highest point of a transverse wave is the **crest**, the lowest the **trough**. The distance from one crest to the next is called the **wavelength**. How far a particle moves away from its rest position is called the amplitude. How often it vibrates per second is given by the frequency in hertz.

When you pluck a guitar string, transverse waves travel back and forth and are reflected at the ends. This creates a **standing wave**, which we hear as a note. At a fixed end a crest is reflected as a trough; at a loose end it stays a crest. The tighter a string is stretched, the faster the waves travel and the higher the note sounds.

In solids the **shear modulus** and the density decide how fast transverse waves spread. Liquids and gases cannot pass on shear forces, which is why no transverse waves travel inside them. In earthquakes there are transverse waves, the so-called **S waves**. Because they do not cross the outer core of the Earth, scientists know that it is liquid.

Light and radio waves are also transverse waves, but they need no material and even travel through space. Only transverse waves can have a particular direction of vibration; this is called **polarisation**. A polarising filter only lets through light with one direction of vibration. Some sunglasses use this against reflections on water, and so do many 3D cinemas.

begriffe.erklaerung: The direction in which the wave moves on.
The direction of vibration of a transverse wave is fixed.
The greatest movement of a particle away from its rest position.
The distance between two crests.
A force that tries to shift layers of a material against each other.

gewusst: In stadiums the Mexican wave often travels on at about 20 seats per second, even though nobody leaves their seat.
Thanks to the S waves of earthquakes we know that the Earth's outer core is liquid, even though nobody has ever been there.
Light is a transverse wave that manages without any rope or water.

teile.einleitung: A water tower is a tall tower with a large water tank at the top. It stores water high up so that it flows into houses with enough pressure. For this it needs no pump at the tap, only gravity.
wichtigste: A water tower stores water high up in a tank.
The water is pumped up into the tank with pumps.
Gravity then pushes the water into the pipes of the houses.
If a house is higher than the tank, no water arrives without an extra pump.
If the tank is almost empty, the water pressure in the houses gets weaker.
Water towers help when many people need water at the same time.
In Switzerland, water stores are often underground reservoirs on a hill.

abschnitte.text: A **water tower** consists of a tower with a big tank on top. Pumps carry the water from springs, lakes or groundwater up into the tank. From there it flows down through pipes to the houses. Many water towers are built of stone, concrete or steel. Some hold several hundred thousand litres of water.

The higher the water stands, the greater the **water pressure** down in the pipes. A difference in height of about 10 metres gives about 1 **bar** of extra pressure. So **gravity** pushes the water into the houses all by itself. A house that is higher than the tank, however, does not get water up to the top floor. There an extra pump is needed.

In the morning and evening, many people need water at the same time, for showering, cooking and washing. The water tower then acts as a **buffer**. It releases a lot of water in a short time without the pumps having to keep up. At night, when little is used, the pumps fill it up again. If the tank is almost empty, the water pressure in the houses falls.

Switzerland has many hills and mountains. That is why tall towers are rarely needed here. Instead, people build a **reservoir**, a big water store, often underground on a hill above the village. It works on the same principle as a water tower. In the ground the water stays cool and dark, which protects its quality.

Many old water towers are splendid buildings and are **landmarks** today. The water tower in Mannheim in Germany is a well known example. In flat countries such as the Netherlands or the USA you still see many water towers. Some have been converted into flats, viewing towers or restaurants. Fire brigades benefit too, because thanks to the pressure, hydrants supply water immediately.

begriffe.erklaerung: How hard the water presses in a pipe.
The force that pulls everything down towards the Earth.
A big water store, often underground on a hill.
A water connection in the street for the fire brigade.

gewusst: The Water Tower at the Chapel Bridge in Lucerne has its name because it stands in the water, not because it stores water.
A water main works like two connected containers: the water wants to stand at the same height everywhere.

teile.einleitung: Ultrasound is sound with such high notes that people can no longer hear it. Bats, dolphins and dogs, however, can detect it. People use ultrasound in medicine, in technology and even in cars.
wichtigste: Ultrasound has a frequency above 20,000 hertz and cannot be heard by people.
A dog hears a dog whistle because it produces ultrasound.
In medicine ultrasound makes organs inside the body visible.
During the examination a gel stops there being air between the probe and the skin.
Ships locate objects under water with sonar.
The parking sensor in a car measures the distance to obstacles with ultrasound.
In an ultrasonic bath tiny collapsing bubbles clean glasses and jewellery.
Industry finds hidden cracks in components with ultrasound.

abschnitte.text: Sound consists of pressure waves that travel through air, water or solid materials. How high a note is depends on the **frequency**, that is, on how often the air vibrates per second. People hear roughly from 20 to 20,000 hertz, and the upper limit falls with age. Everything above that is called **ultrasound**.

**Bats** give out ultrasonic calls while flying and listen to the echo. In this way they find insects in the dark and avoid obstacles; this is called **echolocation**. Dolphins also locate their prey like this. Dogs and cats hear much higher notes than we do, which is why a dog reacts to a dog whistle that we cannot hear.

In an **ultrasound scan** a probe sends sound waves into the body. The waves are reflected back by organs to different degrees, and a computer turns this into a picture. In this way you can look at the heart, liver or kidneys, for example, without any radiation or pain. A gel on the skin is needed because air would reflect the ultrasound back almost completely.

Many cars have **parking sensors** with ultrasonic sensors in the bumper. They measure how long the echo takes and work out the distance to the wall from this. Ships use **sonar** to locate shoals of fish, the seabed or submarines. In industry rails, bridges and aircraft parts are tested with ultrasound for hidden cracks.

In an **ultrasonic bath** tiny bubbles form in the water and collapse in a flash. As they do, they loosen dirt even from fine gaps in glasses and jewellery. This process is called cavitation. An ultrasonic humidifier turns water into a fine, cool mist with rapid vibrations.

Ultrasound is usually produced with **piezoelectric crystals**, which change shape very slightly when a voltage is applied. If the voltage is switched on and off very quickly, the crystal vibrates and sends out ultrasound. The other way round, a crystal produces a voltage when an echo hits it. So the same probe can send and receive.

begriffe.erklaerung: How many vibrations take place per second, measured in hertz.
Finding something by sending out calls and analysing the echo.
A device that locates things under water with sound.
The forming and collapsing of tiny bubbles in a liquid.
A crystal that turns electricity into vibrations and the other way round.

gewusst: Some bats call as loudly as a pneumatic drill, but we hear nothing of it.
Many adults can no longer hear very high notes that children can still hear well.
With very strong, focused ultrasound you can even weld plastic parts together.

teile.einleitung: Dry ice is frozen carbon dioxide, the same substance that we breathe out and that fizzes in sparkling mineral water. It is ice cold, about minus 78 degrees, and never melts into a liquid. Instead it turns directly into gas and produces spectacular fog as it does so.
wichtigste: Dry ice is made of solid carbon dioxide.
At normal air pressure it sublimates at about minus 78 °C.
It is called dry because it does not become liquid when it warms up.
The fog collects on the ground, because carbon dioxide is heavier than air.
If touched with bare hands, it can cause cold burns.
In a tightly closed bottle the gas produced can make it burst.
In small, closed rooms there is a danger of suffocation.
Dry ice is often used for cooling during transport.

abschnitte.text: Dry ice is **carbon dioxide** in solid form, written chemically as CO₂. It looks like white ice or pressed snow and is often sold as cubes, slices or small sticks called pellets. At about minus 78 °C it is much colder than ordinary ice, which melts at 0 °C. It is also heavier than water ice and sinks in water.

When dry ice warms up, it does not become liquid, but turns directly into gas. This process is called **sublimation**. That is why no puddle is left behind, and exactly why it is called dry. Liquid carbon dioxide only exists under much higher pressure, for example in gas cylinders.

If you put dry ice into warm water, thick white clouds rise up. The cold gas cools the air so much that the water vapour in it condenses into tiny droplets. This **fog** is heavier than air, so it creeps along the ground. Theatres, concerts and Halloween parties like to use this effect.

Dry ice cools goods during **transport**, for example ice cream, meat, medicines or laboratory samples. Because it disappears without any meltwater, the parcels stay dry. In industry, machines are blasted clean with tiny pellets of dry ice. It is made by letting liquid carbon dioxide expand, which produces CO₂ snow that is pressed into blocks.

You must never touch dry ice with bare hands, because it causes **cold burns**, similar to burns from hot objects. You need thick gloves or tongs. It must never go into a tightly closed bottle, because the gas can make it burst. In small, badly aired rooms the gas pushes out the air, and there is a **danger of suffocation**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A solid substance turns directly into gas without becoming liquid.
A colourless gas that is produced by breathing and burning.
An injury to the skin caused by extreme cold.
Small pressed sticks or grains.

gewusst: Dry ice is more than 70 degrees colder than the ice in the freezer compartment.
One kilogram of dry ice produces several hundred litres of gas.
The white fog is not the carbon dioxide itself, because this gas is invisible.

teile.einleitung: The twin paradox is a famous thought experiment from Albert Einstein's theory of relativity. One twin travels in a rocket almost as fast as light to a star and back, while the other stays on Earth. On return, the traveller really is younger than their sibling.
wichtigste: According to the special theory of relativity, less time passes for fast moving clocks.
A fast travelling twin is younger on return than their twin on Earth.
It is not a real contradiction, because only the traveller changes inertial frame.
The traveller notices nothing unusual on their own clock during the flight.
The effect applies to all processes, including the ageing of the body.
The physicist Paul Langevin made the thought experiment well known in 1911.
The stretching of time has actually been measured with atomic clocks in aircraft and satellites.

abschnitte.text: Imagine the twins Lea and Luca. Lea flies in a super fast rocket to a distant star and back again, while Luca stays at home. According to Einstein's **special theory of relativity** of 1905, less time passes for Lea during the journey. When she comes back, she is younger than Luca, even though both were born on the same day.

A **paradox** is something that seems to contradict itself. According to the theory of relativity, Lea could also say that the Earth, with Luca on it, is moving away from her, so Luca ought to be younger. The contradiction is resolved because the two are not on an equal footing. Only Lea has to slow down, turn round and speed up again, so she changes her **inertial frame**, whereas Luca does not.

If Lea flies at 80 % of the speed of light, that is 0.8 c, to a star 4 light years away and back, the journey takes 10 years as measured on Earth. For Lea only 6 years pass in that time, because her time runs at a factor of 0.6. On a journey at 0.6 c that takes 10 years on Earth, the traveller ages 8 years. The difference becomes large only at very high speeds; in everyday life it is tiny.

The time a clock itself shows is called **proper time**. The path of a body through space and time is called a **world line**. Between two events, here departure and return, the straight, unaccelerated world line has the longest proper time. That is why Luca, who simply stays on Earth, ages the most.

It has not really been tested with twins, but it has with precise **atomic clocks**. In 1971 the physicists Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating flew atomic clocks round the Earth on airliners, and afterwards the clocks measurably differed from clocks on the ground. Short lived particles that circle at almost the speed of light in accelerators such as at CERN near Geneva also live measurably longer than particles at rest. The satellites of the GPS system have to take such effects into account, otherwise navigation would quickly become inaccurate.

Albert Einstein developed the special theory of relativity in 1905, when he was working at the patent office in Bern. He himself already pointed out that a clock that makes a round trip is slow when it returns. In 1911 the French physicist **Paul Langevin** told the story with a space traveller, which led to the well known picture of the twins. To this day it is one of the most popular examples for explaining the theory of relativity.

begriffe.erklaerung: Einstein's theory about space, time and motion.
The top speed in the universe, about 300,000 kilometres per second.
The stretching of time with fast movement.
A frame of reference that moves steadily, without acceleration.
The time shown by a clock travelling along.

gewusst: Astronauts who spend half a year on the International Space Station age a few thousandths of a second less as a result.
Einstein wrote his famous papers of 1905 in Bern, where today you can visit his flat as a museum.
According to the theory of relativity, no proper time at all would pass for light itself.

teile.einleitung: A convex mirror is a mirror that bulges outwards like the back of a spoon. It shows a smaller picture, but a very large section of the surroundings. That is why it hangs at exits where you cannot see well and is built into many car mirrors.
wichtigste: A convex mirror bulges outwards.
Its image is always smaller and upright.
Light falling on it in parallel is spread apart by it.
Its focal point seems to lie behind the mirror.
It gives a wide field of view and therefore helps at places that are hard to see.
In a curved wing mirror, cars look further away than they really are.
A shiny Christmas tree bauble acts like a convex mirror.

abschnitte.text: An ordinary mirror is flat, but a **convex mirror** is bent outwards. You can think of it as a piece cut from the outside of a shiny ball. Its German name “Wölbspiegel” means “bulging mirror”; the technical term is **convex mirror**. The opposite is the **concave mirror**, which curves inwards like the inside of a spoon. Both kinds of mirror reflect light by the same rules, but with quite different effects.

Light is reflected by a mirror so that the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are equal. Because the surface of a convex mirror is tilted slightly differently everywhere, parallel rays of light spread apart after reflection. If you extend these rays backwards, they meet at a point behind the mirror. This point is called the **focal point**, but it only seems to be there, because no light actually arrives at it. It is therefore called a virtual focal point.

In a convex mirror you always see yourself **upright** and **smaller**. The further away you go, the smaller the image becomes. In return, much more of the surroundings fits into the mirror than into a flat mirror of the same size. The image seems to lie behind the mirror, and you cannot catch it on a screen. That is why it is called a virtual, that is, apparent, image.

At exits, junctions and narrow mountain roads there are often round **traffic mirrors**. They show a large area, so that you can see approaching cars, bikes and pedestrians in time. Many car wing mirrors are also slightly curved so that the blind spot is smaller. Because the image is smaller, vehicles in it look further away than they really are. Some mirrors therefore carry a warning, and drivers should judge distances carefully.

A shiny **Christmas tree bauble** is a small convex mirror in which you see the whole room in miniature. The back of a soup spoon also shows this kind of image. In shops, large curved mirrors hang so that the staff can watch many aisles at once. In buses, such mirrors help the driver keep an eye on the inside of the bus.

begriffe.erklaerung: Bulging outwards, like the outside of a ball.
A mirror that curves inwards and gathers light.
The point where reflected rays of light meet or seem to meet.
An apparent image behind the mirror that cannot be caught on a screen.

gewusst: In the USA, many car mirrors carry the warning that objects in the mirror are closer than they appear.
Round convex mirrors that show a whole room can already be seen in old paintings from the 15th century.
In a convex mirror you can never see an enlarged image of yourself.

teile.einleitung: The state of matter tells you whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas. You know water in all three forms: as ice, as liquid water and as water vapour. Whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas depends mainly on temperature and pressure.
wichtigste: The three most common states of matter are solid, liquid and gas.
An ice cube is solid; water vapour is a gas.
When ice turns into water, this is called melting.
When a liquid becomes solid, for example hot wax, this is called solidifying.
When water turns into steam on boiling, this is called evaporating.
Lava from a volcano is liquid rock.
Under a magnifying glass, snowflakes have six arms or points.

abschnitte.text: All substances are made of tiny **particles** that are constantly moving. In the **solid** state they sit close together in fixed places and only jiggle, which is why a solid has a fixed shape. In the **liquid** state they can slide past each other, so a liquid adapts to any container. In the gas state the particles fly far apart and fill any space.

Each change has a name. Solid becomes liquid by **melting**, and liquid becomes solid by solidifying. Liquid becomes gas by evaporating, and gas becomes liquid by **condensing**, for example when drops form on a cold glass. If a substance goes straight from solid to gas, this is called sublimation, and the reverse is deposition.

At normal air pressure, ice melts at 0 °C and water boils at 100 °C. In the mountains the air pressure is lower, so water boils sooner there; on the Jungfraujoch at about 3450 metres, it boils at about 89 °C. Water is special: ice is lighter than liquid water and therefore floats on top. That is why lakes such as Lake Zurich freeze from the top, and fish survive underneath.

**Snowflakes** form in clouds when water vapour turns directly into ice crystals. Because of the shape of water molecules, the crystals grow in six directions, which is why snowflakes have six arms or points. Hoarfrost on branches and grass also forms directly from water vapour. Glaciers in the Alps are huge amounts of solid water that slowly flow down the valley.

Metals and rocks can melt too if it is hot enough. **Lava** is molten rock at temperatures of about 700 to 1200 °C; as it cools, it solidifies into solid rock. Iron melts at about 1538 °C, chocolate already in your warm hand. As well as the three familiar states, there is **plasma**, an extremely hot gas made of charged particles, as in lightning or in the Sun.

begriffe.erklaerung: The idea that all substances are made of tiny, moving particles.
The temperature at which a solid becomes liquid.
The temperature at which a liquid starts to boil throughout.
The change from gas to liquid.
The direct change from solid to gas.

gewusst: Dry ice made of frozen carbon dioxide never becomes liquid; it sublimes straight into gas.
Real water vapour is invisible; the white clouds above the saucepan are already tiny droplets of water again.
Washing can dry even in frost, because ice sublimes directly into water vapour.

teile.einleitung: Pulling and pushing are two ways of setting something in motion with a force. When you pull, you move something towards you or along behind you; when you push, you press it away from you or along in front of you. Every day you pull and push countless things, often without noticing.
wichtigste: Pulling and pushing are forces that move an object or change its movement.
When you pull, the force points towards you.
When you push, the force points away from you.
You push a shopping trolley, and you pull a drawer open.
A locomotive pulls the carriages behind it.
Wheels and rollers make moving things much easier, because they reduce friction.
Forces are measured in the unit newton.

abschnitte.text: In physics, a **force** is anything that sets a body in motion, slows it down, turns it aside or changes its shape. Pulling and pushing are the simplest examples, which you do with your muscles. When **pulling**, you hold the object and move it towards you; when **pushing**, you press against it and move it away from you. A force always has a strength and a direction, which is why it is drawn as an arrow.

You pull a drawer, a door marked “Pull” or a rope towards you. With a door marked “Push”, you have to press it away from you. You push a pram, a shopping trolley or a wheelbarrow along in front of you. In Switzerland, a cork is pulled out of a bottle with a **corkscrew**, which Swiss Germans call a “Zapfenzieher”.

When you push a heavy box across the floor, the **friction** between box and floor slows it down. Wheels and rollers greatly reduce this friction. That is why the easiest way to move a heavy suitcase is to pull it along behind you on its wheels. On ice you need hardly any force at all, because the friction there is very small.

A **locomotive** pulls a whole train with many carriages, and on some trains it also pushes from behind. A snowplough pushes snow aside, and a bulldozer pushes earth and stones. Tractors pull trailers, ploughs and other machines across the field. In the past, horses pulled carriages, sledges and even boats on rivers.

The strength of a force is measured in **newtons**, named after the English physicist Isaac Newton. One newton is roughly the force with which a 100 gram bar of chocolate presses on your hand. With a spring balance you can see how hard you are pulling on something. In a tug of war, two teams pull in opposite directions, and the stronger one wins.

When you pull on something or push against something, an equal force always acts back on you. Isaac Newton described this in his third law; it is also called the **principle of action and reaction**. If you push yourself off a wall on roller skates, you roll backwards yourself. That is why you need a good grip under your feet when pushing a heavy car.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that moves, slows down, turns aside or changes the shape of a body.
The unit in which forces are measured.
A force that slows down a movement when two surfaces rub against each other.
An arrow that shows the direction and strength of a force.

gewusst: When you push a bike uphill, you need more force, because you have to push part of its weight up as well.
The unit “horsepower” goes back to James Watt, who compared his steam engines with the pulling power of horses.
Tug of war was even an Olympic sport from 1900 to 1920.

teile.einleitung: Wind strength tells you how strongly the wind is blowing. It is usually given on the Beaufort scale from 0 to 12 or as a wind speed in kilometres per hour. That way you know whether only a light breeze is blowing or a dangerous hurricane is raging.
wichtigste: Wind strength describes how strongly the wind is blowing.
The best known scale is the Beaufort scale with the levels 0 to 12.
Force 0 means calm, force 12 means hurricane.
Weather reports often give the wind speed in kilometres per hour.
Sudden, short, strong blasts of wind are called gusts.
A gentle, pleasant wind is called a breeze.
You can also estimate wind strength without an instrument by looking at trees, smoke or waves.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of the 19th century, the British naval officer **Francis Beaufort** developed a scale for sailors. It divides the wind into 13 levels from 0 to 12. Each level describes what you can observe at sea or on land. This **Beaufort scale** is still used today, especially in shipping. People then say, for example, “force 6” or “6 Beaufort”.

At force 0, smoke rises straight up and not a leaf moves. In a light wind the **leaves** rustle and you feel the wind on your face. At the middle levels, thin branches move and dust is whirled up. From about force 8, a **gale**, twigs break off and walking becomes difficult. In a hurricane, whole trees can fall over and roofs can be torn off.

The levels have names. Light to fresh winds are called a **breeze**, followed by a strong breeze and a near gale. Levels 9 to 11 are strong gale, storm and violent storm. Force 12 is a **hurricane**, with wind speeds from about 118 kilometres per hour. Tropical cyclones such as hurricanes often reach much higher speeds still.

Weather stations measure the wind with an **anemometer**. A common type has three small cups that spin faster the stronger the wind is. The speed is given in kilometres per hour, metres per second or knots. It is usually measured 10 metres above open ground. Sudden strong blasts are called **gusts**; they are often much stronger than the average wind.

In Switzerland, MeteoSwiss measures the wind at many stations, including on mountain peaks. On peaks and passes the wind is often much stronger than in the valley. Well known winds are the **föhn**, a warm downslope wind in the Alpine valleys, and the **bise**, a cold north easterly wind on the Swiss Plateau. When there are storm warnings, orange lights flash on the shores of large lakes so that boats get to land in time.

In strong winds you should avoid woods, because branches can fall. Loose objects on the balcony, such as flowerpots or sunshades, should be secured. On lakes, when there is a storm warning, the rule is: get to the shore at once. If you read the weather forecast, you will often also see the expected **peak gusts**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A division of the wind into levels from 0 to 12.
A sudden, short, strong blast of wind.
A light to moderate, pleasant wind.
The strongest wind on the Beaufort scale, force 12.
An instrument for measuring wind speed.

gewusst: A knot means one nautical mile per hour, which is about 1.85 kilometres per hour.
Francis Beaufort originally described the levels by how many sails a warship could still set.
On high Alpine peaks in Switzerland, gusts of well over 200 kilometres per hour have been measured.

teile.einleitung: The ideal gas law links the pressure, volume, temperature and amount of a gas in a single formula. It is p·V = n·R·T and applies quite accurately to air and many other gases. With it you can work out what happens to a balloon, a bicycle pump or a gas cylinder when something changes.
wichtigste: The ideal gas law is p·V = n·R·T.
p is the pressure, V the volume, n the amount of substance in moles and T the temperature in kelvin.
R is the universal gas constant, about 8.314 J/(mol·K).
The temperature must always be put in in kelvin.
Equal volumes of ideal gases at the same pressure and temperature contain the same number of particles; this is Avogadro's law.
One cubic metre of air at 20 °C and 100 kPa contains about 41 mol of gas particles.
With the equation you can even work out which gas it is.

abschnitte.text: An **ideal gas** is a simplified model: the particles are tiny balls that move freely and affect each other only when they collide. Many real gases such as air, nitrogen or helium behave almost exactly like this under normal conditions. The **ideal gas law** p·V = n·R·T describes how pressure, volume, amount of substance and temperature are connected. If you change one quantity, others have to adjust.

The pressure p is measured in pascals, the volume V in cubic metres and the amount of substance n in **moles**. The temperature T must be in **kelvin**; you get it by adding 273.15 to the Celsius temperature. R is the universal **gas constant**, about 8.314 joules per mole and kelvin. So 2 mol of gas at 300 K in 0.05 m³ has a pressure of about 100 kPa, roughly normal air pressure.

If a gas is at 2 bar, 10 litres and 300 K, p·V/T stays the same as long as no gas escapes. At 1 bar and 450 K it therefore takes up 30 litres. At 0 °C and normal pressure, a cubic metre of helium weighs only about 0.18 kg, whereas air weighs about 1.3 kg, which is why helium balloons rise. If 0.4 litres of a gas at 300 K and 100 kPa weigh exactly 0.513 g, this gives a molar mass of 32 g/mol, so it is oxygen.

The equation combines several older laws. In the 17th century **Robert Boyle** and Edme Mariotte found that at the same temperature pressure times volume stays constant. Around 1800, Jacques Charles and Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac studied how gases expand when heated. In 1811 Amedeo Avogadro realised that equal volumes of gas contain the same number of particles, and in 1834 the Frenchman Émile Clapeyron combined everything into one equation.

When you pump up a bicycle tyre, the pressure rises with the number of particles. If a ball is left in the blazing sun, the pressure rises with the temperature, while in cold winter it goes a little soft. A **hot air balloon** rises because the heated air inside expands and is therefore lighter than the cool air outside. Weather balloons get bigger and bigger high up, because the air pressure outside decreases.

At very high pressure or very low temperatures, the equation is no longer exact. Then the particles' own volume and their forces of attraction play a part. Just before they turn into liquid, gases therefore behave differently. For such cases there are more precise equations, such as the **van der Waals equation**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A unit of amount for very many particles, about 6 · 10²³ of them.
A unit of temperature that starts at absolute zero; 0 °C is 273.15 K.
The unit of pressure; normal air pressure is about 100,000 Pa.
A model gas made of tiny particles that affect each other only when they collide.
A fixed natural number R, about 8.314 J/(mol·K).

gewusst: At 0 °C and normal pressure, one mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres, roughly as much as 15 PET bottles of 1.5 litres.
According to the equation, an ideal gas would have no pressure at all at absolute zero, −273.15 °C.
Because the air in the mountains is less dense, a breath on the Jungfraujoch contains far fewer oxygen particles than in Zurich.

teile.einleitung: Waste glass is used glass bottles and jars that are collected so that new glass can be made from them. In Switzerland, waste glass is thrown into collection containers sorted by colour. Glass can be melted down again and again without getting worse.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, waste glass is sorted into the colours clear, brown and green.
Blue and other coloured glass goes with the green glass.
You take the lids off before throwing a jar in.
Mirrors, window glass, drinking glasses and porcelain do not belong in the bottle bank.
On Sundays you usually may not throw glass in, because it is noisy.
New glass bottles are made from melted waste glass.
Glass can be recycled again and again.
The most important raw material for glass is sand.

abschnitte.text: Waste glass includes empty **glass bottles** and jars, for example from wine, cordial, jam or gherkins. They are collected and melted down again in a glassworks. This cycle is called **recycling**. In Switzerland, well over 90 per cent of packaging glass is collected.

Waste glass is sorted into **clear glass**, brown glass and green glass. This is important, because brown pieces can never become clear glass again. Blue, red or other bottles go in with the green glass, because green glass is least affected by other colours. Labels can usually stay on, but lids and corks cannot.

abschnitte.titel: What does not belong in it
abschnitte.text: **Mirrors**, window glass, drinking glasses, light bulbs, porcelain and ceramics do not belong with waste glass. These materials have a different composition or melt at different temperatures. Even small pieces of them can make new bottles faulty. So they belong in the household rubbish or at the municipal recycling centre.

Throwing bottles in makes a lot of noise. That is why in many municipalities you may get rid of waste glass only on working days during the day, and usually not on **Sundays** or at night. The exact times are often shown on the container. When you buy drinks in glass bottles, you pay a small **recycling fee**, which pays for the collection.

Glass is made mainly from **quartz sand**, with soda and lime added. This mixture melts at about 1500 degrees Celsius. If you mix in broken waste glass, everything melts at a lower temperature and a lot of energy is saved. In addition, fewer new raw materials need to be taken from nature.

Glass practically does not break down in nature and would lie around for thousands of years. Recycling saves sand, energy and space in landfill sites. Glass can be melted down any number of times without losing **quality**. Even more environmentally friendly are returnable bottles, which are washed and refilled.

begriffe.erklaerung: Used material is collected and made into new products.
A factory where glass is melted and shaped.
Light coloured sand, the main raw material for glass.
A bottle that is cleaned and refilled.

gewusst: After being melted down, a glass bottle can be back in the shop as a new bottle within a few weeks.
Some Swiss waste glass is also made into foam glass or building material.
Glass is actually a solidified melt without a regular crystal structure.

teile.einleitung: A wind wheel is a wheel with blades that turns in the wind. It comes as a colourful paper toy, called a pinwheel, as an old windmill and as a huge wind turbine that produces electricity. They all work on the same principle: the wind pushes against angled blades.
wichtigste: A wind wheel turns because the wind pushes against its blades.
The stronger the wind, the faster it turns.
For it to turn well, the front must face into the wind.
You can make a toy pinwheel from a sheet of paper with a pin as its axle.
If you run with a pinwheel, it turns even without wind, because you create your own headwind.
Windmills have used the wind for centuries to grind corn.
Large wind turbines turn the movement of the wind into electric current.

abschnitte.text: A toy pinwheel is easy to make. You cut a square sheet of paper from the corners towards the middle and bend every second point into the centre. A pin as the **axle** holds the points in place and joins the wheel to a stick. If you blow on it or run with it, it starts to turn. A small bead between the paper and the stick helps it to run more easily.

The **blades** of a wind wheel are set at an angle to the wind. When the air hits these sloping surfaces, it is deflected to the side and pushes the blades away as it does so. Because all the blades are attached to one axle, the wheel turns. That is why the front must face into the wind. In a stronger wind the push is greater and the wheel turns faster.

More than a thousand years ago, people were already using the wind in **windmills**. The turning of the sails drove millstones that ground corn into flour. In the Netherlands, windmills also pumped water out of low lying land. At Kinderdijk there are still 19 old windmills, which are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In Switzerland, by contrast, waterwheels were used more often, because there are many streams and rivers.

Modern **wind turbines** are huge wind wheels, usually with three rotor blades. The blades drive a **generator**, which turns movement into electric current. Large turbines have rotor blades that can be more than 50 metres long. A computer automatically turns the nacelle at the top of the tower into the wind. In a dangerously strong storm, they are switched off for protection.

In Switzerland, wind energy so far supplies only a small share of electricity. Well known sites are **Mont Crosin** in the Bernese Jura and the Gütsch above Andermatt. At the Griessee in Valais, wind turbines stand at more than 2400 metres. Wind turbines are controversial because they change the landscape, but they produce electricity without exhaust gases, and in winter too.

begriffe.erklaerung: The rod around which a wheel turns.
The turning part of a wind wheel with all its blades.
A machine that turns rotation into electric current.
An old building with sails that grinds corn or pumps water using wind power.

gewusst: The tips of the rotor blades of large wind turbines can move faster than a car on the motorway.
In winter, wind turbines in Switzerland often supply more electricity than in summer, because the wind is stronger then.
When you run with a paper pinwheel, it shows that a headwind works just like real wind.

teile.einleitung: The Trieste was a deep-sea submersible, a so-called bathyscaphe. In 1960 it dived to the deepest point of the oceans in the Mariana Trench, almost 11,000 metres below the sea surface. It had been designed by the Swiss scientist Auguste Piccard.
wichtigste: Bathyscaphe means “deep ship”.
The Trieste was designed by the Swiss Auguste Piccard and named after the city of Trieste in Italy.
Its large float was filled with petrol, which is lighter than water.
The crew sat in a thick steel sphere under the float.
To rise, the Trieste released iron balls used as ballast.
In 1958 the US Navy bought the submersible.
On 23 January 1960 Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh reached the bottom of the Mariana Trench.

abschnitte.text: The Trieste was not a submarine, but a **bathyscaphe**, a diving craft for great depths. The word comes from Greek and means “deep ship”. This type of craft had been invented by the Swiss physicist **Auguste Piccard**, who had already risen into the stratosphere in a balloon in 1931. The Trieste was completed in Italy in 1953 and named after the port city of Trieste, which helped to build it.

At the top was a large **float** full of petrol, because petrol is lighter than water and can hardly be squeezed together. Below it hung a small **steel sphere** with thick walls, in which the crew sat. To dive, tonnes of iron balls served as ballast and provided the weight needed. To rise again, the Trieste released these iron balls, which were held in place by electromagnets.

An ordinary submarine rises by blowing water out of its tanks with compressed air. But in the deep sea the **water pressure** is enormous: at 11,000 metres it is more than a thousand times as great as at the surface. Compressed air could do nothing against it. That is why Piccard relied on petrol for buoyancy and iron ballast that could be dropped.

In 1958 the **US Navy** bought the Trieste and equipped it for even greater depths. On 23 January 1960, Jacques Piccard, Auguste's son, and the US officer Don Walsh dived into the **Challenger Deep** in the Mariana Trench. The descent took about five hours, and at a depth of about 9000 metres an outer window pane cracked. Even so, they reached the bottom and stayed there for about twenty minutes.

At the bottom the two men saw a flat fish, which showed that life is possible even in the very deepest places. Only in 2012 did a person dive that deep again: the film director James Cameron. Today the Trieste is in a US Navy museum in Washington. The Piccard family stayed adventurous: Bertrand Piccard, Auguste's grandson, later went round the Earth in a balloon and in a solar aircraft.

begriffe.erklaerung: Submersible for the deep sea with a float and a pressure sphere.
Extra weight that makes a vehicle sink or keeps it stable.
Force with which water pushes a body upwards.
Deepest trench in the oceans, in the western Pacific.
Force with which water presses from all sides; the deeper, the stronger.

gewusst: Whether it really was a fish at the bottom is still disputed among experts; perhaps it was a sea cucumber.
Jacques Piccard later built the submersible “Auguste Piccard”, which took visitors down into Lake Geneva at Expo 64 in Lausanne.
The windows of the Trieste were made of thick Perspex shaped like a cone.

teile.einleitung: A hot water bottle is a soft container that you fill with hot water. It warms cold feet, heats the bed in advance or eases tummy ache. The fact that it stays warm for so long has to do with a special property of water.
wichtigste: A hot water bottle is filled with hot water.
Classic hot water bottles are made of rubber.
A fabric cover protects you from burning yourself.
After filling it, you must screw the stopper on tightly.
You should not fill it with boiling water, because the rubber can be damaged.
Overnight the water slowly cools down.
In Switzerland the cherry stone cushion is a popular alternative.

abschnitte.titel: What is a hot water bottle?
abschnitte.text: A **hot water bottle** is a flat bag with a screw stopper. You fill it with hot water and, for example, put it in your bed in the evening to warm it up. Many people also use it for cold feet, tummy ache or tense muscles. It is usually kept in a **cover** made of fabric or knitted wool. This makes sure you do not burn yourself on the hot surface.

Water can store a great deal of heat; it has a high **heat capacity**. To warm a litre of water by one degree takes more energy than for almost any other liquid. That is why a hot water bottle gives off its warmth slowly and evenly. Even so, the water slowly cools down overnight until it reaches the temperature of its surroundings. Under a duvet this happens more slowly, because the duvet holds the heat in.

Classic hot water bottles are made of **rubber** or soft plastic. Rubber is stretchy, watertight and does not conduct heat too quickly. In the past people used bed warmers made of metal, ceramic or glass. Even earlier, hot stones or pans of embers were put in the bed. Rubber hot water bottles have existed since the beginning of the 20th century.

You should not pour in boiling water, because the rubber can be damaged and there is a risk of scalding. Usually you fill the bottle only about two thirds full. Then you squeeze the air out and screw the **stopper** on tightly. This stops hot water from leaking out. Old, cracked hot water bottles should be replaced, because they can burst.

In Switzerland the **cherry stone cushion** is a popular alternative. It is a fabric bag full of dried cherry stones. You warm it up in the oven or the microwave. The stones store the heat and give it off slowly. Cooled in the freezer, the same cushion also helps with bumps and bruises.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much heat a substance can store when it gets warmer.
A stretchy, waterproof material, often made from the sap of the rubber tree.
An injury to the skin caused by hot water or steam.
A fabric cushion filled with cherry stones that you warm up or cool down.

gewusst: You can also fill a hot water bottle with cold water and use it as a cooling pad on hot summer days.
A kilogram of water stores several times as much heat as a kilogram of stones.

teile.einleitung: The alkali metals are a group of particularly reactive metals: lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium and francium.
