They are so soft that you can cut them with a knife, and they react violently with water. In nature they are never found pure, only in compounds such as table salt.
wichtigste: The alkali metals are in the first main group of the periodic table.
Hydrogen is also in the first main group, but it is not an alkali metal.
Alkali metals are soft and can be cut with a knife.
With water they react to form hydrogen gas and an alkaline solution.
The violence of the reaction increases from lithium to caesium.
Sodium is kept under paraffin oil, because it reacts violently with air and water.
In a flame they show typical colours: sodium yellow, lithium red.

abschnitte.text: The **alkali metals** are **lithium**, **sodium**, potassium, rubidium, caesium and francium. They are on the far left of the **periodic table** in the first main group. Hydrogen is also there, but it is a gas and not an alkali metal. All alkali metals have just one single electron in their outermost shell, which they give up very easily. That is why they are so reactive. Francium is radioactive and extremely rare.

Alkali metals are shiny silvery but very **soft** metals; sodium can be cut with a knife like cold butter. The fresh cut surface shines only briefly and quickly goes dull in the air. Lithium has the lowest density of all metals, and lithium, sodium and potassium even float on water. Caesium melts at only about 28 °C. Because they react with air and moisture, they are kept under **paraffin oil**.

If you drop an alkali metal into water, it reacts violently. **Hydrogen**, a flammable gas, is produced, along with an alkali, so that the solution becomes **alkaline**. Lithium reacts fairly calmly, sodium whizzes hissing across the water, and potassium even catches fire. From lithium to caesium the reaction becomes more and more violent. Only teachers wearing safety glasses and using very small amounts may demonstrate such experiments.

If you hold compounds of alkali metals in a flame, it glows with a typical **flame colour**. Sodium colours the flame bright yellow, lithium crimson and potassium pale violet. With this **flame test** you can find out which substances are in a sample. Using this method, the scientists Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff discovered the elements caesium and rubidium around 1860. Metal salts also provide the bright colours in fireworks.

You never see pure sodium and potassium in everyday life, but you see their **compounds** all the time. Table salt is sodium chloride, and potassium is found in bananas, potatoes and fertiliser. Lithium is an important part of the **lithium ion batteries** in mobile phones, laptops and electric cars. Many street lamps used to glow yellow because they contained sodium vapour. Atomic clocks, which define the second very precisely, work with caesium.

begriffe.erklaerung: A table in which all chemical elements are arranged according to their properties.
A column in the periodic table with elements that behave similarly.
An alkaline solution that can burn skin and eyes.
The typical colour that an element gives to a flame.
An oil that protects alkali metals from air and water.

gewusst: The name alkali comes from Arabic and means roughly plant ash, from which alkalis used to be obtained.
In 1807 the Englishman Humphry Davy was the first to make pure sodium and potassium, using electric current.
The second is defined by the vibrations of caesium atoms.

teile.einleitung: A gear ratio arises when two gearwheels mesh and one drives the other. Depending on the size of the wheels, the driven wheel turns faster or slower, but with less or more force. Bicycles, clocks, cars and mixers use this principle.
wichtigste: In a gear train, one gearwheel drives another.
The ratio of the numbers of teeth decides how fast the second wheel turns.
If a large wheel drives a small one, the small one turns faster; this is called gearing up.
If a small wheel drives a large one, the large one turns more slowly but with more turning effect.
Two meshing wheels turn in opposite directions.
An idler wheel makes both wheels turn in the same direction.
Gearwheels mesh cleanly only if their teeth are the same size.

abschnitte.text: A **gearwheel** is a wheel with teeth round its edge. When two gearwheels mesh, each tooth of one wheel pushes a tooth of the other along. The driving wheel is called the **driver**, the other the **driven wheel**. For the teeth to mesh cleanly, they must be the same size. But the wheels themselves can have quite different numbers of teeth.

With each turn, a wheel pushes along as many teeth as it has itself. So a wheel with 36 teeth pushes along 36 teeth of a wheel with 12 teeth, which is three turns. If the large wheel turns 10 times a minute, the small one turns 30 times. The **gear ratio** is therefore the ratio of the numbers of teeth. A motor at 3000 revolutions per minute with a gearwheel of 10 teeth turns a wheel with 50 teeth only 600 times a minute.

What you gain in speed of rotation, you lose in force, and the other way round. If a wheel with 15 teeth drives one with 45 teeth, the large one turns at only a third of the speed. But it has three times the **turning effect**, which is called torque. This is called **gearing down**. If the driven wheel turns faster, it is called gearing up.

Several gearwheels one after the other form a **gear train**. If wheel A with 40 teeth drives wheel B with 20 teeth, and B drives wheel C with 10 teeth, then C turns 4 times for each turn of A. Two wheels that mesh directly turn against each other. If you put an **idler wheel** in between, the first and last wheels turn in the same direction. The idler wheel itself does not change the ratio.

On a **bicycle** the gearwheels are connected by a chain, but the principle is the same. A large chainring at the front and a small sprocket at the back give a high gear for riding fast. On a hill you change to a large sprocket at the back; then pedalling is easier, but you go more slowly. In a **clock**, the minute hand turns 12 times while the hour hand goes round once. Swiss watchmakers have been masters for centuries at making tiny gearwheels precisely.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wheel with teeth that passes rotation on to other wheels.
The ratio of the numbers of teeth, which tells you how fast the second wheel turns.
The turning effect of a force, that is, how strongly something turns.
An arrangement of gearwheels that changes speed of rotation and force.
A gearwheel between two others that makes the directions of rotation the same.

gewusst: In ancient Greece, people already built a device made of many small gearwheels, the Antikythera mechanism.
A mechanical wristwatch can contain more than a hundred tiny individual parts.
On a bicycle with many gears, changing gear only changes which gearwheels the chain connects.

teile.einleitung: The watt hour is a unit of energy, for example for the electricity a device uses. One watt hour is the energy that a device with a power of 1 watt needs in one hour. Electricity bills usually show the bigger unit, the kilowatt hour.
wichtigste: The watt hour, Wh for short, is a unit of energy.
A watt is a power; a watt hour is an amount of energy used.
A kilowatt hour is 1000 watt hours.
Energy in watt hours is power in watts times time in hours.
One watt hour equals 3600 joules.
On the electricity bill you pay for the kilowatt hours used.
The capacity of rechargeable batteries is also often given in watt hours.

abschnitte.text: The **watt hour** measures how much electrical energy is used or supplied. A device with a power of 1 watt uses exactly 1 watt hour in one hour. The symbol is **Wh**. The unit is named after the Scottish inventor James Watt, who greatly improved the steam engine.

The **watt** is the unit of power and tells you how much energy a device needs each second. The watt hour, on the other hand, tells you how much energy has been used in total. You can compare it with cycling: your speed is like the power, and the distance you ride is like the energy. So a hairdryer with 2000 watts uses 1000 watt hours in half an hour.

The formula is: **energy** equals power times time. A 10 watt LED lamp that is on for 5 hours uses 50 watt hours. For large amounts you use the **kilowatt hour**; 1 kWh is 1000 Wh. Even bigger units are the megawatt hour and the gigawatt hour, which are used to give the output of power stations.

The electricity meter in the house counts how many kilowatt hours have been used. On the **electricity bill** you pay a price for each kilowatt hour; in Switzerland, for households it is usually just under 30 centimes (as of 2025), varying from municipality to municipality. A household in Switzerland uses several thousand kilowatt hours a year. If you switch appliances off completely instead of leaving them on standby, you save electricity and money.

For **rechargeable batteries** too, it is often stated how many watt hours they can store. A mobile phone battery stores about 10 to 20 watt hours, a laptop battery roughly 50 to 100. The battery of an electric car, by contrast, often stores 50 to 100 kilowatt hours, about a thousand times more. On aeroplanes, power banks are allowed only up to a certain number of watt hours.

In physics, energy is really measured in **joules**. One watt hour equals 3600 joules, because an hour has 3600 seconds. So a kilowatt hour is 3.6 million joules. In everyday life the watt hour is more practical, because you know the power of devices in watts and measure time in hours.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much energy is converted per unit of time, measured in watts.
The ability to do work, for example to move, heat or give light.
1000 watt hours, the usual unit on the electricity bill.
A device that measures how much electrical energy is used.

gewusst: With one kilowatt hour you can make about 50 to 70 cups of coffee.
A person on a bicycle generator needs several hours of hard pedalling for one kilowatt hour.
One watt hour is enough to charge a small part of a mobile phone battery.

teile.einleitung: A windmill is a building that uses the force of the wind to drive a machine. In the past, windmills ground grain into flour or pumped water out of low lying land. They are an early example of how people use energy from nature.
wichtigste: A typical old windmill has four sails.
The wind turns the sails, and a shaft carries the rotation inside.
In a mill, two millstones grind the grains into flour.
The person who works in a mill is called a miller.
There are particularly many old windmills in the Netherlands.
There, windmills also pumped water out of the low lying land.
If the wind comes from another direction, the sails have to be turned into the wind.

abschnitte.text: The wind presses against the angled **sails** and makes them turn. The sails are fixed to a thick **shaft**, which carries the rotation into the inside of the mill. Through wooden gearwheels the movement is redirected and passed on to the millstones. In this way the **kinetic energy** of the wind is turned into useful work.

In the mill there are two round **millstones**, one on top of the other. The lower one is fixed, the upper one turns. The grain trickles into the middle and is ground into **flour** between the stones. The miller made sure that the stones did not run empty and that the flour was fine enough.

For the mill to work, the sails must always face into the wind. With a **post mill**, the whole mill house is turned on a post. With a **tower mill**, only the cap with the sails at the top of the tower is turned. Later, small fantails were invented that turned the mill into the wind automatically.

In the Netherlands, a lot of land lies below sea level. There, for centuries, windmills pumped water out of the land into canals and so kept it dry. The 19 windmills of **Kinderdijk**, which are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, are famous. Windmills are therefore a symbol of that country.

The first windmills were probably built in Persia, where their sails turned horizontally. In Europe there have been windmills since about the 12th century. In Switzerland windmills were rare, because there were many streams and rivers and people mostly built **watermills**. With steam engines and electric motors, windmills lost their importance in the 19th and 20th centuries.

The modern successors of windmills are **wind turbines**. They usually have three slim rotor blades and produce electric current instead of flour. There are some such turbines in Switzerland too, for example in the Jura. But the basic idea is the same as hundreds of years ago.

begriffe.erklaerung: A heavy round stone that grinds grain into flour.
A thick rod that passes on a turning movement.
A windmill in which only the cap with the sails turns.
A modern machine that makes electric current from wind.

gewusst: In the story of Don Quixote, a knight thinks windmills are giants and fights them.
In the past, millers could send messages to the neighbours with the position of the sails, for example about a celebration.
Many families with the surname Müller (Miller) had ancestors who worked in a mill.

teile.einleitung: A submarine is a ship that can not only float at the surface, but also dive and travel under water. To do this it fills tanks with water or blows them empty again with compressed air. With the Swiss scientist Jacques Piccard, Switzerland even has a famous diving story.
wichtigste: Unlike an ordinary boat, a submarine can travel under water.
To dive, it takes water into its tanks.
To surface, it pushes the water out of the tanks with compressed air.
With a periscope you can look from the submerged boat over the water surface.
Submarines have very thick walls, because the water presses hard in the deep.
In 1960 Jacques Piccard dived to the deepest point of the sea in the “Trieste”.
At the 1964 Swiss National Exhibition a tourist submarine travelled in Lake Geneva.
A whale dives and surfaces in a similar way to a submarine and breathes air.

abschnitte.text: Whether something floats or sinks depends on **buoyancy**. A submarine has large **ballast tanks**, which are filled with air while it floats at the surface. If valves are opened, water flows in, the boat becomes heavier and dives. To surface, compressed air is blown into the tanks, the water is pushed out and the boat rises.

With every 10 metres of water depth the **water pressure** rises by about one bar, that is by the weight of the whole layer of air above us. At great depths the water therefore presses on every part of the hull with enormous force. That is why submarines have a very thick, strong pressure hull made of steel. Military submarines usually dive a few hundred metres deep.

With the **periscope** the crew can look over the water when they are just below the surface. At greater depths it is dark, and you can hardly see anything. That is why submarines locate other ships and obstacles with **sonar**, that is, with sound waves. They are driven by electric motors with batteries, diesel engines or, in large boats, a nuclear reactor.

As early as the 17th century the Dutchman Cornelis Drebbel built a simple diving boat with oars. In the 19th century the German Wilhelm Bauer designed the “Brandtaucher”. In the First and Second World Wars submarines became important warships. Today small submersibles are also used for research and for tourist trips.

The Swiss physicist Auguste Piccard developed the submersible **Trieste**. On 23 January 1960 his son **Jacques Piccard**, together with the American Don Walsh, dived into the Mariana Trench in the Pacific, almost 11,000 metres deep. At the Expo 64 national exhibition in Lausanne the tourist submarine “Auguste Piccard” then travelled in Lake Geneva. In this way tens of thousands of people were able to experience the underwater world of the lake.

Whales are mammals and have to come to the surface to breathe. Like a submarine, they dive, stay down for a while and surface again. Sperm whales can dive well over a thousand metres deep. Sonar also has a model in nature, because dolphins locate their prey with ultrasound.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tank that is filled with water for diving and with air for surfacing.
A long tube with mirrors for looking over the water surface.
A device that locates objects under water with sound.
The strong casing that protects the crew from the water pressure.
The force with which water pushes a body upwards.

gewusst: The German short form U-Boot stands for Unterseeboot, meaning undersea boat.
On their record dive Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh stayed at the bottom of the Mariana Trench for only about 20 minutes.
Large nuclear submarines can stay under water for months, because they make their own air and drinking water.

teile.einleitung: The principle of action and reaction is Newton's third law. It says: when one body exerts a force on another, the other exerts an equal and opposite force back. In short, people say “actio equals reactio”.
wichtigste: The principle of action and reaction is Newton's third law.
Every force is matched by an equal opposing force in the opposite direction.
It is summed up with the Latin words “actio equals reactio”.
Force and opposing force do not cancel out, because they act on different bodies.
Rockets move forwards by pushing gas out backwards.
If the Earth pulls an apple with 1 N, the apple also pulls the Earth with 1 N.

abschnitte.text: Forces always come in pairs. If you push against a wall with 20 newtons, the wall pushes back with 20 newtons. The two forces are equal in size but point in opposite directions. This is the **principle of action and reaction**, also called “actio equals reactio”, which means something like action equals counteraction.

In 1687 the English scientist **Isaac Newton** published his famous work on the foundations of mechanics. In it he set out three laws of motion. The first is the law of inertia, the second the law of force with the formula F = m · a. The third is the principle of action and reaction, on which the whole of **mechanics** is still built today.

abschnitte.titel: Why do they not cancel out?
abschnitte.text: Many people ask: if force and **opposing force** are equal, why does anything move at all? The answer: the two forces act on different bodies. The Earth pulls an apple with 1 N, and the apple pulls the Earth with 1 N. But because the Earth is enormously heavy, its movement cannot be noticed at all, whereas the apple falls.

A **rocket** pushes hot gases out backwards with great force. In return, the gases push the rocket forwards, which is why it works even in airless space. If someone jumps from a small boat onto the bank, the boat moves away from the bank. If two children on inline skates push off from each other, both roll apart, but the lighter one faster.

When swimming, you push water backwards and are pushed forwards as a result. When walking, your foot pushes the ground backwards, and the ground pushes you forwards. On black ice this works badly, because hardly any force is passed on. A balloon letting its air out also whizzes off because of **recoil**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that can move, slow down or change the shape of a body, measured in newtons.
The equal and opposite force that always belongs to a force.
Movement forwards because something is pushed out backwards.
The unit of force, named after Isaac Newton.

gewusst: When you jump up, you push the Earth down a tiny little bit.
Squid and jellyfish move by recoil, pushing water out.
A garden hose also jerks backwards if you suddenly turn the water on full.

teile.einleitung: The decay constant, written with the Greek letter λ (lambda), tells you how fast a radioactive substance decays. It is a kind of identifying number for each type of atom. The bigger it is, the faster the substance disappears.
wichtigste: The decay constant λ describes the probability that a nucleus decays per unit of time.
Its SI unit is 1/s, that is, “per second”.
Half life and decay constant are linked by T½ = ln 2 / λ.
A large decay constant means fast decay and a short half life.
The mean lifetime is τ = 1/λ.
The mean lifetime is about 1.44 times as long as the half life.
The activity of a sample is calculated with A = λ · N.

abschnitte.text: Every kind of radioactive atom, a so called **nuclide**, has its own decay constant. It tells you what proportion of the nuclei decays on average per unit of time. It is written with the letter **λ** (lambda). It appears in the law of radioactive decay N(t) = N₀ · e^(-λt) and decides how steeply the curve falls.

Between the decay constant and the **half life**: T½ = ln 2 / λ, where ln 2 is about 0.693. If a nuclide has λ = 0.0693 per year, its half life is 0.693 / 0.0693 = 10 years. The other way round, λ = ln 2 / T½. With a half life of 5 hours, this gives about 0.139 per hour.

The **activity** A of a sample is the number of decays per second. It comes from A = λ · N, that is, decay constant times number of nuclei. So a sample with 5 · 10⁹ nuclei and λ = 1 · 10⁻³ per second has an activity of 5 · 10⁶ becquerels. Substances with a large decay constant therefore radiate much more strongly for the same amount.

The **mean lifetime** τ tells you how long a nucleus exists on average before it decays. It is simply the reciprocal of the decay constant, τ = 1/λ. Because T½ = ln 2 · τ, the mean lifetime is about 1.44 times as long as the half life. After one mean lifetime, about 37 % of the sample is still left.

Carbon 14 has a half life of about 5730 years and therefore a very small decay constant. Iodine 131, which is used in medicine for thyroid diseases, has a half life of about 8 days. Uranium 238 decays extremely slowly; its half life is about 4.5 billion years, roughly the age of the Earth. For storing **radioactive waste**, it is important to know the decay constants of all the substances it contains.

begriffe.erklaerung: A type of atom with a particular number of protons and neutrons.
The Greek letter used to write the decay constant.
The average time a nucleus exists before it decays.
A mathematical operation that belongs with the exponential function; ln 2 is about 0.693.

gewusst: For a nuclide, the decay constant is practically unchangeable, whether the sample is hot, cold or under pressure.
For a single nucleus, the decay constant is a probability; it does not “age” and can decay at any time.
A nuclide with a large decay constant disappears quickly, but radiates particularly strongly during that time.

teile.einleitung: The xylophone is a musical instrument with wooden bars that you strike with beaters. Its name comes from Greek and means something like “wood sound”. It sounds bright and tapping and can be heard in many schools and orchestras.
wichtigste: The bars of a xylophone are made of wood.
It is played with beaters.
The shortest bar sounds highest, the longest lowest.
The xylophone is one of the percussion instruments.
Tubes under the bars of large xylophones make the sound louder.
A similar instrument with metal bars is called a metallophone.
The marimba is a large xylophone with a deep, soft sound.

abschnitte.text: The **xylophone** consists of wooden bars lying side by side on a frame. Each bar is tuned to a particular note. The bars are often arranged like the keys of a piano. The Greek word “xylon” means wood, and “phone” means sound or voice. It is one of the **percussion instruments**, more precisely one of the tuned bar instruments.

When you strike a bar, it starts to **vibrate**. It bends back and forth very fast and makes the air vibrate, which we hear as a note. A short bar vibrates faster and therefore sounds higher, a long bar slower and lower. Instrument makers tune the bars finely by sanding wood away from the underside. Under the bars of large instruments hang **resonator tubes**, which make the sound louder and last longer.

It is played with **beaters**, that is, sticks with a head at the end. Hard heads made of plastic or wood produce a bright, sharp sound. Beaters with a soft head of rubber or yarn sound softer. Professionals often hold two beaters in each hand and can play chords that way. Good bars are often made of hard tropical wood such as rosewood, cheaper models of plastic.

The **marimba** is a large, lower xylophone with a soft, warm sound. Its roots lie in Africa and Central America; in Guatemala it is a national instrument. Instruments with metal bars are called **metallophones**; they include the glockenspiel and the vibraphone. In Indonesia, gamelan orchestras play many metal and wooden instruments together. Similar wooden bar instruments have existed in Asia and Africa for centuries.

abschnitte.titel: At school and in the orchestra
abschnitte.text: In many Swiss schools, children learn their first tunes on xylophones and metallophones from the **Orff instruments**. On these instruments you can take off individual bars so that only the right notes are left. In the symphony orchestra, the xylophone is played in the percussion section. The composer Camille Saint-Saëns used it in “The Carnival of the Animals” to portray rattling fossils. It is also popular in jazz and film music.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tuned wooden bar that makes a note when it is struck.
A stick with a head used to strike bar instruments.
A tube under the bar that makes the note louder.
A bar instrument with metal bars instead of wooden ones.

gewusst: Saint-Saëns used the dry wooden sound of the xylophone to imitate rattling bones.
Many children's xylophones with colourful metal bars are actually metallophones.
A xylophone sounds shorter than a vibraphone, because wood damps the vibration faster.

teile.einleitung: Hydropower is energy obtained from flowing or falling water. Centuries ago, waterwheels already drove mills; today, large power stations use it to produce electricity. In Switzerland, hydropower is the most important source of electricity.
wichtigste: Hydropower is the name for energy produced by flowing water.
In hydroelectric power stations, water drives a turbine that turns a generator.
Hydropower is renewable, because the water cycle is driven by the Sun.
There are run of river power stations, storage power stations and pumped storage power stations.
In Switzerland, about 60 per cent of electricity comes from hydropower (as of around 2024).
The Grande Dixence dam in Valais is the highest gravity dam in the world.
But reservoirs and power stations also change rivers and habitats.

abschnitte.text: Water flowing downhill has energy of motion. Water in a high reservoir has **potential energy**, which is released when it falls down. This energy can be used to drive machines or to produce **electricity**. Because the Sun keeps evaporating water, which falls back as rain and snow, hydropower is a renewable energy.

abschnitte.titel: How does a power station work?
abschnitte.text: In the power station, water flows through a **turbine** and makes it turn. The turbine is connected to a **generator**, which turns the rotation into electricity. The higher the water falls from and the more water flows, the more electricity is produced. Well known types of turbine are the Pelton, the Francis and the Kaplan turbine.

**Run of river power stations** stand on rivers such as the Rhine or the Aare and use the constantly flowing water. **Storage power stations** collect water in reservoirs in the mountains and can supply electricity exactly when it is needed. Pumped storage power stations pump water upwards when there is spare electricity and let it flow down again later. They work like huge batteries.

Switzerland has many mountains, glaciers and lots of rain and snow, and is therefore also called the **water tower of Europe**. There are more than 600 larger hydroelectric power stations here. The Grande Dixence dam in Valais is 285 metres high, making it the highest gravity dam in the world. The Nant de Drance pumped storage power station in Valais, in operation since 2022, is one of the most powerful in Europe.

In ancient times, **waterwheels** already turned millstones for grinding grain. In the Middle Ages they drove saws, hammer mills and spinning mills, in many Swiss valleys too. Towards the end of the 19th century the first hydroelectric power stations for electricity were built. In the 20th century the big dams were built in the Alps, most of them between 1950 and 1970.

Hydropower supplies electricity with almost no **CO2** emissions and can be stored well. But reservoirs flood valleys, and power stations interrupt the natural course of rivers. Fish such as the lake trout can no longer migrate freely, so fish ladders are built. In addition, some streams below water intakes carry only a little water, which is why the law requires a **residual flow**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wheel with blades that is turned by the water.
A machine that makes electricity from rotation.
An artificial lake behind a dam that stores water.
Energy from sources that keep renewing themselves, such as water, sun or wind.
The water that must stay in the stream below a power station.

gewusst: The Grande Dixence dam weighs about 15 million tonnes, more than the Great Pyramid of Giza in Egypt.
A large part of the electricity for SBB trains comes from the railway's own hydroelectric power stations.
The largest hydroelectric power station in the world is the Three Gorges Dam in China.

teile.einleitung: Alkynes are hydrocarbons with at least one triple bond between two carbon atoms. The best known example is ethyne, also called acetylene. With its extremely hot flame, metal can be welded and cut.
wichtigste: Alkynes contain at least one C≡C triple bond.
Alkynes with one triple bond have the general molecular formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂.
The simplest alkyne is ethyne, also called acetylene.
Propyne has the molecular formula C₃H₄.
At the triple bond, the carbon atoms are sp hybridised and the molecule is linear there, at 180°.
Ethyne is obtained from calcium carbide and water.
Ethyne is used with oxygen to weld and cut metal.

abschnitte.text: Alkynes are hydrocarbons, that is, compounds made only of carbon and hydrogen. Their distinguishing feature is a **triple bond** between two carbon atoms, written C≡C. Like the alkenes, they belong to the unsaturated hydrocarbons. Their names end in -yne, for example ethyne, propyne and butyne.

The carbon atoms at the triple bond are **sp hybridised**. As a result, they lie in a straight line with their direct neighbouring atoms, and the bond angle is 180°. The ethyne molecule H-C≡C-H is therefore completely straight. The triple bond is shorter and stronger than a double or single bond, but also very reactive.

**Ethyne** burns with pure oxygen to give a flame of more than 3000 °C. This flame is used in **oxyacetylene welding** to melt, join or cut steel. But pure, compressed ethyne can decompose explosively. That is why in gas cylinders it is dissolved in acetone held in a porous mass.

Ethyne is formed when **calcium carbide**, a grey solid, reacts with water. In a carbide lamp, water drips onto calcium carbide, and the gas produced burns with a bright flame. Such lamps were once used by miners, cavers and cyclists. Calcium carbide was also made in Switzerland, because a lot of electricity from hydropower is needed to make it.

Ethyne was discovered in 1836 by the English chemist Edmund Davy, and the name acetylene was later coined by the Frenchman Marcellin Berthelot. Around 1900, acetylene lamps lit up streets and houses. Today ethyne is a starting material for plastics and other chemicals. In nature, some alkynes occur in plants and fungi.

begriffe.erklaerung: Three shared pairs of electrons between two atoms.
A molecule with double or triple bonds that can still add on atoms.
An old name for ethyne that is still in use.
A model of how an atom's electron orbitals mix to form bonds.
A formula that shows how many atoms of each kind a molecule has.

gewusst: The flame of ethyne and oxygen is one of the hottest flames that can be produced with a fuel gas.
In pure form ethyne has almost no smell; the typical garlic smell comes from impurities in the carbide.
In some areas, people used to fire loud “carbide cannons” at celebrations, using carbide and water.

teile.einleitung: The enthalpy of vaporisation, also called the heat of vaporisation, is the energy needed to turn a liquid into a gas. Water needs an unusually large amount of energy for this, more than almost any other substance. This explains why sweating cools you down and why steam scalds so badly.
wichtigste: The enthalpy of vaporisation is the energy needed to vaporise a liquid.
Among common substances, water has the greatest specific heat of vaporisation.
The reason for this is the hydrogen bonds between water molecules.
The heat of vaporisation of water is about 7 times as big as its heat of fusion.
At the same temperature the heat of condensation is just as big as the heat of vaporisation.
As the temperature rises, the enthalpy of vaporisation decreases.
According to Trouton's rule, the molar entropy of vaporisation of many liquids is about 88 J/(mol K).

abschnitte.text: When a liquid vaporises, its particles have to tear themselves away from each other. This needs energy, which is called the **enthalpy of vaporisation**. If it is given per kilogram, it is called the **specific heat of vaporisation**. For water at 100 °C it is about 2260 kJ per kilogram.

Water molecules hold together strongly through **hydrogen bonds**. That is why much more energy is needed to separate them than with similarly small molecules. Water therefore has one of the greatest heats of vaporisation of all substances. For comparison, it is about 7 times as big as the heat of fusion that you need to melt ice.

When steam condenses back into liquid, exactly the same energy is released, the **heat of condensation**. That is why steam at 100 °C scalds the skin much worse than water at 100 °C. The heat released also plays a part in the weather. When water vapour condenses in thunderclouds, so much heat is released that the air rises even more strongly.

The enthalpy of vaporisation is not always the same size; it decreases as the temperature rises. At skin temperature it is about 2400 kJ/kg for water, so higher than at 100 °C. At the so-called **critical point** it even becomes zero; there is no longer any difference between liquid and gas there. Trouton's rule says that many liquids have a similar entropy of vaporisation of about 88 J/(mol K) at their boiling point; water is above this because of the hydrogen bonds.

The body uses the large heat of vaporisation to cool down. If a runner evaporates 0.5 kg of sweat, this takes about 1.2 MJ of heat from her body. That is as much energy as you need to warm about four litres of water by 70 degrees. Fridges also use this principle: a **refrigerant** vaporises inside and takes in heat as it does so.

begriffe.erklaerung: A technical word for the heat energy involved in a process.
An attraction between water molecules that holds them together.
The energy needed to melt a solid substance.
A substance in a fridge that cools by vaporising.
The state beyond which liquid and gas can no longer be told apart.

gewusst: With the energy needed to vaporise one litre of water, you could heat the same litre from 0 to 100 °C more than five times.
A large part of the solar energy that reaches the Earth is used up in evaporating seawater.
Dogs hardly sweat and cool themselves down by panting instead, that is, by evaporation on their tongue.

teile.einleitung: Water vapour is water in the form of a gas. It forms when water boils or evaporates. Pure water vapour is actually invisible; the white clouds above a saucepan are tiny droplets of water.
wichtigste: Water vapour is water as a gas.
Real water vapour is invisible; visible clouds of steam are made of little droplets.
Warm vapour rises because it is lighter than the air.
Hot steam can scald the skin.
Steam pushes up the lid of a saucepan and makes a whistling kettle whistle.
With steam you can iron, clean, cook vegetables and froth up milk.
Steam engines changed the world in the 18th and 19th centuries.

abschnitte.text: When water is heated strongly, its particles move so fast that they break away from each other. **Water vapour** forms, an invisible gas. When the vapour cools in the air, tiny droplets form and we see white clouds of steam. This change from gas to liquid is called **condensation**, and this is also how clouds and fog form.

One litre of water makes more than a thousand litres of steam. That is why steam pushes up the lid of a saucepan, which then rattles. In a **whistling kettle**, the steam forces its way through a narrow opening and makes a whistling sound. Warm steam is lighter than the surrounding air and therefore rises.

Hot steam can **scald** the skin. When steam condenses on the skin, it also gives off a lot of heat, which is why it is often more dangerous than water at the same temperature. So always open a saucepan lid away from you. You should also not hold your hands or face over a kettle.

In the kitchen you can cook vegetables gently over steam, which keeps the vitamins in better. A steam iron uses hot steam to get creases out of clothes. A steam cleaner cleans floors and tiles without cleaning products. Coffee machines froth up milk with hot steam, and in a **sauna** hot steam forms when you pour water onto the hot stones.

In the 18th century the Scotsman James Watt greatly improved the **steam engine**. It powered factories, locomotives and ships and set off industrialisation. In Switzerland, historic paddle steamers still sail on lakes such as Lake Lucerne and Lake Geneva today. The Brienz Rothorn Railway also climbs the mountain with steam locomotives.

The air always contains some water vapour; this is called **humidity**. Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air. When moist air cools down, clouds, fog or dew form. Water vapour is also an important greenhouse gas that keeps the Earth warm.

begriffe.erklaerung: The change from gas to liquid, for example when steam turns into droplets.
A slow change from liquid to gas, even without boiling.
An injury to the skin caused by hot water or hot steam.
The amount of water vapour contained in the air.

gewusst: Right above the spout of a boiling kettle there is a small clear area; that is where the real, invisible steam is.
A bathroom mirror mists up because water vapour condenses on the cool glass.
The white trails behind aeroplanes are made of frozen water vapour from the engines.

teile.einleitung: Alkanols are alcohols derived from the alkanes, that is, from simple hydrocarbon chains. They carry one or more hydroxyl groups -OH. Well known examples are methanol, ethanol and glycerol.
wichtigste: Alkanols are alkanes in which one hydrogen atom is replaced by an OH group.
Their names end in -ol, for example ethanol or propan-2-ol.
Depending on the position of the OH group, there are primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols.
Propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol.
Because of hydrogen bonds, alkanols boil at much higher temperatures than alkanes of the same weight.
As the chain length increases, their solubility in water decreases.
Methanol is very poisonous and can cause blindness.

abschnitte.text: In theory, alkanols are formed when a hydrogen atom in an **alkane** is replaced by a **hydroxyl group** -OH. Their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH. They are named after the alkane with the ending -ol: methane becomes methanol, ethane becomes ethanol. With longer chains, a number shows on which carbon atom the OH group sits, as in propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol.

If only one other carbon atom is attached to the carbon atom with the OH group, it is a **primary** alcohol such as ethanol. With two neighbours it is a secondary alcohol such as propan-2-ol, and with three a tertiary one such as 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Primary alcohols can be oxidised to aldehydes, secondary ones to ketones. Tertiary alcohols can hardly be oxidised by mild oxidising agents, because there is no hydrogen atom on their carbon atom with the OH group.

The OH group can form **hydrogen bonds** with other molecules. That is why ethanol boils only at 78 °C, while propane, which weighs about the same, boils at −42 °C. Short alkanols such as methanol and ethanol mix with water in any proportion. The longer the carbon chain, the more the molecule behaves like a fat, and the solubility in water decreases.

Some alkanols carry several OH groups; they are called **polyhydric alcohols**. Ethane-1,2-diol, also called ethylene glycol, is used as antifreeze in car radiators. **Glycerol** is called propane-1,2,3-triol by IUPAC and has three OH groups. It is a component of fats and is used in creams, soaps and toothpaste.

**Ethanol** is the alcohol in drinks, but it is also used as a disinfectant, solvent and fuel. Methanol is an important industrial raw material but very poisonous: in the body it is turned into substances that damage the optic nerves and can cause blindness. Propan-2-ol, also called isopropanol, is found in cleaning products and disinfectants. With sodium, ethanol reacts to form sodium ethoxide and hydrogen, similarly to water, only more slowly.

begriffe.erklaerung: The group of atoms -OH made of oxygen and hydrogen.
A hydrocarbon with only single bonds, such as methane or propane.
An attraction between molecules through a hydrogen atom.
An alcohol with several OH groups in the molecule.

gewusst: Methylated spirit contains ethanol that has been made undrinkable with additives.
Glycerol tastes sweet; its name comes from the Greek word for “sweet”.
Because ethanol becomes solid only at about −114 °C, it is used in thermometers for very cold temperatures.

teile.einleitung: Vaporisation is the name for the change of a substance from the liquid to the gaseous state. It happens when water boils, just as it does with a puddle that slowly disappears in the sun. It needs a surprising amount of energy, and a little water turns into a great deal of steam.
wichtigste: The change from liquid to gas is called vaporisation.
Evaporation happens below the boiling point at the surface, whereas boiling happens throughout the whole container.
A cloth that is spread out dries faster because its surface is bigger.
To vaporise 1 kg of water at 100 °C completely, about 2260 kJ is needed.
At 100 °C water turns into steam with a volume about 1700 times bigger.
Hot steam scalds worse than water at the same temperature, because it gives off a lot of heat when it condenses.
The Swiss salt works produce table salt by evaporating the water from brine.

abschnitte.text: In a liquid the particles are always moving and loosely holding together. If they get enough energy, they break free and fly off as a **gas**. This change is called **vaporisation**. The opposite way, from gas back to liquid, is called condensation.

There are two kinds of vaporisation. In **evaporation** only single particles escape at the surface, and this happens even below the boiling point, for example with a puddle. In **boiling** bubbles of steam form throughout the whole pan, rise and burst at the surface. At sea level water boils at 100 °C; on high mountains it boils below 90 °C because of the lower air pressure.

To vaporise 1 kg of water at 100 °C completely, about 2260 kJ is needed. That is more than five times as much energy as you need to heat the same water from 0 °C to 100 °C. While the water is boiling, its temperature does not rise any further; all the energy goes into vaporising. This energy is called the **heat of vaporisation**.

When water turns into steam at 100 °C, its volume becomes about 1700 times bigger. So one litre of water makes about 1700 litres of steam. In the past this enormous expansion drove the **steam engines** of locomotives and ships. Today steam turns the turbines in many power stations.

Deep below Switzerland there are layers of salt from a prehistoric sea. The **Swiss salt works** pump water down, which dissolves the salt, and bring this **brine** back up. Then they evaporate the water in large plants, and the salt is left behind. There are salt works, for example, at Riburg and Schweizerhalle on the Rhine and at Bex in the canton of Vaud.

Hot steam scalds the skin worse than water at the same temperature. When the steam condenses on the skin, it gives off all of its heat of vaporisation again. That is why you should lift the lid of a cooking pot away from yourself when you open it. With a pressure cooker, too, you have to wait until the pressure has been released.

begriffe.erklaerung: The temperature at which a liquid starts to boil everywhere.
The change from gas to liquid.
The energy needed for vaporisation.
Water with a lot of dissolved salt.

gewusst: The visible white steam above a cooking pot actually consists of tiny water droplets; real water vapour is invisible.
At the summit of Mount Everest water boils at only about 70 °C.
In a pressure cooker water only boils above 100 °C, which is why food cooks faster.

teile.einleitung: Alkenes are hydrocarbons with at least one double bond between two carbon atoms. Because of this double bond they are much more reactive than alkanes. The best known alkene is ethene, from which the plastic polyethylene is made and which makes fruit ripen.
wichtigste: Alkenes with one double bond have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ.
A C=C double bond consists of a σ bond and a π bond.
The alkene CH₂=CH-CH₃ is called propene.
In plants, ethene acts as a hormone for the ripening of fruit.
With hydrogen and a nickel catalyst, an alkene becomes an alkane.
Ethene and water give ethanol.
Baeyer's test shows double bonds when violet potassium permanganate loses its colour.

abschnitte.text: Alkenes are **unsaturated** hydrocarbons: at least two carbon atoms are joined by a **double bond**. With one double bond, their formula is CₙH₂ₙ. Their names end in “-ene”, such as ethene, propene and butene. Ethene has the formula C₂H₄, and propene is written CH₂=CH-CH₃.

A double bond consists of two different parts: a stable **σ bond** directly between the atoms and a **π bond** above and below it. The π bond is weaker and easy to attack. That is why alkenes readily react with other substances. In addition, the molecule cannot rotate freely about the double bond, which is why there are cis and trans forms.

Alkenes react most often by **addition**. With hydrogen and a nickel catalyst an alkane is formed, and with water, ethene gives ethanol. With hydrogen bromide and propene, **Markovnikov's rule** applies: the hydrogen goes to the carbon atom with more hydrogen atoms. Double bonds can be detected with bromine water or with **Baeyer's test**, in which violet potassium permanganate loses its colour.

Ethene is a natural **plant hormone**. Ripe apples and bananas give it off, and it makes other fruit ripen faster. That is why a green banana placed next to a ripe apple turns yellow faster. In the trade, bananas are ripened in a controlled way in special **ripening rooms** with ethene.

Ethene and propene are among the most important basic materials of the chemical industry. Through **polymerisation** they are made into polyethylene and polypropylene, from which films, packaging and toys are made. The alkenes are obtained mainly by splitting components of crude oil, which is called **cracking**. Solvents and antifreeze are also made from ethene.

Alkenes with two double bonds are called **dienes**. The diene **isoprene**, chemically 2-methylbuta-1,3-diene, is the building block of natural rubber. Rubber is obtained from the milky sap of the rubber tree and processed into rubber goods, for example tyres. The scents of many plants, such as the limonene in lemon peel, are also built from isoprene units.

begriffe.erklaerung: A molecule with a double or triple bond to which more atoms can still be added.
The weaker part of a double bond, which reacts easily.
Splitting long hydrocarbons into shorter molecules.
A molecule with two double bonds.

gewusst: A single ripe banana in the fruit bowl can make the other fruit ripen faster.
Ethene is one of the most produced organic chemicals in the world.
The orange colour of carrots comes from carotene, a molecule with many double bonds.

teile.einleitung: Wind energy is energy obtained from the force of the wind with large wind turbines. The rotor blades turn in the wind and drive a generator that produces electricity. Wind energy is renewable and is one of the fastest growing sources of electricity worldwide.
wichtigste: Wind energy is the name for energy obtained from the wind with wind turbines.
The wind turns the rotor blades, and a generator turns this into electricity.
Wind energy is renewable and causes no CO2 while running.
If the wind blows twice as fast, a wind turbine delivers about eight times as much power.
Wind farms at sea are called offshore wind farms.
The largest wind farm in Switzerland is on Mont Crosin in the Bernese Jura.
In Switzerland, wind energy so far supplies only a very small share of electricity.

abschnitte.text: Wind is moving air and therefore has **kinetic energy**. It arises because the Sun warms the Earth unevenly, creating differences in air pressure. With **wind turbines**, this energy is turned into electricity. Because new wind keeps blowing, wind energy counts as a renewable energy.

abschnitte.titel: How does a wind turbine work?
abschnitte.text: Modern wind turbines usually have three long **rotor blades** on a tall tower. The wind flows past the blades and sets them turning, much as with an aircraft wing. In the nacelle at the top of the tower, the rotation is passed on to a **generator**. A control system automatically turns the nacelle into the wind and stops the turbine in a storm.

The power depends greatly on the **wind speed**: if the wind blows twice as fast, a wind turbine delivers about eight times as much power. That is why wind turbines are built tall and in windy places such as coasts, hills and passes. Large turbines on land have rotors more than 100 metres across. At sea, in **offshore wind farms**, there are even bigger turbines, because the wind there is stronger and steadier.

More than a thousand years ago, people in Persia were already using windmills to grind grain. In Europe, **windmills** shaped the landscape from the Middle Ages onwards, especially in the Netherlands, where they also pumped water away. Sailing ships had been using the wind for thousands of years. Modern wind turbines for producing electricity spread from the 1980s, above all in Denmark.

In Switzerland, wind turbines so far supply well under one per cent of electricity. The largest wind farm is on **Mont Crosin** in the Bernese Jura. There are other turbines, for example, on the Gotthard Pass and near Andermatt in the canton of Uri. Especially in winter there is often a lot of wind, exactly when solar panels supply little electricity.

Wind turbines produce electricity without **CO2** emissions and without fuel. But they supply electricity only when the wind blows, so storage and other power stations are needed as well. Some people are bothered by how they look in the landscape or by the noise. In addition, birds and bats have to be protected, for example by switching turbines off at certain times.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the long blades of a wind turbine that turn in the wind.
The housing at the top of the tower that holds the generator.
Several wind turbines standing together in one place.
On the open sea, off the coast.

gewusst: The tips of the rotor blades of large wind turbines turn at more than 200 kilometres per hour.
By the laws of physics, a wind turbine can use at most just under 60 per cent of the wind's energy.
The wind turbines on the Gütsch above Andermatt are among the highest in Europe.

teile.einleitung: The wavelength tells you how long a single wave is. It is the distance from one crest to the next crest. Whether water waves, sound or light: all waves have a wavelength, and it decides, for example, how high a note sounds or what colour a light is.
wichtigste: The wavelength is the distance between two neighbouring points in the same phase, for example from crest to crest.
It is written with the Greek letter lambda (λ) and measured in metres.
The formula is: speed of propagation equals wavelength times frequency.
If you double the frequency at the same speed, the wavelength halves.
Low notes have long waves, high notes short waves.
With light, the wavelength decides the colour.
The quantity 2π divided by the wavelength is called the angular wavenumber.

abschnitte.text: If you throw a stone into water, waves with crests and troughs spread out. The distance from one **crest** to the next is the wavelength. To be precise, it is the distance between two neighbouring points that are in the same state of vibration at that moment, that is, in the same **phase**. You can also measure from trough to trough; the result is the same.

Wavelength, frequency and speed are firmly linked: c = λ · f. The **frequency** f tells you how often a wave passes each second, measured in hertz. Sound travels in air at about 343 metres per second, so a note of 686 hertz has a wavelength of 0.5 metres. A water wave travelling at 2 metres per second with a **period** of 3 seconds is 6 metres long. If a source vibrates 10 times a second and the crests are 3 centimetres apart, the waves travel at 0.3 metres per second.

With sound, the wavelength decides the **pitch**. A very low note of 20 hertz has a wavelength in air of about 17 metres, while a note of 1000 hertz has only 0.343 metres. That is why the bass pipes of an organ are much longer than the pipes for high notes. In hospital, **ultrasound** of 5 megahertz is used, which has waves only about 0.31 millimetres long in body tissue and can therefore show fine details.

Light is an electromagnetic wave with tiny wavelengths. **Visible light** ranges from about 380 nanometres for violet to about 780 nanometres for red. A nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre. Ultraviolet and X-rays have even shorter waves; infrared, microwaves and radio waves have longer ones.

The aerials of radios and mobile phones are often built to suit the wavelength they are meant to receive. The size of a **microwave** in the kitchen appliance, about 12 centimetres, also decides how the food is heated. Experts also calculate with the **angular wavenumber**, which is 2π divided by the wavelength. It makes many formulas in physics easier.

begriffe.erklaerung: How often something vibrates each second, measured in hertz (Hz).
The exact state of a vibration, for example right at the top of the crest or down in the trough.
The Greek letter λ, the symbol for wavelength.
Sound with such a high frequency that people cannot hear it.

gewusst: Radio waves for long wave transmitters can be several kilometres long.
The lowest note people can hear has a wave in air as long as a bus.
Bats find their way with ultrasound, whose waves are only a few millimetres long.

teile.einleitung: Thermal insulation makes sure that as little heat as possible escapes from a house in winter. Thick layers of insulating material in the walls, roof and floor work like a warm jumper for the building. This saves heating energy and money and protects the climate.
wichtigste: Thermal insulation slows down the flow of heat through walls, roof, windows and floor.
Good insulating materials trap a lot of air in small pores.
A small U-value means that a part of the building lets little heat through.
The U-value is given in watts per square metre and kelvin.
Places where heat escapes especially quickly are called thermal bridges.
Insulating materials must stay dry, because wet insulation conducts heat much better.
In summer good insulation keeps the house cool for longer.
In Switzerland the Buildings Programme of the Confederation and the cantons supports insulation in renovations.

abschnitte.text: Heat always flows from warm to cold, so in winter from inside to outside. **Thermal insulation** slows down this flow. To do this, insulating materials are fitted to façades, under the roof, in the cellar floor and in window frames. In badly insulated old houses a lot of heat is lost. Well insulated houses often need only a fraction of the heating energy.

Still **air** conducts heat very poorly. Insulating materials such as polystyrene or **rock wool** trap countless small air bubbles in which the air cannot move. Concrete conducts heat about fifty times better than a good insulating material. If an insulating material gets wet, water fills the pores, and water conducts heat much better than air. That is why insulation must always stay dry.

There are artificial insulating materials such as **polystyrene**, often known by the brand name Styrofoam, glass wool and rock wool. There are also natural products such as sheep's wool, wood fibres, cork, hemp and cellulose from waste paper. Straw bales are sometimes used for building too. In windows two or three panes of glass with a layer of gas between them provide insulation. Every material has advantages and disadvantages in price, fire protection and the environment.

The **U-value** shows how much heat flows through one square metre of a part of a building when there is a difference of one degree between inside and outside. Its unit is watts per square metre and kelvin. The smaller the U-value, the better the part insulates. A **thermal bridge** is a weak point, for example a concrete balcony slab that reaches from inside to outside. There the wall is colder on the inside, and mould can form.

In Switzerland a large part of energy use goes on heating buildings. That is why the Confederation and the cantons support renovations with the **Buildings Programme**. Anyone who insulates their façade, roof or windows better can get money back. The Swiss building standard **Minergie** stands for especially economical, well insulated houses. In summer insulation also protects against heat, and the house stays cool for longer.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material that passes on heat only very poorly.
A number that shows how much heat flows through a part of a building.
A place where heat flows out especially quickly.
The modernising of an old building.

gewusst: Polar bears and sheep use the same principle as insulating materials: their fur traps air.
With a thermal imaging camera you can see where heat escapes from a house; it glows red or yellow there.

teile.einleitung: Water pressure is the pressure that water exerts through its own weight on everything inside it. The deeper you dive, the harder the water presses. That is why dams, submarines and divers need special protection.
wichtigste: Water pressure comes from the weight of the water above a point.
For every 10 m of water depth, about 1 bar of pressure is added to the air pressure.
The pressure depends on the height of the water, not on the shape or size of the container.
Water presses equally hard from all sides, including from below and from the side.
Water pressure is greatest at the bottom of a lake.
In the salty sea the pressure is slightly higher than in a mountain lake, because salt water is heavier.
Water towers and reservoirs stand high up so that the water flows into houses with enough pressure.

abschnitte.text: Water has weight: one litre weighs about one kilogram. The more water lies above a point, the more heavily it presses on it. That is why **hydrostatic pressure** rises steadily with depth. At a depth of 10 m the water presses with about 100,000 newtons on every square metre, which is the weight of around 10 tonnes. Pressure is measured in **bar** or pascals.

If you make three holes one above the other in a plastic bottle and fill it with water, it squirts out most strongly and furthest from the lowest hole. That is where the column of water above it is highest. If you squeeze a filled water bag with a hole in it, the water squirts out harder, because the pressure spreads everywhere in the water. The **hydrostatic paradox** is surprising: at the same water height, the pressure on the bottom is the same, whether the container is wide or narrow.

Dams are much thicker at the bottom than at the top, because the pressure is greatest at the bottom of the reservoir. A **gravity dam** such as the Grande Dixence in Valais holds back the water by its enormous own weight. The water supply uses pressure too: reservoirs are often on a hill above the village. That way the water flows into the houses without any pump. On the ground floor it usually comes out of the tap with more pressure than on the top floor.

When diving, you feel the water pressure in your ears after only a few metres. Divers have to **equalise** the pressure so that their eardrums do not hurt. At a depth of 25 m, about 2.5 bar is added to the air pressure, making about 3.5 bar in total. Anyone surfacing from a great depth has to rise slowly so that the body can get used to the falling pressure.

At the deepest point of the ocean, in the Mariana Trench, the pressure is more than 1000 bar. That is like a car standing on each of your fingernails. **Submarines** therefore have very thick, strong walls. The Swiss scientist **Auguste Piccard** developed the bathyscaphe Trieste, in which his son Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh dived almost 11 km down to the bottom of the Mariana Trench in 1960. Deep sea fish survive there because their bodies contain hardly any air.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which water presses on a surface because of its weight.
A unit of pressure; air pressure at sea level is about 1 bar.
Pressure in still water, which increases with depth.
Balancing the pressure in your ears when diving.
A water store, often high up, for the drinking water supply.

gewusst: A diver at a depth of 10 m bears twice as much pressure as at the surface.
A polystyrene cup taken into the deep sea on a diving robot comes back up squashed tiny.
The Swiss Auguste Piccard first flew in a balloon into the stratosphere and then built submersibles for the deep sea.

teile.einleitung: Waste separation means sorting rubbish by type, for example paper, glass, metal, PET or green waste. In this way many materials can be reused instead of being burnt. Switzerland is one of the countries that collect and recycle a particularly large amount of waste, but it also produces a lot of it.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, ordinary household rubbish goes into the rubbish bag.
In many municipalities the rubbish bag costs extra, so that people make less waste.
The contents of the rubbish bag are burnt in a waste incineration plant (KVA).
Burning the rubbish produces heat and electricity.
Tin cans belong in the metal collection, and aluminium coffee capsules in the aluminium or capsule collection.
Clothes in good condition go into the clothing collection.
Anyone who simply throws rubbish on the ground is littering.

abschnitte.text: When separating, you sort rubbish into **recyclable materials**. Paper, cardboard, glass, metal, PET bottles, batteries and green waste are collected separately. New products are made from them; this is called **recycling**. This saves raw materials, energy and space.

Whatever cannot be reused goes into the **rubbish bag**. In many Swiss municipalities you have to pay a fee for each bag, either when you buy the official bag or with a sticker. This principle is called the **polluter pays principle**: whoever makes more rubbish pays more. It is meant to encourage people to avoid waste and to separate it better.

In Switzerland, the contents of rubbish bags are not dumped in landfill but burnt in a **waste incineration plant**, KVA for short. There are about 30 of them across the country. Burning produces heat, which is used to generate electricity and to heat houses through **district heating**. Metals are also recovered from the slag that is left over.

Empty tin cans belong in the **metal collection**, and aluminium cans and aluminium coffee capsules in the aluminium or capsule collection. Glass bottles are taken to the bottle bank, sorted by colour. PET drinks bottles are returned to the shop, and all shops that sell batteries must take them back. Clothes in good condition go into the **clothing collection**, where they are used again.

Even better than separating waste is not making any. Your own **water bottle** instead of lots of disposable bottles helps a great deal. Using shopping bags several times, repairing things and avoiding food waste also cut down rubbish. In Switzerland, each person produces about 700 kilograms of municipal waste a year (as of around 2020), and about half of it is collected and recycled.

Anyone who simply throws rubbish on the ground or in the grass is **littering**. Discarded cans, cigarette ends and packaging pollute streets, lakes and meadows. Animals can injure themselves on bits of plastic or eat them. In many cantons there are fines for this, and municipalities organise clean up days, in which school classes help too.

begriffe.erklaerung: New products are made from used materials.
A waste incineration plant, where rubbish is burnt and energy is produced.
Plant waste such as vegetable peelings, leaves and grass cuttings.
Carelessly leaving rubbish lying around or throwing it away.

gewusst: In biogas plants, gas and electricity can be produced from green waste.
Glass can be melted down and reshaped almost any number of times.
In nature, depending on the weather, a banana skin often takes months to rot away completely.

teile.einleitung: The International Prototype of the Kilogram is a small metal cylinder near Paris. For more than 100 years it set exactly how heavy a kilogram is. Since 2019 it is no longer needed for this, because today the kilogram is defined using a constant of nature.
wichtigste: The prototype kilogram is made of platinum and iridium.
From 1889 it set the unit of mass, the kilogram, for the whole world.
It is kept under three glass bell jars.
Originally the kilogram had been defined as the mass of one litre of water.
Since 2019 the kilogram has been based on the Planck constant.
With a Kibble balance you can determine the kilogram using this constant of nature.
Many countries, including Switzerland, owned exact copies of the prototype kilogram.

abschnitte.text: The prototype kilogram is a cylinder about the size of a table tennis ball, made of an **alloy** of 90 per cent platinum and 10 per cent iridium. Its height and diameter are each about 39 millimetres. This mixture of metals is very hard, does not rust and hardly changes. That is why it was well suited as a **standard**, that is, as a reference piece for all other weights.

The prototype kilogram is kept at the **International Bureau of Weights and Measures** in Sèvres near Paris. It sits in a safe under three glass bell jars placed one inside the other. Only rarely was it taken out to compare the copies of the individual countries with it. In Switzerland today the Federal Institute of Metrology, **METAS**, in Bern-Wabern is responsible for exact measures.

After the French Revolution, in 1795, the kilogram was defined as the mass of one litre of water. But water has a different density depending on its temperature, which made the measurement inaccurate. That is why in 1889, at the first **General Conference on Weights and Measures**, it was decided to use a piece of metal as the standard. The countries received exact copies, so-called national prototypes.

Comparisons showed that the prototype kilogram and its copies were no longer quite the same weight. Over 100 years the difference was about 50 micrograms, which is less than a grain of sand. For science, however, this was still too inaccurate. An object can always change a little, for example through dust or cleaning.

Since 20 May 2019 the kilogram has been defined by the **Planck constant**, an unchanging constant of nature. With a **Kibble balance** the weight of a body is compared with an electromagnetic force that can be measured exactly. In this way any well-equipped laboratory in the world can determine the kilogram itself. The prototype kilogram is now a valuable exhibit of history.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much matter a body contains, measured in kilograms.
A number in nature that never changes.
A very accurate balance that compares weight with an electric force.
A mixture of different metals.

gewusst: For a long time the prototype kilogram was the last measure in the world based on a real object.
Anyone who touched the prototype kilogram had to wear gloves and use special tweezers.
The small cylinder would fit easily into a closed hand.

teile.einleitung: The fire triangle shows which three things a fire needs to burn: fuel, oxygen and enough heat. If just one of these ingredients is missing, the fire goes out. Every way of putting out a fire is based on this.
wichtigste: A fire needs fuel, oxygen and enough heat.
Together the three conditions form the fire triangle.
If one side of the triangle is missing, the fire goes out.
Water puts out a fire mainly by cooling it down.
A fire blanket takes the oxygen away from the fire.
You must never put out burning oil or fat with water.
In Switzerland you can reach the fire brigade on the number 118.

abschnitte.text: The fire triangle is a simple model with three sides. The first side is the **fuel**, something that can burn, such as wood, paper, gas or petrol. The second side is the **oxygen** from the air. The third side is the **ignition temperature**, that is, enough heat for the fuel to start burning. Only when all three come together does a fire start.

A piece of wood lies in the air and still does not burn by itself. Only when it is strongly heated does it start to burn. Every substance has its own **ignition temperature**: paper catches fire at just over 200 degrees Celsius, other substances need much more. A match provides the heat to start with; after that the fire keeps itself alive with its own heat.

To put out a fire, you take one side of the triangle away. With **water** you cool the fuel below its ignition temperature. With a **fire blanket**, sand or foam the fire is smothered, because no more oxygen can reach it. In forest fires the fire brigade sometimes cuts firebreaks so that the fire runs out of fuel. Turning off a gas tap also takes the fuel away from the fire.

If oil is burning in a pan in the kitchen, you must **never pour water** on it. The water turns into steam in a flash and carries burning fat with it, creating a dangerous jet of flame. The right thing to do is to put a lid on the pan or use a fire blanket and switch off the cooker. Then the fire has no oxygen.

In Switzerland you call the emergency number **118** if there is a fire. In many municipalities the fire brigades are made up of volunteers, and in big cities there are also professional fire brigades. Many houses have **smoke alarms**, which give an early warning. The important thing is: in a fire, first get yourself to safety, then raise the alarm.

Experts sometimes extend the triangle to a **fire tetrahedron**, with four sides. The fourth condition is the chemical **chain reaction** that keeps the fire going. Some extinguishing powders interrupt exactly this reaction. For everyday life, though, the triangle is enough to understand how fire starts and how it is put out.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that can burn, for example wood, paper or gas.
The temperature at which a substance starts to burn by itself.
A fireproof blanket used to smother small fires.
A sudden, very large flame that shoots up dangerously high.

gewusst: Even a cup of water on burning fat can produce a jet of flame metres high.
A candle under an upturned glass goes out because it runs out of oxygen.
Blowing puts out a candle because it blows the flame away and cools the wick.

teile.einleitung: Centrifugal force is the force you feel when you are swung round in a circle. It pushes outwards, for example on a roundabout or in a car on a tight bend. In physics it is a so called fictitious force, which appears only from the point of view of someone who is turning along with the motion.
wichtigste: Centrifugal force acts outwards in a rotation, away from the centre.
It depends on the mass, the speed and the radius of the bend.
If you go through the same bend twice as fast, the centrifugal force becomes four times as great.
The tighter the bend at the same speed, the greater the centrifugal force.
It is a fictitious force that only an observer turning along with the motion feels.
Seen from outside, the centripetal force keeps a body on its circular path.
Salad spinners, spin dryers and centrifuges use centrifugal force.

abschnitte.text: When you sit on a **chair swing ride**, the seats fly outwards at a slant. You feel a force pushing you away from the centre. This force is called **centrifugal force**. The word comes from Latin and means roughly “fleeing the centre”. You also feel it on a bus when it goes fast round a bend and you are pushed to the side.

Actually every body wants to fly on in a straight line; this is called **inertia**. For it to stay on a circular path, a force must constantly pull it towards the centre, the **centripetal force**. For a stone on a string this is the string, for a car the grip of the tyres on the road. Someone turning along with the motion, on the other hand, feels a force outwards. Because this appears only in the rotating frame, centrifugal force is called a fictitious force.

The centrifugal force is greater the heavier a body is, the faster it moves and the tighter the bend. The formula is F = m·v²/r. Because the speed is squared, double the speed gives four times the force. If something turns in a circle at the same rate but with double the radius, the force doubles. A stone of 0.5 kg on a string 1 m long, circling twice a second, feels about 79 newtons, as much as the weight of 8 kg.

A **salad spinner** turns the wet lettuce so fast that the water flies outwards through the holes. A washing machine spins washing dry in the same way. If you swing a bucket of water fast over your head, the water does not fall out, because it is pressed into the bucket. Cyclists lean inwards on bends so that they do not tip over outwards. Roads and railway tracks are often built sloping on bends so that vehicles can get round more safely.

In the laboratory, a **centrifuge** separates substances according to their density by spinning very fast; heavy parts collect on the outside. In this way, for example, the components of blood can be separated. The Earth turns too, which is why it is slightly flattened at the poles and a little fatter at the equator. The diameter at the equator is about 43 km bigger than from pole to pole. Because of the Earth's rotation, you even weigh a tiny bit less at the equator than at the poles.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force you feel outwards in a rotation.
A force that pulls a body towards the centre of a circular path.
A force that only an observer who is moving along with the motion feels.
The tendency of a body to keep moving in a straight line.
A machine that separates substances by spinning fast.

gewusst: Modern laboratory centrifuges produce forces several thousand times stronger than gravity.
Fighter pilots and astronauts train in large human centrifuges so that they can withstand strong forces.
On a roller coaster with a loop, centrifugal force keeps you in your seat even upside down.

teile.einleitung: The weather forecast tells you whether the sun will shine tomorrow, whether it will rain or snow and how warm it will be. Behind it there is a lot of physics: experts measure temperature, air pressure, wind and humidity and use computers to calculate how the weather will develop. In Switzerland, this is mainly the job of MeteoSwiss.
wichtigste: Switzerland's weather service is called MeteoSwiss.
Weather experts are called meteorologists; in German they are jokingly also called “weather frogs”.
In Switzerland, temperature is given in degrees Celsius and must be measured in the shade.
By precipitation the forecast means rain, snow or hail.
A 90 per cent chance of rain means it will very probably rain.
Weather satellites supply pictures of the clouds from above.
In Switzerland, severe weather warnings come in five danger levels.

abschnitte.text: A weather report describes the current weather and predicts what it will be like over the next hours and days. This prediction is called the **forecast**. You find it on the radio, on television, in the newspaper and in apps. It usually gives the temperature, clouds, **precipitation**, wind and sometimes the snow line or the pollen count.

For a forecast to work, accurate measurements are needed. Air temperature is measured in the **shade** and about 2 metres above the ground, otherwise the sun would heat up the thermometer. MeteoSwiss runs a dense network of automatic measuring stations from the lowlands up to high mountain peaks. In Payerne in the canton of Vaud, **weather balloons** rise every day and radio back data from high up.

**Weather satellites** circle high above the Earth and supply pictures of the clouds from above. Weather radars detect where it is raining or hailing right now; Switzerland has five radar stations for this. All the measurements flow into huge computers that use physical formulas to calculate the weather of the future. These **weather models** divide the air into many small cubes and work out for each one how wind, heat and moisture change.

The weather can never be predicted with complete certainty, which is why people speak of **probability**. With a 90 per cent chance of rain, you should definitely take an umbrella. With 20 per cent it usually stays dry. For the next two to three days, forecasts are quite reliable; ten days ahead they are much less accurate.

MeteoSwiss warns of thunderstorms, gales, heavy rain, snow, black ice and heat. The **warning levels** range from 1 for no or little danger to 5 for very great danger. The warnings appear on the federal natural hazards platform and in the MeteoSwiss app. This allows people, farmers, mountain guides and fire brigades to prepare in good time.

Someone who studies and predicts the weather is a **meteorologist**. In German such people are jokingly called “Wetterfrosch”, a weather frog. The expression comes from the fact that people used to put tree frogs in jars with a little ladder and believed they would climb up when the weather was fine. Today we know that this does not work reliably, and frogs are no longer kept like that.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of the weather and of the Earth's atmosphere.
A prediction of what something will be like in the future.
Water that falls from the sky as rain, snow or hail.
The weight of the air pressing down on us; it helps with weather forecasting.

gewusst: On the Säntis and the Jungfraujoch, weather stations measure round the clock even in icy storms.
A weather model has to carry out billions of calculations in a few hours.
Weather sayings such as “Abendrot, Gutwetterbot” (red sky at night, good weather ahead) sometimes have a grain of truth, but are much less accurate than modern forecasts.

teile.einleitung: A distance time graph is a drawing that shows where something is at what time. At a glance you can see whether a bike is going fast, rolling slowly or standing still. Physicists use such graphs to describe movements precisely.
wichtigste: Time is usually on the horizontal axis and the distance travelled on the vertical axis.
A straight line sloping upwards means movement at a constant speed.
The steeper the line, the greater the speed.
A horizontal line means the body is standing still.
