A line sloping down to the right shows that the body is moving back towards its starting point.
A curve that gets steeper and steeper shows accelerated movement.
Where two lines cross, both bodies are at the same place at the same time.

abschnitte.text: A distance time graph is a **coordinate system** with two axes. To the right, on the horizontal axis, you plot the **time**, for example in seconds. Upwards, on the vertical axis, is the distance, for example in metres. So every point on the graph says: at this moment the body was at this place. If you join up many such points, you get a line that shows the whole movement.

If the line rises straight and evenly, the body is moving at a steady speed; this is called **uniform motion**. A shallow line means a slow speed, a steep line a fast speed. A horizontal line means: time goes on, but the distance does not change, so the body is standing still. If the line falls to the right, the distance from the start gets smaller and the body is turning back.

From a straight line you can calculate the **speed**: you divide the distance travelled by the time taken. If a line goes from 0 metres at 0 seconds to 50 metres at 10 seconds, that gives 50 divided by 10, so 5 metres per second. If the line starts at 20 metres and reaches 60 metres after 4 seconds, 40 metres were covered in 4 seconds, which is 10 metres per second. In maths this value is called the **gradient** of the straight line.

Not every movement is even. If a car keeps getting faster, it covers more distance every second, so the line bends upwards and gets steeper and steeper. This curved line is part of a **parabola** and shows accelerated movement. If a body slows down, on the other hand, the curve gets flatter and flatter until it is horizontal and the body stands still.

If you draw two movements on the same graph, you can compare them directly. If Lea sets off and Tim starts a little later but faster, Tim's line begins further to the right and is steeper. Where the two lines **cross**, both are at the same place at the same time, so that is exactly where Tim catches up with Lea. In this way, overtaking, meeting points or timetables can be planned quite easily.

Railway companies such as SBB plan their timetables with very similar diagrams, called **train graphs**. In them you can see where trains pass each other and where one train has to wait for another. Sports apps on mobile phones also often draw graphs of distance and time while you jog or cycle. In physics lessons, you measure movements with a stopwatch and tape measure and plot the values yourself.

begriffe.erklaerung: A line on the graph from which you read values such as time or distance.
How much distance a body covers in a certain time, for example in metres per second.
How steeply a line rises; here it corresponds to the speed.
A movement in which the speed always stays the same.

gewusst: In a distance time graph a line can never go straight up vertically, because then a body would be in several places in zero seconds.
On railway train graphs, time is often on the vertical axis, exactly the other way round from physics lessons.
As early as the 14th century, the scholar Nicole Oresme drew movements as diagrams.

teile.einleitung: Wind is moving air that flows from one place to another. It arises because the Sun warms the Earth unevenly, which creates differences in air pressure. Wind can be as gentle as a breeze or as destructive as a hurricane.
wichtigste: Wind arises because air flows from high to low air pressure.
The bigger the difference in pressure, the stronger the wind blows.
A very strong wind is called a gale or storm.
The föhn is a warm downslope wind in the Alpine valleys.
In the winter of 1999, the storm Lothar blew down many forests in Switzerland.
An anemometer measures the speed of the wind.
A weathercock shows where the wind is blowing from.

abschnitte.text: The Sun warms land, water and air by different amounts. Warm air expands and rises, and an **area of low pressure** forms there. Cold air sinks and forms an **area of high pressure**. The air then flows from high to low pressure, and we feel this as wind.

In an area of high pressure the air sinks and warms up, clouds dissolve, and the weather is often fine. In an area of low pressure the air rises and cools, which is why it often brings clouds and precipitation. The closer a high and a low are to each other, the stronger the wind. Because the Earth turns, the air does not flow straight but in big swirls.

The **föhn** is a warm, dry downslope wind that blows mainly in the Alpine valleys on the northern side, for example in the Reuss valley or the Rhine valley. The **bise** is a cold wind from the north east that is felt especially on the Swiss Plateau and around Lake Geneva. During the day the valley wind blows up the valley in mountain valleys, and at night the mountain wind blows down the valley. On clear nights at large lakes the wind usually blows from the land to the lake, and during the day rather the other way round.

A very strong wind is called a **gale** or storm, and an even stronger one a **hurricane force wind**. On 26 December 1999 the storm Lothar swept across Switzerland and blew down millions of trees in a short time. Over an open lake the wind usually blows more strongly than in a town, because there are fewer obstacles and less friction. That is why Swiss lakes have storm warning lights that flash when there is danger.

With a **wind gauge**, also called an anemometer, you measure wind speed. A weathercock on the church tower shows where the wind is blowing from. At motorway bridges and airfields there are **windsocks**, which show direction and strength. Wind strength is often given on the Beaufort scale, from 0 for calm to 12 for hurricane.

Thousands of years ago, wind was already driving sailing ships across the seas and turning windmills. Today **wind turbines** produce electricity; in Switzerland, for example, on Mont Crosin in the Bernese Jura or on the Gotthard Pass. Wind also dries washing quickly, because it carries the moisture away. Paragliders and gliders use rising air currents too, so that they can stay in the air for a long time.

begriffe.erklaerung: The weight of the air pressing down on the Earth.
A warm, dry downslope wind in the Alps.
A cold wind from the north east in Switzerland.
The technical word for a wind gauge.
A scale of wind strength from 0 to 12.

gewusst: When the föhn blows, the Alps often look particularly clear and close from the Swiss Plateau.
Switzerland's strongest gusts of wind are usually measured on high mountain peaks.
The Beaufort scale was originally developed for sailors, who were meant to judge the wind strength from the state of the sea.

teile.einleitung: Physics is the natural science that explores how the world around us works. It studies motion, forces, energy, light, sound, heat, electricity and magnetism. The laws of physics explain why a ship floats, why an apple falls and why in a thunderstorm we see the lightning first.
wichtigste: Physics explores the basic laws of nature.
Forces are measured in the unit newton.
At about 300,000 kilometres per second, light is much faster than sound.
Below 0 °C, water freezes into ice.
Unlike magnetic poles, that is a north pole and a south pole, attract each other.
Metals such as copper conduct electric current well.
Physicists work with experiments, measurements and mathematics.

abschnitte.text: The word physics comes from the Greek word for nature. Physicists observe nature, carry out **experiments** and describe their results with formulas. Important branches are **mechanics** (motion and forces), optics (light), acoustics (sound), the study of heat and the study of electricity. Physics is the basis for technology such as cars, mobile phones and power stations.

A force can move something, slow it down or change its shape, and it is measured in **newtons**. Every body has **inertia**: it wants to stay in its state of motion. That is why you tip forwards on the bus when it suddenly brakes, because your body wants to keep moving. A large steel ship floats because it displaces so much water that **buoyancy** carries it.

At about 300,000 kilometres per second, light is the fastest thing there is. In air, sound travels at only about 340 metres per second, which is why you hear the thunder only after the lightning. Electric **current** flows well through metals such as copper, which is why cables are usually made of copper. With magnets, north and south poles attract each other, and like poles repel.

Substances can be solid, liquid or gas; these are the three **states of matter**. Water freezes into ice below 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at normal pressure. The Celsius temperature scale was invented by the Swede Anders Celsius. Heat always flows from the warmer to the colder body.

In the 17th century Isaac Newton described the laws of motion and gravity. In Bern in 1905, Albert Einstein developed the special **theory of relativity** while working at the patent office. Marie Curie studied radioactivity and received two Nobel Prizes. In Geneva there is **CERN**, one of the largest research centres for particle physics in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit in which forces are measured.
The property of a body of wanting to stay at rest or in motion.
The force with which water or air pushes a body upwards.
Whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas.

gewusst: If you count the seconds between lightning and thunder and divide by three, you know roughly how many kilometres away the storm is.
Light takes about 8 minutes to get from the Sun to the Earth.
The LHC particle accelerator at CERN is an underground ring about 27 kilometres round.

teile.einleitung: When you look into a mirror, your reflection seems to be standing behind the glass. But in reality there is nothing there. An image like this, which forms only in our eye and cannot be caught on a screen, is called a virtual image.
wichtigste: With a virtual image the light rays only seem to come from it.
A virtual image cannot be caught on a screen or a wall.
The image in a plane mirror is virtual, upright and the same size.
A magnifying glass produces an enlarged virtual image when the object is inside the focal length.
Curved traffic mirrors show a virtual, upright and smaller image.
Diverging lenses always produce virtual images.
The opposite is a real image, like the one a projector throws onto a screen.

abschnitte.text: A **virtual image** forms when light rays spread apart after a mirror or a lens. Our eye extends these rays backwards in its mind. We see the image where these imagined lines meet. But no light actually comes together there. That is why a sheet of paper at this spot stays dark.

abschnitte.titel: The image in a plane mirror
abschnitte.text: A flat mirror shows a virtual, upright image of the same size. The image lies exactly as far behind the mirror as the object stands in front of it. So if a person stands 2 metres in front of the mirror, their reflection is 4 metres away from them. Left and right appear swapped, or more precisely front and back. That is why “AMBULANCE” is often written in mirror writing on ambulances.

A **magnifying glass** is a **converging lens**. If an object lies inside the focal length, an enlarged, upright, virtual image forms. You can estimate the magnification like this: 25 centimetres, the near viewing distance, divided by the focal length. So a magnifying glass with a focal length of 5 centimetres magnifies about 5 times. If a stamp is 3 centimetres in front of a magnifying glass with a focal length of 4 centimetres, the image lies 12 centimetres in front of the lens.

An outward curved **convex mirror** shows a virtual, upright and smaller image. In return you can see a large area at once. That is why such mirrors hang at exits where it is hard to see and are used as rear-view mirrors on lorries. A **diverging lens** also always gives smaller virtual images. A lens with a focal length of minus 10 centimetres forms the image of an object 10 centimetres away at 5 centimetres in front of the lens.

The counterpart is the **real image**. There the light rays really come together, and you can see the image on a screen. Real images are produced, for example, by projectors, cameras and the lens of the eye on our retina. We meet virtual images in the bathroom mirror, in glasses for short-sighted people and in binoculars. Magic tricks and stage effects also use virtual images to make things float.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance between the lens and the point where parallel light rays meet.
A lens that is thicker in the middle and brings light rays together.
A lens that is thinner in the middle and makes light rays spread apart.
An image where the light rays really meet and which can be caught on a screen.

gewusst: To see all of yourself in a mirror, a mirror half as tall as you is enough, no matter how far away you stand.
A mirage over a hot road is also a virtual image; the supposed puddle is reflected sky.

teile.einleitung: The tunnelling effect is an astonishing phenomenon of quantum physics. Tiny particles such as electrons can cross a barrier even though their energy is not really enough to do so. It is as if a ball rolled through a hill instead of over it.
wichtigste: In the tunnelling effect a particle gets over an energy barrier even though in classical physics its energy is not enough.
Inside the barrier the particle's wave function dies away exponentially.
With the same barrier, heavier particles tunnel much less often than light ones.
Flash memory uses electrons that tunnel through a thin insulating layer when data is written.
Leo Esaki developed the tunnel diode.
In the Sun protons tunnel through the Coulomb barrier, which makes nuclear fusion possible.
In the Josephson effect Cooper pairs tunnel between two superconductors.
In the ammonia molecule the nitrogen atom tunnels through the plane of the hydrogen atoms.

abschnitte.text: In our everyday world a ball only gets over a hill if it has enough momentum. But in **quantum physics** the tiniest particles also behave like waves. Such a wave does not stop at once at a wall, but gets weaker inside it. If the **barrier** is thin enough, a small remainder still arrives on the other side, and the particle can turn up there.

Inside the barrier the **wave function** dies away exponentially, that is, it gets smaller very quickly. That is why tunnelling is only likely with very thin barriers of a few millionths of a millimetre. Mass also plays a big part: heavy particles tunnel much less often than light electrons. That is why a person can never tunnel through a wall.

Inside the **Sun** the positively charged protons push each other away. In classical physics the temperature would be too low to overcome this Coulomb barrier. But some protons tunnel through it and fuse, and that is how the Sun shines. Around 1928 George Gamow also used the tunnelling effect to explain radioactive **alpha decay**.

In 1981 Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer invented the **scanning tunnelling microscope** at the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon near Zurich. A fine metal tip moves just above a surface, and electrons tunnel through the tiny gap. The tunnelling current is turned into a picture on which you can even see individual atoms. For this the two received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986.

In **flash memory**, for example in USB sticks and mobile phones, electrons tunnel through a wafer-thin insulating layer when data is written. The Japanese Leo Esaki built the **tunnel diode** and received the Nobel Prize for it in 1973. In the Josephson effect pairs of electrons tunnel between two superconductors; this is used for extremely sensitive measuring instruments. Tunnelling also plays a part in quantum computers.

begriffe.erklaerung: An obstacle for which a particle really has too little energy.
A mathematical description of where a quantum particle is likely to be.
The physics of the very smallest particles.
A device that makes individual atoms visible using tunnelling current.
A material that conducts electricity without resistance.

gewusst: Without the tunnelling effect the Sun would not shine.
The scanning tunnelling microscope, with which you can see atoms, was invented in Switzerland.
Every time you save a photo on a USB stick, billions of electrons tunnel.

teile.einleitung: Aldehydes are a group of organic compounds that carry a special group of carbon, oxygen and hydrogen atoms, the aldehyde group -CHO. Many of them have a strong smell and are responsible for the scent of vanilla, cinnamon or bitter almonds. Others, such as formaldehyde, are important basic materials for industry.
wichtigste: Aldehydes have the aldehyde group -CHO at the end of a carbon chain.
In IUPAC naming they have the ending -al.
The simplest aldehyde is methanal, also called formaldehyde.
Mild oxidation of ethanol produces ethanal.
Aldehydes can be oxidised further to carboxylic acids.
They can be detected with Fehling's test and Tollens' test.
Benzaldehyde smells of bitter almonds, and vanillin is the main flavour substance of vanilla.

abschnitte.text: Aldehydes belong to the **carbonyl compounds**, because they contain a carbon atom with a double bond to oxygen. In aldehydes this carbon also carries a hydrogen atom, and together this forms the **aldehyde group** -CHO. The name comes from “alcohol dehydrogenatus”, that is, alcohol from which hydrogen has been removed. According to IUPAC rules, aldehydes are given the ending -al, as in methanal, ethanal or propanal.

The simplest aldehyde is **methanal**, better known as formaldehyde, a gas with a pungent smell. It is used to make synthetic resins and glues and is harmful to health, which is why there are strict limits for it indoors. Ethanal, also called acetaldehyde, is formed in the body when alcohol is broken down. Propanal and butanal are raw materials for plastics and solvents.

Aldehydes are formed when **primary alcohols** are mildly oxidised; ethanol becomes ethanal in this way. If they are oxidised further, **carboxylic acids** are formed; ethanal, for example, becomes acetic acid. Because aldehydes are oxidised so easily, they act as reducing agents themselves. This property is used to detect them in the laboratory.

In **Fehling's test**, a blue copper solution is added to the sample and heated. If an aldehyde is present, a brick red precipitate of copper oxide forms. In **Tollens' test**, silver is deposited as a shiny silver mirror on the glass wall. These tests can also detect certain sugars such as glucose, which have an aldehyde group.

Many aldehydes have a pleasant smell and are used as flavourings. **Vanillin** is the main flavour substance of the vanilla pod and today is mostly made artificially. **Benzaldehyde** smells of bitter almonds and marzipan, and cinnamaldehyde gives cinnamon its scent. Aldehydes are also used in perfumes to create fresh notes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of atoms that determines the properties of a class of substances.
A reaction in which a substance gives up electrons, often while taking up oxygen.
An organic acid with the group -COOH, such as acetic acid.
An international organisation that sets the rules for chemical names.

gewusst: Part of the headache after too much alcohol is blamed on ethanal, which is formed when it is broken down in the body.
Glucose gives a positive Fehling's test, because it has an aldehyde group.
Vanillin used to be obtained from waste from papermaking too.

teile.einleitung: Activation energy is the energy a chemical reaction needs to get going at all. You can picture it as a hill over which you have to push a ball before it rolls down the other side by itself. It explains why wood does not burn by itself, even though there is oxygen everywhere.
wichtigste: Activation energy is the energy a reaction needs to start.
A piece of wood does not burn by itself, because it lacks the activation energy.
With a match, the heat from friction supplies the activation energy.
In a petrol engine, the spark from the spark plug supplies the activation energy.
In an energy diagram it appears as an energy hill before the products.
The state at the top of the energy hill is called the transition state.
Svante Arrhenius introduced the term in 1889.

abschnitte.text: Many reactions give off energy, for example the burning of wood. Even so, they do not simply happen by themselves but need a push. This starting energy is called **activation energy**. Only once it has been supplied can the reaction carry on, often keeping itself going with the heat it releases.

In an **energy diagram**, you draw the energy of the substances during the reaction. First the curve climbs up an energy hill, then it falls to the products. The height of the hill measured from the starting substance is the activation energy. At the top is the **transition state**, a very short lived state in which old bonds are half broken and new ones half formed.

For two particles to react, they must collide. Only if a collision has enough energy and the particles are lined up correctly does a new substance form. At higher temperatures the particles move faster, and more collisions are strong enough. That is why reactions usually happen much faster in warmth, and food keeps longer in the fridge.

When you strike a **match**, friction produces heat that sets the match head alight. In a petrol engine, a spark from the **spark plug** ignites the mixture of petrol and air. You light a wood fire with paper and small shavings, which catch fire more easily. A gas cooker needs a spark or a flame before the gas burns.

A **catalyst** is a substance that lowers the activation energy without being used up itself. It offers a different reaction path with a lower energy hill. The catalytic converter in a car helps to turn poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful substances. In living things, **enzymes** work as catalysts and make reactions possible at body temperature.

The Swedish chemist **Svante Arrhenius** introduced the concept of activation energy in 1889. He described with a formula how strongly the speed of a reaction depends on temperature. This Arrhenius equation is still used in chemistry and technology today. Arrhenius received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1903.

begriffe.erklaerung: A process in which new substances are formed from substances.
A short lived state at the top of the energy hill.
A substance that makes a reaction easier and is not used up in the process.
A protein that works as a catalyst in living things.

gewusst: A sugar cube can hardly be lit with a match, but with a little ash on it, it burns, because substances in the ash act as a catalyst.
As a rule of thumb, many reactions run about twice as fast for every 10 °C more.
Without activation energy, all the wood and paper on Earth would burn up at once.

teile.einleitung: Supercooled water is water that is colder than 0 °C and still stays liquid. That sounds impossible, but it happens all the time in clouds and in freezing rain. As soon as the water gets a nudge, it freezes in a flash.
wichtigste: Supercooled water is liquid water below 0 °C.
It stays liquid because there are no nuclei for crystals to form on.
Without nuclei, pure water can stay liquid down to about minus 40 °C.
If water at minus 5 °C suddenly starts to freeze, its temperature rises to 0 °C.
Freezing rain consists of supercooled drops that freeze at once when they land.
Clouds with supercooled droplets are dangerous for aeroplanes, because the droplets freeze on the wings.
Rime forms from freezing supercooled fog droplets.
Silver iodide was used as an artificial freezing nucleus in experiments to prevent hail.

abschnitte.text: Normally water freezes into ice at 0 °C. But for an ice crystal to grow, it needs a starting point, a so-called **nucleus**. This can be a grain of dust, a scratch in the glass or a tiny piece of ice. If there is no such nucleus, the water stays liquid even though it is colder than 0 °C; it is **supercooled**.

Very pure water in small droplets can stay liquid down to about minus 40 °C. Only then do the ice crystals form entirely by themselves. Normal tap water contains more nuclei and usually freezes just a few degrees below zero. Supercooling is an **unstable state**: even a jolt can make the water freeze.

If supercooled water at minus 5 °C suddenly starts to freeze, its temperature rises to 0 °C. This is because heat is released when water freezes, the **heat of fusion**. Part of the water turns into ice and warms up the rest until 0 °C is reached. Reusable hand warmers use this effect too, but with a salt solution instead of water.

Many clouds consist of supercooled water droplets even at temperatures below zero. When an aeroplane flies through them, the droplets freeze on the wings and fuselage; this is called **icing**. That is why aeroplanes have de-icing systems, and on the ground in winter they are sprayed with de-icing fluid. When supercooled fog drifts against trees and masts, thick white **rime** grows there.

When rain falls from a warm layer of air into a cold layer near the ground, the drops can become supercooled. When they hit roads, cars or branches, they freeze at once. This **freezing rain** covers everything with a glass-clear, slippery layer of ice. It is very dangerous, because roads can become as slippery as a mirror within minutes and branches can break under the weight.

Researchers tried to make supercooled clouds freeze artificially. To do this they scattered **silver iodide**, whose crystals are very similar to ice crystals and act as freezing nuclei. The aim was to prevent hail or to make it rain. Whether this works reliably is still disputed today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny starting point on which an ice crystal can grow.
Colder than the freezing point, but still liquid.
The heat that is released when something freezes.
A thick coating of ice made of frozen fog droplets.
Ice that forms on aeroplanes, power lines or trees.

gewusst: If you carefully put a bottle of very clean water into the freezer, it can stay liquid and suddenly turn into ice when you knock it.
In winter, in many clouds above Switzerland, liquid droplets float at minus 10 °C or colder.
On masts and summit crosses rime can form ice flags a metre long, which always grow into the wind.

teile.einleitung: Cloud physics studies how clouds form and grow and how they produce rain, snow or hail. Clouds are made of countless tiny water droplets or ice crystals floating in the air. Anyone who understands cloud physics can predict the weather better.
wichtigste: Clouds form when moist air rises, cools and water vapour condenses.
For this, the water vapour needs tiny particles, the condensation nuclei.
A typical cloud droplet is only about 0.01 mm across.
In 1803 Luke Howard proposed the Latin cloud names such as cumulus and stratus.
Droplets grow by colliding and merging, which is called coalescence.
In the Bergeron Findeisen process, ice crystals grow at the expense of supercooled droplets.
The typical thundercloud with an anvil is called cumulonimbus.

abschnitte.text: Air always contains invisible **water vapour**. When air rises, it expands and cools. Cold air can hold less water vapour, so part of it turns back into liquid water. This process is called **condensation**. The temperature at which this begins is called the **dew point**.

In pure air, water vapour hardly forms droplets. It needs tiny particles it can settle on, the **condensation nuclei**. These are, for example, dust, salt crystals from the sea, soot or pollen. On each of these particles a droplet about 0.01 mm across grows. Billions of such droplets together are what we see as a cloud.

Cloud droplets are so light that even weak upward air currents carry them. For rain to fall, much bigger drops are needed; one raindrop takes about a million cloud droplets. In warm clouds, droplets collide and merge, which is called **coalescence**. In cold clouds there are often **supercooled droplets** that stay liquid despite temperatures below zero. Ice crystals beside them grow at their expense, which is the **Bergeron Findeisen process**, and the crystals fall as snow or melt into rain.

In 1803 the Englishman **Luke Howard** proposed Latin names for clouds. **Cumulus** means heap and refers to puffy clouds; **stratus** means layer. Cirrus means a curl of hair and refers to high feathery clouds of ice; nimbus stands for rain. Today ten cloud genera are distinguished. The **cumulonimbus** is the mighty thundercloud whose top often spreads out like an anvil.

In winter, **high fog**, which belongs to the stratus genus, often lies over the Swiss Plateau for weeks. Cold air then collects down low, warmer air lies above it, and the sun shines on the mountains. In summer, puffy clouds over the Alps and the Jura often grow into thunderstorms. You can estimate the height of the cloud base: about 125 m for each degree of difference between the temperature and the dew point. So at 20 °C and a dew point of 12 °C, the base is about 1000 m above the ground.

begriffe.erklaerung: When water vapour cools and turns into liquid water.
A tiny particle on which a cloud droplet forms.
The temperature at which water vapour in the air starts to condense.
The merging of droplets into bigger drops.
Liquid, even though the temperature is below zero degrees.

gewusst: A medium sized puffy cloud can contain several hundred tonnes of water and still floats.
Water droplets in clouds can stay liquid down to about minus 40 degrees.
Fog is nothing other than a cloud that touches the ground.

teile.einleitung: The World Wide Web, Web or WWW for short, is the network of web pages that you can look at with a browser and that are connected by links. It was invented between 1989 and 1991 at the CERN research centre near Geneva. The Web is not the same as the internet, but one of the most important services that use the internet.
wichtigste: In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee submitted his first proposal for a linked information system at CERN.
Originally the Web was meant to help researchers share information.
Berners-Lee developed the language HTML, the protocol HTTP and web addresses.
The first web browser was called WorldWideWeb and was later renamed Nexus.
The first web server ran on a NeXT computer at CERN.
The world's first website could be reached at info.cern.ch.
In 1993 CERN released the web software to everyone free of licence fees.

abschnitte.text: The **internet** is a worldwide network of computers connected by cables and radio. The **World Wide Web** is a service on this network, just as email is. It consists of billions of web pages linked by **hyperlinks**. If you click on a link, you jump to another page, no matter on which computer in the world it is stored. To display web pages, you need a program called a **browser**.

At **CERN** near Geneva, thousands of researchers from many countries work together. The British computer scientist **Tim Berners-Lee** noticed that information on different computers was hard to find. In March 1989 he proposed a system in which documents are connected by links. Together with the Belgian computer scientist **Robert Cailliau**, he developed the idea further. At the end of 1990, the first web server and the first browser were running at CERN.

Berners-Lee created three basic building blocks that are still used today. **HTML** is the language in which web pages are written. **HTTP** sets out how browsers and servers talk to each other, and the **URL** is the address of a page. His first browser was called WorldWideWeb, later Nexus, and ran on a NeXT computer. The first website at info.cern.ch explained what the Web is and how to use it.

On 30 April 1993 CERN decided to release the web software to everyone without **licence fees**. This meant anyone could build web pages and browsers without paying. Soon afterwards, browsers with pictures appeared, and the Web grew explosively. In 1994 Berners-Lee founded the **World Wide Web Consortium**, W3C for short, which still sets rules for the Web today. Many experts believe that releasing it freely is the reason why the Web became so successful.

Today billions of people use the Web for learning, shopping, playing and reading the news. Search engines help to find the right thing among the countless pages. Web pages can contain text, pictures, videos and whole games. It is important to check information critically, because not everything on the Web is true. Personal data such as your address or passwords should also be passed on only with great care.

begriffe.erklaerung: A program with which you can look at web pages.
A clickable reference that leads to another page.
The language in which web pages are built.
A computer that stores web pages and sends them out on request.
The address of a web page that you type into the browser.

gewusst: The computer of the first web server had a sticker on it asking people not to switch it off.
The first website still exists at CERN today as a reconstruction you can look at.
Tim Berners-Lee was knighted by the British Queen for his invention.

teile.einleitung: A waterfall forms where a river or stream plunges over a rock edge into the depths. Gravity pulls the water downwards, often with a thundering roar and fine spray. Switzerland has many famous waterfalls, from the mighty Rhine Falls to the high falls of the Lauterbrunnen valley.
wichtigste: In a waterfall, water plunges downwards because of gravity.
The Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen are the most famous large waterfall in Switzerland.
The Lauterbrunnen valley in the Bernese Oberland has particularly many waterfalls, for example the Staubbach Falls.
The Trümmelbach Falls near Lauterbrunnen thunder down inside a mountain.
The Giessbach Falls on Lake Brienz drop in 14 steps.
The highest waterfall in the world is Angel Falls in Venezuela.
The energy of falling water can be used in hydroelectric power stations.

abschnitte.text: Waterfalls form where a river flows over a **step in the land**. Often there is hard rock on top and softer rock below, which the water wears away faster. This creates an edge over which the water plunges. **Gravity** pulls the water down, making it go faster and faster. At the foot of the fall, the crashing water often digs out a deep basin called a **plunge pool**.

Many waterfalls in the Alps owe their existence to the **glaciers** of the Ice Ages. The glaciers scoured out wide, steep **U-shaped valleys**. The side streams could not cut down as deeply and today plunge over high rock walls into the main valley. The best known example is the Lauterbrunnen valley in the Bernese Oberland, where there are dozens of waterfalls. There, the Staubbach Falls drop almost 300 metres freely and turn into a fine dust of water.

The **Rhine Falls** near Schaffhausen are about 150 metres wide and about 23 metres high. They are considered one of the waterfalls with the most water in Europe. The **Trümmelbach Falls** near Lauterbrunnen are special because they thunder down inside the mountain, carrying meltwater from the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau. On Lake Brienz, the **Giessbach Falls** plunge down to the lake in 14 steps. There are many others too, such as the Reichenbach Falls near Meiringen.

The highest waterfall in the world is **Angel Falls** in Venezuela, whose water falls almost 1000 metres. Niagara Falls on the border between Canada and the USA are famous for their huge amounts of water. The Iguazú Falls between Argentina and Brazil are made up of hundreds of separate falls. The local people call the Victoria Falls in Africa “the smoke that thunders”. They lie on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe.

Falling water has a lot of **energy**, which on impact is turned into movement, noise and a little heat. This energy is used in **hydroelectric power stations**, where water falls through pipes onto turbines. In Switzerland, most electricity comes from hydropower. Fine spray often forms at waterfalls, and in sunshine a **rainbow** appears in it. Because the rocks are wet and slippery, you should always stay on the paths at waterfalls.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which the Earth pulls all things downwards.
A deep basin at the foot of a waterfall that the water has hollowed out.
A wide valley with steep sides that a glacier has scoured out.
A plant that produces electricity from the energy of flowing or falling water.

gewusst: Waterfalls slowly move backwards, because the water wears away the rock edge bit by bit.
At the Rhine Falls you can take a boat to a rock in the middle of the roaring water.
In winter, smaller waterfalls can freeze solid and are then climbed by ice climbers.

teile.einleitung: A displacement can, also called an overflow can, is a container with a spout at the side that is used in physics lessons. With it you can measure the volume of irregularly shaped objects such as stones or keys. The idea behind it is simple: an object in water pushes aside exactly as much water as the space it takes up itself.
wichtigste: A displacement can is used to find the volume of irregular objects.
Before measuring, it must be so full that water has only just stopped running out.
The overflowing water is caught with a measuring cylinder.
If 35 ml of water flows out, the object has a volume of 35 cm³.
A floating object such as a cork must be pushed right under the water.
Air bubbles on the object can make the measurement wrong.
With the volume and the mass you can calculate the density of an object.

abschnitte.text: A **displacement can** is usually a beaker made of plastic, glass or metal with a small spout at the side. If you pour in too much water, the extra flows out through the spout. Underneath you put a **measuring cylinder**, which catches the water flowing out. This lets you read off exactly how much water has overflowed.

First you fill the can until water runs out of the spout and wait until it stops dripping. Then you put the empty measuring cylinder under the spout. Now you carefully put the object into the water so that it is completely under. The water that now overflows has exactly the same **volume** as the object.

One millilitre of water equals exactly one cubic centimetre, so 1 ml = 1 cm³. If 35 ml flows out, the stone has a volume of 35 cm³. If the stone weighs 91 g, you divide the mass by the volume and get a **density** of 2.6 g/cm³. This fits many rocks well, such as granite.

For small objects you can also manage without a displacement can. You fill a measuring cylinder with, for example, 50 ml of water and put a key in it. If the water level rises to 72 ml, the key has a volume of 22 cm³. You simply work out the difference, which is why this is called the **difference method**.

If **air bubbles** stay stuck to the object, they push aside extra water, and the result is too big. That is why you should shake the object gently or wet it beforehand. A cork floats and has to be pushed right under the water with a thin needle. Drops that stay hanging on the spout can also make the result slightly wrong.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much space an object takes up.
A narrow glass with a scale for reading off amounts of liquid.
How much mass there is in a certain volume.
To push water aside or upwards because an object needs space.

gewusst: According to legend, Archimedes had the idea of measuring the volume of a crown with displaced water while he was in the bath.
One litre of water fits exactly into a cube with sides of 10 cm.
A stone with a density of 2.6 g/cm³ is about two and a half times as heavy as the same amount of water.

teile.einleitung: Centripetal force is the force that keeps a body on a circular path. Without it, everything that turns in a circle would simply fly on in a straight line. It acts on a roundabout, when cycling round a bend, in the hammer throw and even on the Moon, which circles the Earth.
wichtigste: Centripetal force always points towards the centre of the circle.
It is calculated with the formula F = m · v² / r.
It is given in newtons.
If the centripetal force is missing, the body flies on tangentially, that is, straight ahead.
On a bike on a flat bend, the friction between tyres and road supplies the centripetal force.
The bends of cycling tracks slope inwards so that part of the force comes from the track.
This slope is called banking.

abschnitte.text: A moving body actually wants to carry on in a straight line; this is called **inertia**. For it to go round in a circle instead, a force must constantly pull it towards the centre. This force is called **centripetal force**, from the Latin for “striving towards the centre”. It does not change the speed but constantly changes the direction of the movement.

Centripetal force is calculated with F = m · v² / r. Here m is the **mass**, v the speed and r the radius of the circle. A cyclist and her bike together weigh 60 kilograms and ride at 10 metres per second round a bend with a radius of 20 metres. Then she needs 60 times 100 divided by 20, that is 300 **newtons**. Twice as fast means four times as much force, which is why fast bends are dangerous.

In the **hammer throw**, the thrower spins round several times, pulling on the wire. The wire supplies the centripetal force for the heavy hammer. As soon as he lets go, this force is missing, and the hammer flies on **tangentially**, that is, straight ahead in the direction it was moving at that moment. In just the same way, drops of water fly off a wet bicycle wheel.

On a bike on a flat road, the centripetal force comes from the **friction** between tyres and ground. If the road is icy, this friction is missing, and you slide straight on out of the bend. That is why cycling tracks and motorway bends slope inwards; this slope is called **banking**. Runners in the 200 metres also lean inwards on the bend so that their feet produce a force towards the centre of the bend.

The Moon also needs a centripetal force to circle the Earth. Here it is supplied by the Earth's **gravity**. In the same way, the pull of the Sun keeps the Earth and the other planets in their orbits. Satellites fly so fast that gravity keeps them exactly on a circular orbit.

On a roundabout it feels as if you are being pushed outwards. This felt force is called **centrifugal force**. In physics it is a fictitious force, because really the body only wants to carry on straight ahead while the seat pulls it towards the centre. A spin dryer uses this: the washing is kept going round by the drum, but the water flies out through the holes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tendency of a body to keep its movement.
Along a line that touches the circle at only one point.
The unit of force, named after Isaac Newton.
The inward slope of a bend.

gewusst: Without the Sun's gravity, the Earth would fly off straight into space.
On roller coaster loops, centripetal force makes sure you stay in your seat even upside down.
Cycling tracks often have slopes of more than 40 degrees on the bends.

teile.einleitung: Ultraviolet radiation, UV radiation for short, is light that we cannot see with our eyes. It has shorter wavelengths than violet light and comes mainly from the Sun. UV radiation can cause sunburn, but it also helps the skin to make vitamin D.
wichtigste: UV radiation has shorter wavelengths than visible violet.
Johann Wilhelm Ritter discovered it in 1801.
There are three kinds: UV-A, UV-B and UV-C.
The ozone layer holds back a large part of the Sun's UV radiation.
UV-C practically does not reach the ground at all.
Too much UV on unprotected skin leads to sunburn, but with UV the skin also makes vitamin D.
In the Alps UV radiation is stronger than in the Swiss Plateau.

abschnitte.text: Light is an electromagnetic wave, and every colour has its own **wavelength**. Violet has the shortest wavelength that we can still see. Shorter still, between roughly 100 and 400 nanometres, lies **ultraviolet radiation**, which means “beyond violet”. It carries more energy than visible light and can therefore change substances.

In 1800 William Herschel had discovered invisible infrared beyond red light. The German physicist **Johann Wilhelm Ritter** wondered whether there was also something on the other side of the spectrum. In 1801 he showed that silver chloride turns dark especially quickly beyond violet. With this, UV radiation had been discovered.

The radiation is divided into **UV-A, UV-B and UV-C**. UV-A has the longest wavelength, goes deep into the skin and makes it age. UV-B has more energy and mainly causes sunburn, but it also makes it possible to form **vitamin D**. The dangerous UV-C is completely absorbed by the **ozone layer** and the air and practically does not reach the ground.

In the Alps UV radiation is stronger than in the Swiss Plateau, because the layer of air above is thinner and filters less. It increases by about ten per cent for every 1000 metres of height. Fresh snow also reflects a large part of the radiation. Without good sunglasses, painful **snow blindness** can happen when skiing or hiking.

The best protection comes from shade, clothes, a hat, sunglasses and sun cream. The UV index tells you how strong the radiation is at the moment; from values of about 3 you should protect yourself. UV-C lamps kill germs and clean drinking water. Under **black light** highlighter pens and fluorescent paints glow visibly, and this is also how banknotes are checked to see if they are genuine.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance between two wave crests; it decides what kind of light it is.
A layer in the atmosphere that absorbs a lot of UV radiation.
A substance absorbs invisible UV light and glows visibly instead.
A number that shows how strong the Sun's UV radiation is at the moment.
A vitamin for strong bones that the skin can make with sunlight.

gewusst: Bees can see UV light and recognise patterns on flowers that are invisible to us.
Even on cloudy days a large part of the UV radiation comes through the clouds.
Scorpions glow bluish green under UV light.

teile.einleitung: A cycle ergometer is an exercise bike that measures exactly how much power someone produces when pedalling. You find it in gyms, with athletes and in doctors' surgeries. With it you can work out very nicely how much work and energy goes into pedalling.
wichtigste: A cycle ergometer is an exercise bike that measures power.
It works out the power from pedalling force and pedalling speed.
Doctors often use it for an exercise ECG.
Anyone who pedals at 150 W for 20 minutes does 180 kJ of work.
That is 0.05 kWh or about 43 kcal.
To produce 1 kWh, you would have to pedal at 250 W for 4 hours.
Three minutes at 200 W give 36,000 J of work.

abschnitte.text: The word **ergometer** means work meter, from the Greek ergon for work. A cycle ergometer looks like a bike without wheels that stands fixed on the floor. A brake, often with magnets or eddy currents, produces a resistance that can be set exactly. A screen shows the **power** in watts, the time and often also the pulse.

The device measures how hard you press on the pedals and how fast they turn. From the **pedalling force** and the pedalling speed it works out the power. The unit watt is named after the Scottish inventor James Watt. One watt means that one joule of work is done per second.

**Work** is power times time. If someone pedals for 20 minutes, that is 1200 seconds, at 150 W, this gives 180,000 J or 180 kJ. In kilowatt hours this is 0.15 kW times a third of an hour, so 0.05 kWh. For a whole **kilowatt hour** you would have to pedal at 250 W for 4 hours.

One kilocalorie is about 4.2 kJ, so 180 kJ is roughly 43 kcal. But the body uses much more energy than arrives at the pedal. Muscles turn only about a quarter of the energy from food into movement; the rest becomes **heat**. That is why you sweat so much when training.

abschnitte.titel: At the doctor's and in sport
abschnitte.text: In doctors' surgeries and hospitals the ergometer is used for the **exercise ECG**. The activity of the heart is recorded while the effort is increased step by step. This shows how the heart and circulation react to exertion. Athletes use ergometers to test their fitness and plan their training precisely.

A trained person can produce about 200 to 250 W for an hour, and professional cyclists manage clearly more. In Switzerland a kilowatt hour of electricity costs only a few centimes. So if you pedal for a whole afternoon, you produce energy worth a few centimes. This shows how much work there is in the electricity from the socket.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much work is done per second, measured in watts.
Power times time, measured in joules.
The work that 1000 watts do in one hour.
A heart test carried out during physical effort.
An old unit of energy, about 4.2 kilojoules.

gewusst: To make a 60 watt light bulb shine for an hour, you would have to pedal hard the whole time.
Professional cyclists can produce over 1500 W for short sprints.
Most ergometers simply turn the pedalling energy into heat.

teile.einleitung: A distorting mirror is a mirror with a curved surface that changes your reflection in funny ways. Sometimes you look huge and thin, sometimes small and fat. At funfairs and in museums, distorting mirrors cause a lot of laughter.
wichtigste: A distorting mirror distorts your reflection.
Its surface is not flat but curved.
Parts that bulge outwards make the image narrower and smaller; parts that curve inwards enlarge it.
If a mirror is curved differently at the top and the bottom, you look thin at the top and fat at the bottom.
Only the image is distorted; your body stays the same.
Christmas baubles, spoons and soap bubbles also act like distorting mirrors.
A room full of distorting mirrors is called a hall of mirrors.

abschnitte.text: An ordinary mirror is completely flat and shows you as you are, only reversed left to right. A **distorting mirror**, on the other hand, is curved, often even wavy. This stretches some parts of your reflection and squashes others. The result is a distorted, often very funny picture.

A mirror always reflects light so that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection; this is the **law of reflection**. On a curved surface, every spot points in a slightly different direction. An outward bulging, **convex** area makes the image smaller, while an inward curving, **concave** area enlarges it. If a mirror is curved only across its width, you become wider or narrower, but not taller or shorter.

A shiny Christmas bauble is a spherical mirror in which you look small with a big nose. On the back of a spoon you see yourself small and upright; on the inside your image is upside down. On a soap bubble or a shiny teapot your reflection also appears small and distorted. In crumpled aluminium foil the image is so broken up that you can hardly recognise yourself.

For more than a hundred years there have been **halls of mirrors** at funfairs, rooms with many different distorting mirrors. You go from mirror to mirror and look different each time. Science museums such as the Technorama in Winterthur also show curved mirrors where you can try out optics. Distorting mirrors are also used by artists and photographers for special effects.

Not all curved mirrors are there for fun. A **traffic mirror** at exits where you cannot see well bulges outwards and shows a large area of the road at once. Car wing mirrors are also often slightly curved so that you can see more. In return, the cars in them look smaller and further away than they really are.

begriffe.erklaerung: A picture of you that a mirror creates with reflected light.
Bulging outwards, like the outside of a ball.
Curving inwards, like the inside of a spoon.
The rule for how light bounces back from a smooth surface.

gewusst: With a small distorting mirror made of shiny metal foil, you can make your own hall of mirrors at home.
In a concave mirror your image can suddenly be upside down if you stand far enough away.
As early as the 19th century, distorting mirrors were a popular attraction at fairs.

teile.einleitung: Heat transfer is the name for all the processes by which heat gets from one place to another. There are three kinds: conduction, convection and radiation. Whether cooking, heating or sunbathing, heat transfer is always involved.
wichtigste: Heat is transferred in three ways: by conduction, convection and radiation.
On its own, heat always flows from the warmer to the colder.
Conduction needs contact between particles.
In convection, a flowing liquid or gas carries the heat.
Thermal radiation also works through a vacuum.
The Sun's warmth reaches us by radiation.
A vacuum flask slows down all three kinds of heat transfer.

abschnitte.text: When two things are at different temperatures, heat flows from the warmer to the colder. This goes on until both are equally warm. This balancing out is called **heat transfer**. Depending on the situation it happens by conduction, convection or radiation, and often by all three at once.

In **conduction**, particles pass their movement on to their neighbours without the substance itself moving. This needs contact, that is, a material through which the heat travels. If you put a metal spoon in hot tea, the handle soon gets warm too. Metals conduct heat well; air, wood and plastic conduct it poorly.

In **convection**, the warm substance itself moves. Warm air is lighter than cold air and therefore rises; this is how a radiator spreads heat round a room. In a saucepan, warm water rises from the bottom and colder water sinks. Wind and ocean currents such as the Gulf Stream also carry huge amounts of heat.

Every warm body gives off invisible **infrared radiation**. This **thermal radiation** needs no material and even travels through the vacuum of space. That is how the Sun's warmth reaches the Earth across about 150 million kilometres. At a campfire you feel it on your face, even when the air around you is cool.

The most important difference: conduction needs contact, radiation also works through a vacuum. That is why a cup of tea on a table can conduct heat into the table, but in space it can cool down only by radiation. Light coloured and shiny surfaces reflect thermal radiation, dark surfaces absorb it. Survival blankets therefore have a shiny silver side.

A **vacuum flask** has two walls of glass or steel with a vacuum between them. The vacuum prevents conduction and convection, and the mirrored walls reflect the radiation. This keeps tea hot or juice cold for hours. The Scottish scientist James Dewar invented this principle in 1892.

begriffe.erklaerung: Heat travels through a material from particle to particle.
Heat is carried along by a flowing liquid or gas.
Invisible radiation that carries heat even through empty space.
A space that is almost completely empty, with no air.

gewusst: Without thermal radiation, no warmth from the Sun would reach us, because the space in between is almost empty.
With thermal imaging cameras you can see the thermal radiation of people and animals even in the dark.
A hairdryer warms your hair mainly by convection: it blows warm air onto it.

teile.einleitung: Pliers are a tool with two handles and two jaws with which you can hold, bend or cut things. They multiply the force of your hand many times over. The secret behind them is the law of the lever.
wichtigste: Pliers consist of two levers joined by a pivot.
The front parts that grip are called jaws.
Long handles and short jaws make the jaws grip very tightly.
You have the most force when you hold the pliers at the ends of the handles.
With pincers you pull nails out of wood.
With side cutters you cut through thin wire.
Electricians' pliers have thick plastic handles for protection against electricity.

abschnitte.text: Pliers consist of two parts joined in the middle by a **pivot**. At the back are the long **handles**, at the front the short **jaws**. When you squeeze the handles together, the jaws close. Depending on the shape of the jaws, the pliers can hold, bend, squeeze or cut.

Each half of the pliers is a **lever** that turns about the pivot. According to the law of the lever, a long lever arm needs little force to produce a large force at the short lever arm. If, for example, the handles are five times as long as the jaws, the jaws press about five times as hard. That is why you hold the pliers at the end of the handles, where you have the most **force**.

With **pincers** you pull nails out of wood or nip them off. **Side cutters** have sharp blades and cut thin wire. Combination pliers can grip, bend and cut, while long nose pliers reach into tight spots. With pipe wrenches you tighten large pipes and nuts.

Electricians use pliers with thick plastic **insulation** on the handles. Plastic does not conduct electricity and so protects against an electric shock. Dentists also need forceps to pull teeth that can no longer be saved. In the kitchen you know grill tongs, which you use to turn hot sausages.

Pliers are among humanity's oldest tools. In the Bronze Age, **blacksmiths** already used tongs to take red hot metal out of the fire and hold it. The Romans already had pliers for many different jobs. Today most pliers are made of hardened steel.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bar that moves about a pivot and increases force.
The front parts of a pair of pliers that grip.
The point where the two halves of the pliers are joined.
A layer that does not let electricity through.

gewusst: From the point of view of physics, a pair of scissors is also a kind of pliers made of two levers.
The beaks of some birds work like pliers, for example when cracking nuts.
Crabs and lobsters have claws, which in German are also called “Zangen”, pliers.

teile.einleitung: A heat pump is a device that takes heat from the surroundings and releases it inside the house. It draws the heat from the air, the ground or groundwater and needs only a little electricity to do so. In Switzerland, heat pumps are very often fitted in new houses today.
wichtigste: A heat pump takes heat from the surroundings and releases it in the house.
It works like a fridge in reverse.
The heat source can be outdoor air, the ground or groundwater.
A refrigerant absorbs heat, is compressed and gives off the heat again at a higher temperature.
From one unit of electricity it makes about three to five units of heat.
Heat pumps do not burn oil or gas and are therefore climate friendly.
Many heat pumps can also cool in summer.

abschnitte.text: A heat pump is a **heating system** that does not produce heat itself but pumps it into the house from outside. Even cold winter air still contains heat energy that can be used. The heat pump raises this heat to a higher temperature that is enough for heating and hot water. To do this it needs electricity for a **compressor**.

Inside the heat pump, a **refrigerant** flows round a closed circuit. It evaporates even at very low temperatures and in doing so absorbs heat from the surroundings. The compressor squeezes the vapour, which makes it very hot, just as a bicycle pump gets warm when you pump up a tyre. In the house the hot refrigerant gives its heat to the heating water, cools down, is allowed to expand, and the cycle starts again.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the heat come from?
abschnitte.text: An **air source heat pump** takes heat from the outdoor air; you can recognise it by the fan outside the house. A **ground source heat pump** uses heat from the ground; for this, holes more than 100 metres deep are often drilled. Deep down it is roughly the same temperature all year round. Other systems use groundwater, lake water or waste heat.

A **fridge** is actually a heat pump too. It pumps heat out of the inside and releases it at the back into the kitchen, which is why it is warm there. The heat pump in a heating system does the same, only it brings heat from outside to inside. Some systems can switch over and cool the house in summer.

From one kilowatt hour of electricity, a good heat pump makes about three to five kilowatt hours of heat. This figure is called the **seasonal performance factor**. Ground source heat pumps are usually more efficient than air source heat pumps, because the ground is warmer than the air in winter. Heat pumps work best with underfloor heating, which needs only moderately warm water.

In Switzerland, heat pumps are now fitted in most new detached houses. Many old oil and gas heating systems are also being replaced by heat pumps, often with grants from the cantons. Because Swiss electricity comes mostly from hydropower and nuclear energy, heat pumps cause little **CO2**. They are therefore seen as an important technology for protecting the climate.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that evaporates even at low temperatures and carries heat.
A pump that squeezes a gas together and so heats it up.
A pipe deep in the ground through which liquid flows and picks up heat from the earth.
Shows how much heat a heat pump delivers per unit of electricity over a year.

gewusst: Even at minus 10 °C outside, an air source heat pump can still take heat from the air.
As early as the 19th century, Lord Kelvin described the idea of a heat pump.
From 1938, Zurich's town hall was heated by one of the first large heat pumps in Europe, which took heat from the River Limmat.

teile.einleitung: Central heating is a heating system in which a single heat source heats all the rooms of a house. The heat is usually carried by hot water through pipes to the radiators or into the floor. Today almost all homes in Switzerland have this kind of heating.
wichtigste: With central heating, one heat source heats all the rooms.
The heat is usually distributed by heating water in pipes.
A circulation pump makes the water flow round the circuit.
In the flow pipe, hot water goes to the radiators; in the return pipe, cooled water comes back.
An expansion vessel is needed because water expands when it is heated.
Thermostatic valves on the radiators control the room temperature.
The Romans already heated with the hypocaust, a kind of underfloor heating.

abschnitte.text: In the past, many rooms had their own stove, which was heated with wood or coal. With **central heating**, on the other hand, there is only one **heat source**, usually in the cellar. This can be an oil or gas boiler, a wood fired boiler or a **heat pump**. A connection to a district heating network is also possible. From there the heat is distributed throughout the whole house.

The boiler heats water that flows through a closed system of pipes. In the **flow pipe**, the warm water goes to the radiators. There it gives off its heat to the room and cools down. Through the **return pipe** it flows back to the boiler and is heated again. A **circulation pump** keeps this circuit moving.

Water expands when it is heated. An **expansion vessel** takes up the extra volume so that the pressure in the pipes does not rise too much. On the radiators there are **thermostatic valves**, which let more or less warm water through and so control the room temperature. A sensor on the outside wall of the house measures the outdoor temperature so that the heating supplies warmer water when it is cold. Sometimes you have to bleed air out of the radiators, because otherwise they gurgle and do not get properly warm.

The ancient Romans already knew a form of central heating, the **hypocaust**. A fire outside the room sent hot air under a floor that stood on small brick pillars. This was used especially to heat baths and grand houses. Remains of such systems can be seen in Switzerland, for example at **Augusta Raurica** near Basel. Water based heating as we know it today spread in the 19th and 20th centuries.

In Switzerland, for a long time heating oil was the main fuel. Today **heat pumps**, which use heat from the air, the ground or groundwater, are usually installed in new buildings. They go particularly well with **underfloor heating**, because it needs only lukewarm heating water. The large surface of the floor still gives off the heat well. Heating economically, for example with a slightly lower room temperature and short bursts of airing instead of tilted windows, saves money and protects the environment.

begriffe.erklaerung: The appliance that produces the heat for the whole house, for example a boiler.
The pipe in which hot water flows to the radiators.
The pipe in which cooled water flows back to the boiler.
A knob on the radiator that controls the room temperature.
The underfloor heating of the ancient Romans, with hot air under the floor.

gewusst: According to a widely used rule of thumb, lowering the room temperature by one degree saves about six per cent of heating energy.
The numbers on a thermostatic valve are not degrees; setting 3 usually corresponds to about 20 degrees.
At Augusta Raurica you can see the small brick pillars on which the floor of the Roman baths once rested.

teile.einleitung: A rack railway is a mountain railway that uses a gearwheel on very steep stretches. The gearwheel meshes with a toothed rail between the tracks, the rack. Switzerland is famous for its rack railways up the Rigi, the Pilatus or to the Jungfraujoch.
wichtigste: Rack railways have a gearwheel under the carriage that meshes with a rack.
This lets them climb steep slopes without slipping.
Since 1871, Europe's first rack railway has run up the Rigi.
The Pilatus Railway is considered the steepest rack railway in the world.
Switzerland's highest rack railway goes up to Jungfraujoch station.
The Brienz Rothorn Railway still often runs with steam locomotives today.
Because the lines are so steep, rack railways usually travel slowly.

abschnitte.text: An ordinary railway moves forward only through the friction between wheel and rail. Beyond a certain gradient, the smooth wheels would spin or the train would slide back. That is why on a rack railway there is a toothed **rack** between the rails. A **gearwheel** on the locomotive meshes with it, much as a bicycle cog meshes with the chain. In this way the train can go up and down safely and can also brake.

There are several kinds of rack, often named after Swiss engineers. The **Riggenbach system** looks like a ladder with rungs and was developed by Niklaus Riggenbach. In the **Abt system** by Roman Abt, two or three racks lie side by side with their teeth staggered, which makes the ride smoother. The Strub system is a simple rack with teeth on top. In the Locher system on the Pilatus, two horizontal gearwheels grip a rack from the left and the right.

On 21 May 1871 the **Vitznau Rigi Railway** began operating, the first mountain railway with a gearwheel in Europe. It was built by Niklaus Riggenbach and brought many visitors up the “Queen of the Mountains”. The **Pilatus Railway** from Alpnachstad up the Pilatus opened in 1889. With a gradient of up to 48 per cent, it is considered the steepest rack railway in the world. This means that over 100 m of track it climbs as much as 48 m.

The **Gornergrat Railway** runs from Zermatt up the Gornergrat, with a view of the Matterhorn. The **Wengernalp Railway** links Lauterbrunnen and Grindelwald with the Kleine Scheidegg. From there, the **Jungfrau Railway** runs through a tunnel in the Eiger and Mönch up to the Jungfraujoch, the highest railway station in Europe at 3454 m. The Brienz Rothorn Railway on Lake Brienz is known for its steam locomotives. Many of these railways were built between 1870 and 1912, when tourism in the Alps was booming.

The world's first mountain railway with a gearwheel ran up Mount Washington in the USA from 1869. After that, rack railways were built in many mountainous countries, for example in Austria, Germany and France. In Germany, the Zugspitze Railway runs up the country's highest mountain. Some railways use the gearwheel only on steep sections and otherwise run normally; they are called **mixed railways**. An example in Switzerland is the Zentralbahn over the Brünig Pass.

begriffe.erklaerung: A toothed rail between the tracks that the gearwheel meshes with.
A wheel with teeth round its edge that mesh with other teeth.
How steeply a line climbs, often given as a percentage.
A railway that uses the gearwheel only on steep sections.

gewusst: The carriages of the Pilatus Railway are built like steps, so that passengers can sit comfortably despite the gradient.
The Jungfrau Railway opened in 1912; building it took 16 years.
On the Rigi, rack railways climb from two sides, from Vitznau and from Arth-Goldau.

teile.einleitung: A wind turbine, also called a wind power plant or windmill, is a device that turns the force of the wind into electric current. Its huge rotor blades turn in the wind and drive a generator. In this way electricity is produced without burning coal, oil or gas.
wichtigste: A wind turbine turns the kinetic energy of the wind into electric current.
The wind turns the rotor blades, which drive a generator through a shaft.
Modern turbines are often more than 150 metres tall and usually have three rotor blades.
Wind power is a renewable energy, because the wind never runs out.
Many wind turbines together are called a wind farm.
The largest wind farm in Switzerland is on Mont-Crosin in the Bernese Jura.
One disadvantage is that wind turbines supply electricity only when the wind blows.

abschnitte.text: A wind turbine uses the wind to produce electricity. It consists of a tall **tower**, a machine housing at the top of the tower and the **rotor**, usually with three blades. In the machine housing, the so called **nacelle**, are the gearbox and the generator. The electricity is fed into the grid through cables.

The rotor blades are shaped like the wings of an aircraft. When wind flows past them, **lift** is produced, which sets the rotor turning. The rotation is passed on to a **generator**, which produces electricity like a big bicycle dynamo. Electronics automatically turn the nacelle into the wind and turn the blades out of the wind in a storm so that nothing breaks.

Modern wind turbines on land have hub heights of more than 100 metres and rotor diameters of more than 100 metres. The blade tips move at more than 200 kilometres per hour. Twice the wind speed brings about eight times as much **power**, which is why wind turbines are put in windy places such as coasts, hills and mountain ridges. At sea, particularly large turbines stand in **offshore wind farms**.

Many centuries ago, people were already using the wind with **windmills**, for example to grind grain or to pump water in the Netherlands. At the end of the 19th century, the first wind turbines that produced electricity were built. From the 1980s, wind turbines were greatly developed, above all in Denmark and Germany. Today China, the USA and Germany are among the countries with the most wind turbines.

In Switzerland, wind power so far supplies only a small share of electricity, less than one per cent (as of about 2024). Well known sites are the **Mont-Crosin** wind farm in the Bernese Jura, the Gotthard Pass and the Rhone valley in Valais. Many projects are controversial, because wind turbines change the landscape and can endanger birds and bats. In winter, when solar panels supply less electricity, there is often more wind, which is why wind power is seen as a good addition.

begriffe.erklaerung: A machine that makes electric current from rotation.
The turning part of the wind turbine with the rotor blades.
The machine housing at the top of the tower.
Energy from sources that do not get used up, such as wind, sun or water.

gewusst: A single rotor blade of a large turbine can be longer than a football pitch is wide.
A modern wind turbine on land can produce electricity for several thousand households a year.
The wind farm on the Gotthard Pass stands more than 2000 metres above sea level.

teile.einleitung: A turbine is a wheel with many curved blades that is turned by flowing water, steam, gas or wind. It turns the kinetic energy of the flow into a turning movement. In power stations it drives generators that produce electricity.
wichtigste: A turbine is a wheel with blades that turns.
The curved parts that the water hits are called blades.
In a power station the turbine is connected to the generator.
In nuclear power stations hot steam flows through the turbine.
In gas-fired power stations hot gas turns the turbine.
Aeroplanes fly with turbines in their engines.
The water wheel is an ancestor of the water turbine.
A water turbine turns faster when more water flows through it with more force.

abschnitte.text: A turbine is a **turbomachine**. A stream of water, steam, gas or air hits the curved **blades** of a rotor and makes it turn. The turning movement is passed on through a shaft. The word comes from the Latin turbo, which means whirl.

More than 2000 years ago people were already using **water wheels** to drive mills. In the 19th century these became much more powerful water turbines. Around 1827 the Frenchman Benoît Fourneyron built one of the first usable water turbines. Soon afterwards came the Francis turbine, the Pelton turbine and the Kaplan turbine.

Switzerland gets more than half of its electricity from **hydropower**. In the Alps water rushes from reservoirs down through penstocks to the turbines. Where the drop is large, the **Pelton turbine** is used, in which jets of water shoot onto spoon-shaped cups. In river power stations with only a small drop, on the other hand, Kaplan turbines turn, which look like large ships' propellers.

In nuclear and coal-fired power stations water is heated into hot steam, which flows through a **steam turbine**. In 1884 the Englishman Charles Parsons built an important early steam turbine. In gas-fired power stations hot combustion gases drive a **gas turbine** directly. The turbine turns the generator, and this produces electricity.

The engines of large aeroplanes contain gas turbines. At the front a large fan sucks in air, which is compressed, burned with fuel and pushed out at the back. The hot gases turn a turbine, which in turn drives the compressor and the fan. That is why in everyday language the whole engine is often simply called a turbine.

A **wind turbine** is also a kind of turbine, turned by the flow of air. Cars have turbochargers, which use exhaust gases to drive a small turbine wheel. The more water or gas flows through with more force, the faster and more powerfully a turbine turns. Large power station turbines can supply as much electricity as a whole city needs.

begriffe.erklaerung: A curved vane on the turbine wheel that the flow hits.
A machine that turns a turning movement into electricity.
A water turbine with cups for large drops.
The difference in height that the water falls down.
A machine that gets energy from a flowing substance.

gewusst: In Valais there are power stations where the water falls well over a thousand metres down to the turbines.
The Pelton turbine was invented by the American Lester Pelton, who wanted to supply gold mines with energy.
The turbines of large aircraft engines turn many thousands of times a minute.

teile.einleitung: Hydrogen is the lightest element and could become an important energy carrier of the future. It can be made from water using electricity, stored, and later turned back into electricity or heat. The only exhaust is water, but a lot of energy is lost along the way.
wichtigste: Hydrogen is the lightest element in the periodic table.
In electrolysis, water is split into hydrogen and oxygen with the help of electricity.
A fuel cell produces electricity directly from hydrogen and oxygen.
Green hydrogen is made with electricity from renewable energy.
Most hydrogen today is grey hydrogen made from natural gas.
In fuel cell cars, hydrogen is usually stored at about 700 bar.
Making hydrogen and turning it back into electricity loses much more energy than a battery does.

abschnitte.text: **Hydrogen** has the chemical symbol H and comes right at the start of the periodic table. A hydrogen atom consists of just one proton and one electron. Hydrogen is the most common element in the universe; the Sun is made mostly of it. On Earth it is found almost only in compounds, for example in water. As a gas it is colourless, odourless and very easily set alight.

Hydrogen is not an energy source like the sun or wind but an **energy carrier**. You first have to put energy in to make it. In **electrolysis**, electric current splits water into hydrogen and oxygen. The hydrogen can be stored and transported. Later it gives the energy back, for example in a fuel cell.

Depending on how it is made, hydrogen is given a colour. **Green hydrogen** is made with electricity from the sun, wind or hydropower and is climate friendly. **Grey hydrogen** comes from natural gas, and a lot of carbon dioxide is produced in the process. It makes up most of the production today. With blue hydrogen, the carbon dioxide is captured and stored.

A **fuel cell** lets hydrogen and oxygen react with each other in a controlled way and produces electricity directly. Only water vapour comes out of the exhaust. In the tanks of fuel cell cars, hydrogen is usually stored at about 700 bar, which is about 300 times more pressure than in a bicycle tyre. In Switzerland, lorries running on hydrogen have been on the roads since 2020. Hydrogen is also being tested for trains, ships and industry.

Hydrogen can store energy from the summer and make it usable in winter. A big **disadvantage** is that a lot of energy is lost in making, storing and turning it back into electricity. In the end often only about a third is left, whereas with a battery it is much more. In addition, hydrogen and oxygen form the explosive **oxyhydrogen**. That is why tight tanks, sensors and strict safety rules are needed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that stores and transports energy, for example petrol or hydrogen.
A process in which electricity breaks a substance such as water down into its parts.
A device that produces electricity from hydrogen and oxygen.
An explosive mixture of hydrogen and oxygen.
A unit of pressure; the air around us is at about 1 bar.

gewusst: A kilogram of hydrogen contains about three times as much energy as a kilogram of petrol.
The airship Hindenburg was filled with hydrogen and went up in flames in 1937.

teile.einleitung: A thermal power station is a power station that produces electricity with the help of heat. Chemical energy from fuels or nuclear energy is first turned into heat, then into movement and finally into electrical energy. Coal, gas, nuclear and waste power stations are examples.
wichtigste: A thermal power station produces electricity from heat.
The heat comes from fuels such as coal, gas, wood or rubbish, or from nuclear energy.
The heat turns water into steam, which drives a turbine.
The turbine turns a generator, which produces electricity.
A large part of the heat stays unused and has to be carried away.
In Switzerland the nuclear power stations are the most important thermal power stations.
Coal and gas power stations emit a lot of carbon dioxide.

abschnitte.titel: What is a thermal power station?
abschnitte.text: A thermal power station converts energy in several steps. First **chemical energy** from a fuel or **nuclear energy** becomes heat. The heat produces movement, and this becomes electrical energy. Worldwide, most electricity comes from such power stations.

In a boiler the heat is used to heat water until it becomes hot **steam** under high pressure. The steam flows through a **turbine** and makes its bladed wheels spin fast.
