The turbine is connected to a **generator**, which produces electricity like a giant bicycle dynamo. After that the steam is cooled, turns back into water and is pumped back into the boiler.

Coal power stations burn hard coal or brown coal. **Gas power stations** burn natural gas, and modern combined cycle power stations use the heat twice over. In nuclear power stations the splitting of uranium supplies the heat. Waste incineration plants, wood-fired power stations and some solar thermal power stations are also thermal power stations.

A thermal power station can never turn all the heat into electricity, often only about a third to just under two thirds. The rest of the heat has to be carried away, for example by a river or a **cooling tower**. The white clouds above cooling towers are not smoke but water vapour. If the waste heat is used for district heating, this is called combined heat and power.

In Switzerland it is mainly the nuclear power stations Beznau, Gösgen and Leibstadt that supply electricity from heat. The Mühleberg nuclear power station in the canton of Bern was shut down at the end of 2019. Gösgen and Leibstadt have large cooling towers that can be seen from far away. In addition, many **waste incineration plants** produce electricity and heat whole neighbourhoods through district heating networks.

Thermal power stations supply electricity reliably, whether the sun is shining or the wind is blowing. But coal and gas power stations emit a lot of **carbon dioxide** and so add to climate change. Nuclear power stations emit hardly any CO2, but they produce radioactive waste that has to be stored safely for a very long time. That is why there is discussion all over the world about how electricity should be produced in future.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wheel with many blades that is turned by steam, water or wind.
A machine that turns a turning movement into electric current.
A tall tower in which surplus heat is released into the air.
Hot water from a power station that heats houses through pipes.

gewusst: The cooling towers of Gösgen and Leibstadt are among the tallest structures in Switzerland and can be seen from far away.
The first public steam power stations for electricity started operating in London and New York in 1882.
The white plume above a cooling tower consists of tiny water droplets, like a cloud.

teile.einleitung: When you sit in front of a campfire, you feel the heat on your face, even though the hot air rises upwards. This is due to thermal radiation. It is invisible light that every body gives off, and it even brings the Sun's warmth to us through empty space.
wichtigste: All bodies give off thermal radiation, depending on their temperature.
Thermal radiation is mostly infrared radiation, which our eyes cannot see.
William Herschel discovered infrared radiation in the year 1800.
Thermal radiation does not need air and even travels through the vacuum of space.
A black body absorbs all the radiation that falls on it completely.
If the absolute temperature doubles, the power radiated rises sixteenfold.
Shiny surfaces such as a survival blanket reflect thermal radiation.

abschnitte.text: **Thermal radiation** is a form of electromagnetic radiation, just like light and radio waves. Every body gives it off, an ice cube just as much as the Sun. At room temperature it lies in the range of **infrared radiation**, which we cannot see but can feel on our skin. Very hot bodies such as red hot iron or the filament of an old light bulb also glow visibly red, yellow or white. Heat can also spread by conduction and by convection, but radiation is the only way that needs no material at all.

In the year 1800 the astronomer **William Herschel** split sunlight into its colours with a prism. He placed thermometers in the different colours. Next to the red light, where nothing could be seen at all, the temperature rose the most. In this way he discovered invisible **infrared radiation**. Herschel was born in Germany and lived in England, where he also found the planet Uranus.

An ideal **black body** absorbs all the radiation that hits it and is itself a particularly good radiator. Dark, matt surfaces come close to this, whereas shiny surfaces reflect radiation. The power radiated grows with the fourth power of the absolute temperature; this is described by the **Stefan-Boltzmann law**. So if you double the temperature in kelvin, the radiation rises by a factor of 16. That is why a fire radiates so much more strongly than a warm stove.

Under a **sunshade** it is more pleasant, even though the air is almost the same temperature, because it blocks the Sun's radiation. A car in the sun gets very hot inside: light comes in through the windows, but the thermal radiation from the hot seats hardly gets out. The Earth's greenhouse effect works in a similar way. A silver **survival blanket** reflects the body's thermal radiation and keeps injured people warm. A vacuum flask is also mirrored on the inside.

With a **thermal imaging camera** you can make thermal radiation visible. Warm spots appear bright or red, cold ones dark or blue. Fire brigades use this to find people in smoke filled rooms or hidden pockets of embers. On a house, the camera shows where heat escapes through poor insulation. Some snakes, such as pit vipers, sense the thermal radiation of their prey with special sense organs.

begriffe.erklaerung: Invisible radiation beyond red that you feel as heat.
An imaginary body that absorbs all radiation and is a particularly good radiator.
Temperature in kelvin, counted from absolute zero at about minus 273 °C.
A camera that makes thermal radiation visible as a picture.

gewusst: You yourself are constantly giving off heat; in a thermal imaging camera you glow brightly.
All the energy that reaches the Earth from the Sun comes as radiation through empty space.

teile.einleitung: A watermill uses the force of flowing water to drive machines. For centuries such mills ground grain into flour, sawed wood or forged iron. They are the ancestors of today's hydroelectric power stations.
wichtigste: A watermill is driven by a waterwheel.
If the water falls onto the wheel from above, it is called overshot.
A channel, the mill race, leads the water to the millwheel.
Through gearwheels, the waterwheel turns the millstone.
In sawmills tree trunks were sawn up, and in hammer mills iron was forged.
Old waterwheels were mostly built of wood.
Today's hydroelectric power stations use a turbine instead of a millwheel.

abschnitte.text: A **mill race** leads water from a river or stream to the millwheel. The water presses on the paddles or fills small buckets, and the wheel starts to turn. Through a shaft and **gearwheels**, the rotation is carried into the inside of the mill. There the heavy upper **millstone** turns above a fixed lower stone. The grain is ground into flour between them.

With an **overshot** wheel, the water falls into the buckets from above, and the weight of the water turns the wheel. It suits small streams with a steep drop, as are often found in hills and mountains. With an **undershot** wheel, the water flows against the paddles at the bottom, which suits wide, flat rivers. In between there is the breastshot wheel. Old waterwheels were mostly built of wood and often had to be repaired.

Water power did not drive only grain mills. In the **sawmill**, in Switzerland often called a “Sagi”, tree trunks were sawn into planks. In the **hammer mill**, the waterwheel lifted a heavy hammer that struck red hot iron. Other mills pressed oil, pounded rags into paper or drove looms. That is why whole villages and trades grew up along streams and rivers.

The Greeks and **Romans** already knew about watermills. At Barbegal in southern France, the Romans ran a site with 16 waterwheels. In the Middle Ages watermills spread across the whole of Europe, and almost every village had one. The miller was an important man, because everyone needed flour for their bread. With the steam engine and later the electric motor, many mills lost their job.

Today's **hydroelectric power stations** use a **turbine** instead of a millwheel. It turns much faster and drives a generator that produces electricity. In Switzerland, more than half of the electricity comes from hydropower. Many old mills are museums today or have been converted into small power stations. In some you can still watch the wheel turning and flour being ground.

begriffe.erklaerung: A channel that leads water to the millwheel.
A heavy, round stone used to grind grain into flour.
A waterwheel onto which the water falls from above.
A fast turning bladed wheel in modern power stations.

gewusst: The common surname Müller (Miller in English) is a reminder of how many people used to work in mills.
A big waterwheel often turned only a few times a minute, but it had a lot of power.

teile.einleitung: A seesaw is a long board that rests on a pivot in the middle so that it can rock up and down. In many playgrounds, two children sit at the ends and take turns going up and down. Along the way you experience one of the most important laws of physics: the law of the lever.
wichtigste: The point in the middle around which the seesaw moves is called the pivot.
If your side goes down, the other side goes up.
Two children of the same weight sitting the same distance out keep the seesaw balanced.
Whoever slides closer to the pivot acts lighter; whoever sits further out acts heavier.
You go up by pushing off with your legs.
Pieces of rubber or car tyres under the ends soften the bump.
If one child suddenly jumps off, the other falls down hard.

abschnitte.text: A seesaw is a **two sided lever**: a long beam resting on a bearing in the middle. This bearing is called the **pivot**. On each side there is a seat, often with a handle in front of it to hold on to. Playground seesaws are usually made of wood or metal and are firmly anchored in the ground.

Whether the seesaw tips depends not only on weight but also on how far from the pivot someone sits. The rule is: weight times distance must be the same on both sides; then there is **balance**. This **law of the lever** was already described by the Greek scholar Archimedes more than 2000 years ago. So if two children of the same weight sit the same distance out, the seesaw stays level.

A heavy adult and a light child can still seesaw together. The adult slides closer to the pivot, and the child sits right at the end. Two small children can even lift an adult if together they sit right at the end and he sits further in. The longer **lever arm** makes up for the smaller weight.

When you reach the bottom, you push off the ground with your **legs**. This makes your side go up, and the other side sinks. When your side hits the bottom, you feel a jolt, because you are suddenly **brought to a stop**. That is why pieces of rubber or old car tyres often lie under the ends to cushion the bump.

On the seesaw you should always hold on to the **handle** with both hands. If one child suddenly jumps off while the other is up in the air, that child falls down hard and can be hurt. So you say so before you get off. Feet and hands never belong under the board when it comes down.

You find the principle of the seesaw in many places. A **beam balance**, as was once used at markets, works in exactly the same way. A well sweep, a pair of scissors or a crane also use the lever. In playgrounds there are also spring seesaws that rock on a thick coil spring.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point around which something turns.
A rigid beam that turns about a point and passes on forces.
The distance from the pivot to the point where the force acts.
The state in which both sides exactly even each other out.

gewusst: Archimedes is said to have claimed that with a long enough lever he could move the world.
A child of 20 kilograms can balance an adult of 60 kilograms if the child sits three times as far from the pivot.
In English it is called a “seesaw”; in German it is called a “Wippe”.

teile.einleitung: The water pistol is a popular toy for hot summer days. Press the trigger and a jet of water shoots out. Behind it lies exciting physics about pressure, pumps and the path of water through the air.
wichtigste: In a simple water pistol, a small pump pushes water out.
The faster and harder you press, the stronger the jet.
With big water pistols, you first pump air together in the tank.
The squeezed air pushes the water out; over time the jet gets weaker.
A jet of water always falls downwards in a curve.
The jet flies furthest when you aim at a slant upwards.
You should never aim at other people's eyes.

abschnitte.text: A simple **water pistol** has a tank, a trigger and a small **pump**. When you pull the trigger, a piston pushes water out through a narrow nozzle. Small **valves** make sure the water flows in one direction only. When you let go, the pump sucks new water in from the tank. The faster and harder you press, the stronger the jet.

With big water pistols, you pump several times before squirting. This squeezes the **air in the tank**, and the pressure rises. When you open the valve, the air pushes the water out powerfully. The more water flows out, the more room the air has, and the pressure falls. That is why the jet gets weaker if you squirt for a long time, and if the tank has a hole, the air escapes and the jet stays weak.

If you squirt straight ahead, the jet of water falls downwards in a **curve**. Gravity pulls the water down while it flies forwards. This path is called a **parabola**. Without air resistance, the jet flies furthest if you aim upwards at an angle of 45 degrees. Fountains and garden hoses show such curves too.

The famous water pistol **Super Soaker** was invented by the American engineer **Lonnie Johnson**. He worked for the space agency NASA and was experimenting with a pump in the 1980s. A powerful jet of water shot across his bathroom. From 1990 the Super Soaker was sold and became one of the most successful toys in the world. It uses exactly the principle of squeezed air.

With a water pistol you should never aim at other people's **eyes**, because a strong jet can injure the eyes. You also do not squirt at animals, electrical appliances or people who do not want to play. It is best to fill it with clean water. After playing, you empty the tank so that no germs grow. In summer, a water fight is a welcome way to cool down.

begriffe.erklaerung: A narrow opening through which water shoots out fast.
A small flap that lets water or air through in one direction only.
How hard something presses on a surface, for example air in the tank.
The curved path of something that is thrown or squirted.

gewusst: The inventor of the Super Soaker has registered more than a hundred patents.
As it flies, a jet of water breaks up into many small drops, which you can see well against the light.

teile.einleitung: A diverging lens is a lens made of glass or plastic that is thinner in the middle than at the edge. It makes rays of light spread apart instead of focusing them. It is found in glasses for short sighted people, in door viewers and in telescopes.
wichtigste: A diverging lens is thinner in the middle than at the edge.
Its shape is called concave.
Parallel rays of light spread apart behind it.
It has a negative power and a virtual focal point.
On its own, it makes smaller, upright, virtual images of a real object.
You cannot focus sunlight to a hot spot with it.
A door viewer often contains a diverging lens.

abschnitte.text: Lenses are transparent bodies that bend light by **refraction**. There are two basic kinds: converging lenses, which are thicker in the middle, and **diverging lenses**, which are thinner in the middle. The typical shape is called **concave**, that is, curved inwards. There are biconcave lenses, which are curved on both sides, and plano concave ones, which are flat on one side.

Light is bent when it passes from air into glass and back again. In a diverging lens the rays are bent outwards, so that parallel rays spread apart behind the lens. If you imagine these rays extended backwards, they meet at a point in front of the lens, the **virtual focal point**. Because the lens does not gather the light, you cannot make a fire with it.

With **short sightedness**, the eye is a little too long or bends the light too strongly. The sharp image then forms in front of the retina, and distant things look blurred. Glasses with diverging lenses spread the light out a little beforehand, so that the image forms exactly on the retina again. The strength of such lenses is given as a negative number in dioptres, for example −2 dioptres.

In the **door viewer** in a front door, a diverging lens makes sure that you can see a large area in front of the door through a small hole. The people appear smaller, but upright. In Galileo Galilei's telescope, a diverging lens served as the eyepiece, the lens next to the eye. In camera lenses too, diverging lenses are combined with converging lenses to reduce image faults.

The **power** of a lens tells you how strongly it bends light and is measured in dioptres. It is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres. For diverging lenses it is negative, for converging lenses positive. So a lens with a focal length of −0.5 m has a power of −2 dioptres.

begriffe.erklaerung: Curved inwards, thinner in the middle.
The bending of light when it passes from one material into another.
An image that you see only through the lens and cannot catch on a screen.
The unit for the power of a lens.
You see near things sharply but distant things blurred.

gewusst: You can often tell that someone wears glasses for short sightedness because their eyes look smaller behind the lenses.
If you hold a diverging lens and an equally strong converging lens together, their effects cancel out.
An air bubble in water also acts like a diverging lens.

teile.einleitung: When a car brakes, a bike stops or you land after a jump, you slow down. In physics this decrease in speed is called deceleration. It is really an acceleration that acts against the direction of movement.
wichtigste: Deceleration means that speed decreases.
Like acceleration, it is measured in metres per second squared, that is m/s².
A deceleration of 5 m/s² means: every second you become 5 m/s or 18 km/h slower.
In an emergency stop on a dry road a car manages about 8 m/s².
You work out the braking time by dividing the speed by the deceleration.
A crumple zone lengthens the braking distance in an impact and so lowers the deceleration.
Large decelerations mean large forces on the body.

abschnitte.text: **Deceleration** tells you how quickly something slows down. In physics it is a **negative acceleration**. You calculate: deceleration equals the decrease in speed divided by the time. A bike that stops evenly from 6 m/s in 2 seconds has a deceleration of 3 m/s². A train decelerating at 0.5 m/s² becomes 5 m/s slower in 10 seconds.

If a vehicle travels at 10 m/s and brakes at 2 m/s², it stands still after 5 seconds. To convert from m/s to km/h you multiply by 3.6. That is why 5 m/s² means exactly 18 km/h less every second. You work out the **braking distance** with the formula: speed squared divided by twice the deceleration. So at double the speed the braking distance becomes four times as long.

In an **emergency stop** on a dry road a car reaches about 8 m/s². On a wet road or on snow the deceleration is much smaller, because the tyres grip less well. A car at 100 km/h needs about 50 metres on a dry road before it stops. On top of this comes the **reaction distance**, which the car travels before the foot is even on the brake. That is why keeping enough distance is so important.

The shorter a braking distance, the greater the deceleration and the greater the forces. A **crumple zone** in a car deforms in an impact and so lengthens the distance over which it slows down. Airbags and seat belts also make sure the body is slowed down more gently. When you bend your knees after a jump, the slowing down takes longer and is gentler. This protects joints and bones.

Decelerations are often compared with the **acceleration due to gravity**, g, which is about 9.81 m/s². So an emergency stop in a car is almost 1 g. In an accident 30 g and more can occur for a brief moment. Space capsules returning to Earth are strongly slowed down in the atmosphere, and the crew feels several g. Parachutes reduce speed so that the landing is not too hard.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much distance something covers in a certain time.
How quickly the speed changes.
The distance a vehicle needs from the start of braking until it stands still.
A part of a car that squashes together on purpose in an impact.

gewusst: If you drive twice as fast, you do not need twice the braking distance, but four times as much.
Woodpeckers withstand very large decelerations when hammering on wood without injuring themselves.

teile.einleitung: The slipstream is the area behind a body in which there is less wind. Anyone who rides or runs close behind someone else has to fight less against air resistance and saves a lot of energy. Cyclists, runners, racing drivers and even migrating birds use this trick.
wichtigste: In the slipstream, air resistance is much smaller.
In a group of cyclists, the rider at the front works hardest against air resistance.
That is why cyclists in a breakaway group regularly take turns at the front.
Racing drivers use the slipstream of the car in front to overtake.
In many triathlons, riding in someone's slipstream on the bike course is forbidden, because it gives an unfair advantage.
For slow walkers, the slipstream hardly matters.
Large migrating birds often fly in a V shape to save energy.

abschnitte.text: When a body moves through the air, it has to push the air aside. You feel this work as **air resistance**. Behind the body there is an area with swirls and lower air pressure, the **slipstream**. Anyone in it is slowed down less and is even pulled along a little.

Air resistance grows sharply with speed, roughly with its square. If you go twice as fast, it is about four times as great. For slow **walkers** it is therefore tiny, but for racing cyclists at 40 to 50 kilometres per hour it is the biggest brake. That is why cyclists can save a great deal of energy in the slipstream.

In the **peloton**, the big main field of a cycle race, most riders are sheltered in the slipstream. The rider at the front works hardest. In a **breakaway group**, the riders therefore regularly take turns at the front so that each one can recover at the back. Before the finish, teammates form a **lead out train** to bring their sprinter forward in the slipstream.

In motor races, drivers stay close behind the car in front, gain speed in the slipstream and then pull out to **overtake**. In running, **pacemakers** set the pace and shield the runners from the wind. In Vienna in 2019, with the help of many pacemakers, Eliud Kipchoge became the first person to run a marathon in under two hours. Because the conditions were special, the time does not count as an official world record.

Because the slipstream helps so much, it is not allowed everywhere. In many **triathlons**, competitors have to keep a minimum distance on the bike course, otherwise they get a time penalty. This is called the drafting ban. In road cycling, on the other hand, riding in the slipstream is an important part of tactics.

Large migrating birds such as geese, cranes or pelicans often fly in a **V shape**. Each bird uses swirls of air from the bird in front, which give it lift, and so saves energy on the long flight. The birds take turns at the front, much like cyclists. Lorries and trains also save energy when they travel close behind each other, but on the road this is dangerous because of the safe distance needed.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which the air slows down a moving body.
The big main field in a cycle race.
A runner who sets the pace at the front and helps others.
Riders who pull away from the main field and ride at the front.

gewusst: A cyclist in the middle of the peloton often needs much less effort than the rider at the front.
The rider at the front also benefits a little when someone rides close behind.
In team pursuit speed skating, the athletes also skate close behind one another.

teile.einleitung: A hydroelectric power station produces electricity from the force of flowing or falling water. In Switzerland, hydropower is the most important source of electricity, thanks to the many mountains, lakes and rivers. The water drives a turbine, and a generator turns this into electricity.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, most electricity comes from hydropower; in 2024 it was about 60 per cent.
A hydroelectric power station uses the potential and kinetic energy of water.
Water drives a turbine, which produces electricity with a generator.
There are river power stations, storage power stations with reservoirs and pumped storage power stations.
Hydropower is renewable, because it keeps raining and snowing.
Hydroelectric power stations produce hardly any CO2 and no smoke.
Fish ladders help fish to swim past river power stations.

abschnitte.text: Water that lies high up has **potential energy**. When it flows or falls down, this becomes **kinetic energy**. The water flows through a **turbine** and turns it like a windmill. The turbine is connected to a generator, which turns the rotation into electric current. The more water flows and the further it falls, the more electricity is produced.

A **river power station** stands on a river and uses a lot of water with a small drop, for example on the Rhine and the Aare. A **storage power station** collects water in a reservoir high in the mountains and, when needed, lets it plunge far down through pipes. A pumped storage power station pumps water into a higher lake when there is plenty of spare electricity. When a lot of electricity is needed later, it lets the water flow down again. In this way it works like a giant battery.

For big drops in the Alps, the **Pelton turbine** is used. In it, a sharp jet of water shoots onto spoon shaped buckets on a wheel. For small drops and lots of water, as in river power stations, the **Kaplan turbine** is suitable; it looks like a ship's propeller. In between, the Francis turbine is often used. The Pelton turbine was invented in the USA in the 19th century.

Switzerland is sometimes called the water tower of Europe, because many big rivers rise here. In Valais and the Grisons there are numerous reservoirs, such as the Lac des Dix behind the **Grande Dixence** dam. The Nant de Drance pumped storage power station in Valais went into operation in 2022 and lies deep inside the mountain. On the Rhine at Rheinfelden stands one of the oldest large river power stations in Europe. In winter, the storage lakes supply particularly valuable electricity, when other sources supply less.

Hydroelectric power stations produce hardly any CO2 and are therefore good for the climate. They can supply electricity very quickly when it is needed. But dams greatly change valleys and rivers, and fish can no longer migrate freely. That is why **fish ladders** are built and care is taken that enough **residual flow** stays in the streams. In the past, people used waterwheels to grind corn in mills or to drive saws.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wheel with blades that turns because of flowing water.
A machine that turns rotation into electricity.
An artificial lake behind a dam that stores water.
A power station that pumps water up and later lets it down again to produce electricity.
Water that must stay in the stream below a power station so that animals and plants can live.

gewusst: The largest hydroelectric power station in the world is the Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze in China.
A pumped storage power station uses more electricity for pumping than it produces later, but it is still useful as a store.
The Romans already used waterwheels to grind grain.

teile.einleitung: Alkanes are the simplest compounds of carbon and hydrogen. Their atoms are joined only by single bonds, which is why they are called saturated hydrocarbons. They include methane in natural gas, propane in barbecue gas bottles and many components of petrol.
wichtigste: Alkanes consist only of carbon and hydrogen, joined by single bonds.
Unbranched alkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, and cycloalkanes CₙH₂ₙ.
Boiling points rise with chain length, because the van der Waals forces increase.
Pentane is the first unbranched alkane that is liquid at room temperature.
Alkanes are non polar and practically do not dissolve in water.
Burning one molecule of propane takes 5 oxygen molecules.
2,2,4-trimethylpentane has an octane number of 100 and is the reference for petrol.

abschnitte.text: Alkanes are **hydrocarbons** whose carbon atoms are joined only by single bonds. Each carbon atom forms four bonds. Because there is no room for more hydrogen atoms, alkanes are called **saturated**. The formula of unbranched alkanes is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, and ring shaped **cycloalkanes** have the formula CₙH₂ₙ.

The alkanes form a **homologous series**, in which each member has one more CH₂ group. The first ones are called methane, ethane, propane and butane. After that come names with Greek number words: pentane, hexane, heptane (C₇H₁₆), octane and so on. Hexane has the formula C₆H₁₄ and a molar mass of about 86 grams per mole.

Short alkanes up to butane are gases at room temperature; from **pentane** onwards they are liquid, and very long chains are solid like candle wax. Boiling points rise with chain length, because the **van der Waals forces** between longer molecules are stronger. Branched molecules such as the ball shaped 2,2-dimethylpropane boil at a lower temperature than pentane, because they have less contact area. Alkanes are non polar and **hydrophobic**, which is why they do not mix with water.

Alkanes burn well and release a lot of energy. Complete combustion produces **carbon dioxide** and water. A propane molecule C₃H₈ needs 5 oxygen molecules for this, producing 3 molecules of CO₂ and 4 molecules of water. If there is not enough oxygen, poisonous carbon monoxide and soot are also produced.

**Methane** is the main component of natural gas and biogas. Propane and butane are filled into gas bottles for barbecues, camping and lighters. Petrol, diesel and heating oil are mixtures of many alkanes obtained from crude oil in refineries. **2,2,4-trimethylpentane**, with an octane number of 100, serves as the standard for the knock resistance of petrol.

Burning alkanes from crude oil and natural gas produces carbon dioxide, which contributes to **climate change**. Methane itself is also a powerful greenhouse gas, which is released by cows and from swamps too. That is why people are looking for alternatives, such as electricity from renewable sources. But long alkanes such as paraffin are still used for candles, ointments and waxes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance made only of carbon and hydrogen.
Having only single bonds, so that no more hydrogen atoms can be added.
A series of substances that each differ by one CH₂ group.
Water repellent, not mixing with water.
A measure of how knock resistant a petrol is.

gewusst: Natural gas has no smell of its own; a scent is added so that leaks are noticed.
Paraffin candle wax consists of alkanes with about 20 to 40 carbon atoms.
Saturn's moon Titan has lakes of liquid methane and ethane.

teile.einleitung: The law of radioactive decay describes how the amount of a radioactive substance decreases over time. It says that in equal periods of time, the same proportion of the remaining atomic nuclei always decays. With it you can, for example, work out the age of bones, wood or rock.
wichtigste: The number of undecayed nuclei decreases exponentially.
After one half life, only half of the nuclei are left.
The decay of a single nucleus is random and cannot be predicted.
Only with very many nuclei does the exact law emerge.
Temperature and pressure have practically no influence on the half life.
Activity is measured in becquerels; one becquerel is one decay per second.
After 7 half lives, less than 1 % of the sample is left for the first time.

abschnitte.text: Some atomic nuclei are unstable and at some point change by themselves, giving off **radiation** as they do so. This process is called **radioactive decay**. The law of radioactive decay describes how many nuclei are still left after a certain time. It is N(t) = N₀ · e^(-λt), where N₀ is the starting number of nuclei and λ is the decay constant.

The **half life** is the time after which half of the nuclei have decayed. After two half lives a quarter remains, after three an eighth and after four a sixteenth. So if only 1/16 of a sample is left after 12 hours, four half lives of 3 hours each have passed. A sample with 6400 Bq has only 400 Bq left after four half lives.

Nobody can predict when a single nucleus will decay; it is pure **chance**. You can picture it like lots of dice that you keep throwing, removing each one that shows a six. With a single die you never know when it will go, but with thousands of dice, almost exactly a sixth disappears in each round. That is why the law of radioactive decay holds very precisely as soon as a sample contains billions of nuclei.

On an ordinary graph, the curve first falls steeply and then flatter and flatter, without ever quite reaching zero. This shape is called an **exponential function**. If you plot the number of nuclei on a logarithmic axis, it becomes a falling straight line. From the gradient of this line you can read off the half life.

The law of radioactive decay is used to find the age of finds. In **radiocarbon dating**, you measure how much carbon 14 is still present in wood, bone or cloth; its half life is about 5730 years. In this way, for example, the age of the glacier mummy Ötzi was determined as about 5300 years. For very old rocks, substances such as uranium with half lives of billions of years are used.

The Frenchman **Henri Becquerel** discovered radioactivity in 1896, and the unit becquerel is named after him. Shortly afterwards, Marie and Pierre Curie studied radioactive elements such as radium and polonium. Around 1902, Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy realised that atoms change in the process and that the amount decreases exponentially. In Switzerland today, the Federal Office of Public Health monitors radioactivity in the environment.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tiny centre of an atom, made of protons and neutrons.
The time after which half of the radioactive nuclei have decayed.
The unit of activity, one decay per second.
A decrease in which the same proportion always disappears in equal times.
The number of decays in a sample per second.

gewusst: According to the law of radioactive decay, a radioactive sample never disappears completely; it only gets weaker and weaker.
In your body too, a few thousand atomic nuclei decay every second, for example of potassium 40; this is completely natural.
Half lives range from tiny fractions of a second to billions of years.

teile.einleitung: An addition reaction is a chemical reaction in which atoms or molecules attach themselves to a double or triple bond. The multiple bond opens up, and two substances become a single product without anything left over. Such reactions are important for making plastics, margarine and many other substances.
wichtigste: In an addition, atoms attach to a multiple bond without any by product being formed.
Typical are additions to alkenes with a C=C double bond and to alkynes with a triple bond.
Bromine water loses its colour on contact with a C=C double bond.
Ethene and bromine give 1,2-dibromoethane, and ethene and hydrogen chloride give chloroethane.
According to Markovnikov's rule, propene and hydrogen bromide give mainly 2-bromopropane.
The addition of hydrogen is called hydrogenation and is used to harden fats.
When very many ethene molecules join together, the plastic polyethylene is formed.

abschnitte.text: The word **addition** means adding on. In organic chemistry, atoms attach themselves to a **multiple bond** between carbon atoms. The double bond becomes a single bond, and a new atom bonds to each of the two carbon atoms. Because all the atoms end up in the product, no by product is formed.

With **bromine water** you can test whether a substance has double bonds. Bromine water is yellowish brown. If you add an alkene such as ethene, the bromine attaches to the double bond and colourless 1,2-dibromoethane is formed. So the **loss of colour** shows that a C=C double bond was present.

abschnitte.titel: How it happens and the rules
abschnitte.text: In the addition of bromine, a ring shaped intermediate, the **bromonium ion**, forms first. Then a second bromine particle attacks from the other side. With unsymmetrical alkenes such as propene, **Markovnikov's rule** applies: the hydrogen atom goes to the carbon atom that already carries more hydrogen. So propene and hydrogen bromide give mainly 2-bromopropane.

The addition of hydrogen is called **hydrogenation**. It needs a catalyst, for example nickel or platinum. In the food industry, liquid vegetable oils are turned into solid fats in this way; this is called **fat hardening**. With ethyne and its triple bond, 1 mol of ethyne needs 2 mol of hydrogen until ethane is formed.

When very many small molecules join through their double bonds to form long chains, this is called **polymerisation**. In this way ethene becomes **polyethylene**, the most common plastic in the world. Plastic bags, films and many bottle tops are made of it. Polypropylene and polystyrene are formed in a similar way.

If **water** adds to ethene, ethanol, that is alcohol, is formed; this is called hydration. With hydrogen chloride, ethene becomes chloroethane. Additions also happen at other double bonds, for example at the C=O bond in aldehydes. The opposite of addition is **elimination**, in which atoms are split off and a double bond is formed.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two atoms share two pairs of electrons.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up itself.
The addition of hydrogen to a multiple bond.
Many small molecules join together to form long chains.

gewusst: The bromine water test is one of the best known school experiments in organic chemistry.
Vladimir Markovnikov was a Russian chemist of the 19th century.
Almost all plastic bags are made of polyethylene, which is formed by addition.

teile.einleitung: A class 1 lever, also called a two sided lever, is a simple machine in which the pivot lies between the effort and the load. Examples are the seesaw in the playground, scissors and the beam balance. With it you can move a lot with little force if you choose the distances cleverly.
wichtigste: In a class 1 lever, the pivot lies between the effort and the load.
Effort and load act in the same direction, for example both downwards.
The law of the lever applies: effort times effort arm equals load times load arm.
Scissors, pliers, seesaws and beam balances are class 1 levers.
The shorter the load arm, the greater the force on the load.
A beam balance needs two arms of the same length.
An oar with the rowlock as pivot also acts like a class 1 lever.

abschnitte.text: A **lever** is a rigid bar that can turn about a point, the **pivot**. In a class 1 lever, this pivot lies between the place where you push and the load. The distance from the pivot to the effort is called the **effort arm**, and the distance to the load the load arm. Because the two forces are on different sides, they act in the same direction, and the lever tips one way or the other depending on their strength.

A lever is balanced when effort times effort arm equals load times load arm. If 60 N hang on the left at a distance of 30 cm, then 45 N must hang on the right at a distance of 40 cm, because 60 · 30 = 45 · 40 = 1800. If you press with 100 N on the handles of a pair of combination pliers, 15 cm from the joint, 750 N acts on a wire 2 cm from the joint. So you save force, but in return you have to move through a longer distance.

A pair of **scissors** consists of two class 1 levers with the joint as the pivot. Thick cardboard is best cut close to the joint, because there the load arm is short and the cutting force becomes large. Pliers, nutcrackers with the joint in the middle and pincers work in the same way. On a **seesaw**, a light child can balance a heavy one by sitting further out.

Levers have been used for thousands of years, for example for lifting heavy stones when building. In the 3rd century BC the Greek scholar **Archimedes** described the law of the lever. He is credited with saying that with a long lever and a fixed point he could move the Earth. The draw well with a long sweep is also an ancient class 1 lever.

In a **beam balance**, both arms are the same length, so it is balanced exactly when the same mass lies on both sides. Such balances were already used in ancient Egypt and are a symbol of justice. In rowing, the oar rests in the rowlock on the boat, which can serve as the pivot. The rower pulls on the handle, and the blade presses into the water on the other side.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point about which a lever turns.
The distance from the pivot to the point where the force acts.
The distance from the pivot to the load.
A one sided lever, in which effort and load are on the same side of the pivot, as with a wheelbarrow.

gewusst: Your head sits on your spine as if on a class 1 lever; your neck muscles keep it balanced.
The golden rule of mechanics applies to the lever: what you save in force, you have to add in distance.
With a long crowbar, a child can move a stone that they could never lift with their hands.

teile.einleitung: Scales are a measuring device for finding out how heavy something is. They come in many forms, from the old beam balance to digital kitchen scales. Scales are also a well-known symbol of justice.
wichtigste: With scales you measure how heavy something is.
When shopping, people often weigh fruit and vegetables.
Digital scales show the weight with digits on a display.
Before you put something on them, the scales should show zero.
Whole lorries are weighed on large weighbridges.
Goldsmiths need very accurate scales for tiny amounts.
Scales are a symbol of justice.

abschnitte.text: **Scales** measure the mass of an object, that is, how many kilograms or grams it has. To do this they use the weight with which the Earth pulls on the object. Before you put something on them, the scales should show **zero**, otherwise the result will not be right. With the tare button you can, for example, set a bowl to zero and weigh only what is in it.

The oldest form is the **beam balance**: a beam rests in the middle, and a pan hangs from each end. You put weights on one side until the beam is level. In a **spring balance** the weight stretches a spring, and a pointer shows the value. Today's digital scales measure with an electronic sensor and show the weight in digits.

When shopping, people weigh fruit and vegetables so that they pay the right price. At the post office every parcel is weighed, because the postage depends on the weight. At the paediatrician's, babies are weighed regularly to see whether they are growing well. Whole lorries drive onto large **weighbridges**, for example at gravel works or at checkpoints.

Goldsmiths, pharmacies and laboratories need scales for tiny amounts. An **analytical balance** measures to an accuracy of a ten-thousandth of a gram. It often stands behind glass, because even a draught would disturb the result. The company Mettler from the Zurich region became known all over the world for such precision balances.

Beam balances were already being used in ancient Egypt, several thousand years ago. Because scales treat both sides equally, they became a symbol of **justice**. The figure of Justitia holds scales in one hand and a sword in the other. A sign of the zodiac, Libra, is also named after the scales.

begriffe.erklaerung: Scales with a beam and two pans that have to be in balance.
Scales in which a spring is stretched more or less depending on the weight.
The weight of the packaging or bowl, which is subtracted.
A figure who represents justice with scales and a sword.

gewusst: On the Moon a spring balance would show only about a sixth, but a beam balance would show the same as on Earth.
Today lorries can be weighed on the road while driving at full speed.
The most accurate scales in the world even notice if you leave a fingerprint on the object being weighed.

teile.einleitung: Tensile strength tells you how hard you can pull on a material before it breaks. It is one of the most important figures for materials such as steel, aluminium, ropes or plastics. Engineers need it so that bridges, cranes and cable cars are safe.
wichtigste: Tensile strength is the highest stress in a tensile test, based on the original cross section.
For metals it is usually given in N/mm².
The force at breaking is the tensile strength times the cross sectional area.
The number in the steel name S235 gives the minimum yield strength in N/mm².
After reaching their tensile strength, tough metals narrow at one point and break there.
Concrete can take a lot of compression but little tension, which is why it is reinforced with steel.
In glass, tiny surface cracks greatly reduce the tensile strength.

abschnitte.text: When you pull on a bar, the force is spread over its cross sectional area. Force divided by area is called **mechanical stress**. The **tensile strength** is the highest stress a material can withstand when pulled. It is often abbreviated to Rm and given in newtons per square millimetre.

Tensile strength is measured in the **tensile test**. A standard test piece is clamped in a testing machine and pulled apart slowly, harder and harder, until it breaks. The machine records the force and the lengthening, and from this the stress strain diagram is produced. At first the test piece stretches elastically like a spring; after that it stays permanently deformed, and tough metals finally narrow at one point.

A steel bar with a cross section of 50 mm² and a tensile strength of 500 N/mm² breaks at about 50 · 500 = 25,000 newtons, that is 25 kN. That is roughly the weight of 2.5 tonnes. An interesting quantity is the **breaking length**: how long a freely hanging wire could be before it breaks under its own weight. For steel with 500 N/mm², this is about 6.5 kilometres.

Concrete can withstand very high compressive forces but breaks even under small tensile forces. That is why steel bars are put into the concrete, which gives **reinforced concrete**. The concrete takes the compression and the steel the tension; this is how bridges, ceilings and dams are built. For structural steel, the name, such as S235 or S355, gives the minimum yield strength, above which the steel is permanently deformed.

Structural steel has about 360 to over 500 N/mm², depending on the grade; high strength steel wires for cable car ropes reach several times that. Pure aluminium is fairly soft, but aluminium alloys in aircraft building are very strong and light at the same time. **Carbon fibres** and spider silk are particularly strong in tension compared with their weight. In theory glass would be extremely strong, but tiny scratches on the surface act like notches where cracks begin.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force divided by the area on which it acts.
A test in which a test piece is pulled apart until it breaks.
The stress above which a material is permanently deformed.
Tough and deformable; the material stretches noticeably before breaking.
Steel bars inside concrete that take up tensile forces.

gewusst: Compared with its weight, spider silk is stronger in tension than many steels.
Carrying ropes for cable cars in the Alps are designed with a large safety margin; they hold several times the actual load.
Despite being so thin, a hair can withstand about 1 newton, which is about 100 grams.

teile.einleitung: Water is the most important substance for all life on Earth. Pure water is transparent and has no smell and no taste. It can occur as a solid in the form of ice, as a liquid, or as a gas in the form of water vapour.
wichtigste: Pure water is transparent, odourless and tasteless.
At 20 degrees Celsius water is liquid; at 0 °C it freezes and at 100 °C it boils.
Liquid water takes the shape of any container you pour it into.
Our body is made up of slightly more than half water.
Schoolchildren should drink about one litre a day.
The chemical formula of water is H2O.
Switzerland is known as the water tower of Europe.

abschnitte.text: Water is made of tiny **molecules**, each built from two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. That is why its chemical formula is **H2O**. In a glass, pure water is transparent, but in a deep lake or in the sea it has a bluish shimmer. Water is measured in litres, for example in a measuring jug.

At 20 degrees Celsius water is liquid and takes the shape of any bowl you pour it into. At 0 °C it freezes into **ice**, and at 100 °C it starts to boil at sea level. On high mountains water boils at less than 100 °C, because the air pressure is lower. What is special is that ice is lighter than liquid water and therefore floats on top.

Our body is made up of slightly more than half water, and babies have even more. We constantly lose water through sweating, breathing and going to the toilet. That is why schoolchildren should drink about one litre a day, ideally water or unsweetened tea. In hot weather and during sport you need even more.

About 70 per cent of the Earth's surface is covered with water. Most of it is salty seawater; only a few per cent is **fresh water**. Water is constantly on the move in the **water cycle**: it evaporates, forms clouds, falls as rain and flows back to the sea through rivers. A sponge put in water soaks it up, because water creeps into fine hollow spaces.

Switzerland is called the **water tower of Europe**, because big rivers such as the Rhine, the Rhone, the Inn and the Ticino rise here. Glaciers, lakes and groundwater store huge amounts of water. Drinking water comes mostly from groundwater and springs and is usually so clean that you can drink it straight from the tap. But if a fountain says “Kein Trinkwasser” (not drinking water), you should not drink from it.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest particle of a substance; for water it is made of three atoms.
Water with very little salt, as in lakes, rivers and groundwater.
The constant journey of water between the sea, the air, the land and rivers.
Water that collects underground in soil and rock.

gewusst: Water is one of the few substances that is lighter as a solid than as a liquid, which is why lakes freeze from the top.
The water you drink today may once have been inside a dinosaur or in a cloud over the Pacific.
On a tap, the red side usually means warm water and the blue side cold water.

teile.einleitung: Centripetal acceleration is the acceleration towards the centre that every body on a circular path experiences. Without it, a roundabout, a car on a bend or the Moon would simply fly on in a straight line. It explains why you feel pushed outwards on a bend.
wichtigste: Centripetal acceleration always points towards the centre of the circular path.
It is calculated with a = v² / r from the speed along the path v and the radius r.
With the angular velocity ω, a = ω² · r.
With double the radius and the same speed, it becomes half as big.
With double the speed, it becomes four times as big.
The force that causes it is called the centripetal force.
The Moon also experiences a centripetal acceleration of about 0.0027 m/s² on its orbit round the Earth.

abschnitte.text: A body on a circular path is constantly changing its direction, even if it stays at the same speed. In physics, every change in velocity, including a change of direction, is an **acceleration**. In circular motion this acceleration always points towards the centre, which is why it is called **centripetal acceleration**. The word comes from Latin and means roughly “striving towards the centre”.

The most important formula is a = v² / r, where v is the **speed along the path** and r the radius. So a body at 10 m/s on a circle with a radius of 20 m has 100 / 20 = 5 m/s². With the **angular velocity** ω, that is, the angle turned per second, a = ω² · r. A child sitting 2 m from the axis of a roundabout that turns once in 4 seconds therefore experiences about 4.9 m/s².

A car at 72 km/h, that is 20 m/s, experiences a centripetal acceleration of 4 m/s² on a bend with a radius of 100 m. The tyres supply the necessary force through **static friction** on the road. If the road is wet or icy, the friction is sometimes not enough, and the car slides straight on out of the bend. That is why tight bends have signs with lower speed limits, and railway lines or race tracks have tilted, **banked bends**.

A **centrifuge** uses very large centripetal accelerations to separate substances. A laboratory centrifuge at 3000 revolutions per minute produces about a thousand times the acceleration due to gravity g at a distance of 10 cm. Heavy particles such as blood cells quickly settle at the bottom. The spin cycle of a washing machine and loops on roller coasters also work on this principle.

Heavenly bodies also move on almost circular paths. For the Moon, the Earth's **gravity** supplies the necessary centripetal force. Its centripetal acceleration, at about 0.0027 m/s², is very small, because its orbit is huge. Isaac Newton realised that the same gravity makes an apple fall and keeps the Moon in its orbit.

In the 17th century the Dutch physicist **Christiaan Huygens** was one of the first to derive the formula for circular motion. Isaac Newton built his laws of mechanics and gravitation on it. Today engineers need the formula when building roads, roller coasters, turbines and satellite orbits.

begriffe.erklaerung: The path of a body that moves round a centre at the same distance.
The force that keeps a body on the circular path and points towards the centre.
Tells you how fast something turns, that is, what angle it sweeps through each second.
An apparent force outwards that you feel on a spinning roundabout.
The acceleration in free fall on Earth, about 9.81 m/s².

gewusst: The feeling of being pushed outwards really comes from your body wanting to carry on straight ahead.
Fighter pilots and astronauts train in large centrifuges so that they can withstand high accelerations.
The Earth turns in such a way that at the equator you experience a small centripetal acceleration of about 0.03 m/s².

teile.einleitung: Adenosine triphosphate, ATP for short, is the most important energy molecule in all living things. It is often called the “energy currency” of the cell, because almost every process in the body is paid for with it. Whether you run, think or grow, ATP is always being used.
wichtigste: ATP consists of adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups.
When one phosphate group is split off to give ADP, about 30 kJ/mol are released under standard conditions.
Most ATP is made during cellular respiration in the mitochondria.
ATP synthase is driven by a proton gradient.
Glycolysis yields a net 2 ATP from one molecule of glucose.
Each day a person turns over about as much ATP as they weigh.
Karl Lohmann discovered ATP in 1929.

abschnitte.text: ATP is a molecule made of three parts: the base **adenine**, the sugar **ribose** and a chain of three phosphate groups. Adenine and ribose together are called adenosine, hence the name adenosine triphosphate, that is, “adenosine with three phosphates”. The bonds between the phosphate groups store usable energy. Much like a charged battery, ATP gives off this energy when a phosphate group is split off.

When a phosphate group is split off ATP with water, **ADP**, adenosine diphosphate, is formed, and about 30 kJ per mole are released under standard conditions. If two phosphate groups are split off, AMP, adenosine monophosphate, is left. With the energy released, muscles move, nerve cells send signals and cells build new substances. Afterwards ADP is immediately “recharged” into ATP.

Most ATP is made during **cellular respiration**, in which sugar is broken down with oxygen into carbon dioxide and water. The first step, glycolysis, takes place in the cytoplasm and yields a net 2 ATP per glucose. Much more ATP is then made in the **mitochondria**, the power stations of the cell. There, enzymes pump protons across the inner membrane, and these flow back through ATP synthase, which turns like a tiny turbine as they do so.

The body stores only very little ATP; the supply in a muscle is enough for just a few seconds of maximum effort. That is why ATP has to be made constantly, and each molecule is reused many hundreds of times a day. In total, a person turns over about as much ATP each day as they weigh. In plants, ATP is also made during **photosynthesis** using the energy of sunlight.

The German biochemist **Karl Lohmann** discovered ATP in muscle extracts in 1929, at about the same time as American researchers. In 1941 Fritz Lipmann showed that ATP is the central energy carrier of the cell. How exactly ATP synthase works was worked out by, among others, Paul Boyer and John Walker, who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1997. Today we know that all known living things, from bacteria to humans, use ATP.

begriffe.erklaerung: Adenosine diphosphate, the “discharged” form of ATP with two phosphate groups.
A part of the cell in which most of the energy is obtained.
The breakdown of nutrients with oxygen to obtain energy.
An enzyme that makes ATP like a tiny rotary motor.
The first step in breaking down glucose in the cell.

gewusst: ATP synthase is one of the smallest motors in the world and really does turn round in a circle.
Glow worms use ATP to produce their light.
Building blocks like those in ATP are also found in the genetic material RNA.

teile.einleitung: In a horizontal throw an object is thrown exactly horizontally, for example a ball off a table or a stone from a bridge. It then flies on a curved path, a parabola, to the ground. The amazing thing is that it lands at exactly the same time as a ball that is simply dropped.
wichtigste: Without air resistance a body thrown horizontally flies on a parabola.
The horizontal speed stays the same during the flight.
Vertically, the body falls faster and faster, as in free fall.
A thrown ball and a dropped ball from the same height land at the same time.
Double the throwing speed gives double the range.
The horizontal and vertical movements combine according to the principle of superposition.

abschnitte.text: In a **horizontal throw** a body is given only a horizontal speed at the start. As soon as it leaves the hand, gravity pulls it downwards. The path of flight therefore becomes steeper and steeper and has the shape of a **parabola**. This is exactly true if you ignore air resistance.

The throw is made up of two movements that do not disturb each other. Horizontally, the body flies on at a constant speed. Vertically, it falls faster and faster, as in **free fall**. The fact that these movements simply combine is called the **principle of superposition**, and Galileo Galilei already recognised it.

For the time of the fall, t = square root of 2h / g. From a height of 1.25 m, with g = 10 m/s², the flight lasts exactly 0.5 seconds. The range is s = v · t: a ball from a height of 5 m flies for 1 second, so at 8 m/s it goes 8 metres. A stone from a height of 20 m flies for 2 seconds, and at 15 m/s it therefore goes 30 metres.

If you throw one ball horizontally and at the same time drop a second one from the same height, both land at the same time. This is because the horizontal movement does not change the time of the fall. If you throw twice as fast, you get twice as far, because the time of flight stays the same. If you throw from a higher place, you get further, because the ball is in the **air** for longer.

A jet of water from a garden hose held horizontally shows the parabola especially nicely. A marble rolling over the edge of a table also makes a horizontal throw. At fountains you can watch the curved arcs of water well. In reality **air resistance** slows down light objects, so that they fly a little less far.

begriffe.erklaerung: A curved line that describes the shape of the path of flight.
Falling only under the influence of gravity, without air resistance.
Several movements combine without disturbing each other.
The horizontal distance from the point of release to the landing point.

gewusst: A bullet fired horizontally hits the ground at the same time as a bullet dropped from the same height, if the ground is flat and you ignore the air.
Isaac Newton imagined firing a cannonball horizontally so fast that it never lands, but circles the Earth.
That is exactly how the International Space Station flies: it is constantly falling, but keeps missing the Earth.

teile.einleitung: The trajectory parabola is the path along which a thrown body flies if air resistance is ignored. It has the shape of a parabola, an even curve. Galileo Galilei already realised this in the 17th century.
wichtigste: Without air resistance, a thrown body flies along a parabola.
The movement is made up of an even horizontal movement and an accelerated vertical movement.
In a horizontal throw, the vertex of the parabola lies exactly at the point of release.
In 1638, in his “Discorsi”, Galileo Galilei showed that the path of a throw is a parabola.
You reach the greatest height with a release angle of 90 degrees and the greatest distance with 45 degrees.
Without air resistance, a ball arrives back at release height with the same speed as when it was thrown.
With air resistance, the descending part of the curve becomes steeper and shorter.

abschnitte.text: Galileo realised that a throw can be split into two parts. Horizontally, without air resistance, the body flies on at a **constant speed**. Vertically it is accelerated evenly downwards by gravity, just as in free fall. Both movements happen at the same time without disturbing each other; this is called **superposition**. Together they produce the curve of the parabola.

If you throw a ball exactly horizontally, the highest point, the **vertex**, lies at the point of release. The ball then falls faster and faster. For the distance fallen, h = g · t² / 2. Example: if a ball is thrown at 5 m/s, it needs 0.4 seconds to travel 2 m horizontally. In that time, with g = 10 m/s², it drops 0.8 m.

In an **angled throw**, the body flies upwards at a slant. The equation of the path is y = x · tan α − g · x² / (2 · v0² · cos² α). Here α is the **release angle** and v0 the initial speed. A ball thrown at 20 m/s at 30 degrees has a vertical starting speed of 10 m/s and therefore rises exactly 5 m with g = 10 m/s². Straight up, that is at 90 degrees, you reach the greatest height, and at 45 degrees the greatest distance.

In reality, the air slows down every thrown body. This makes it fly less far, and the path becomes lopsided. The descending part becomes **steeper and shorter** than the rising part. This path is called a **ballistic curve**. For heavy balls the difference is small, but for a shuttlecock it is very large.

Jets of water from a **fountain** or a garden hose show the trajectory parabola beautifully, because every droplet carries out a little throw. Basketball shots, football crosses and ski jumpers also roughly follow a parabola. Without air resistance, the path is symmetrical, and the ball arrives back at release height as fast as it set off. Galileo described all this in 1638 in his book “Discorsi”, which is regarded as the foundation stone of modern mechanics.

begriffe.erklaerung: An evenly curved line, like the one produced when throwing.
The highest point of a trajectory parabola.
Several movements working together without disturbing each other.
The horizontal distance from release to landing at the same height.

gewusst: Without air resistance, throws at 30 degrees and 60 degrees with the same speed go equally far.
If you drop one ball and at the same moment throw a second one horizontally, both reach the ground at the same time.
On the Moon, because of the weaker gravity, a ball would fly a much wider parabola.

teile.einleitung: A vacuum is a space in which there is no air and almost no particles. It is never completely empty, but the fewer particles are left, the better the vacuum. Space is the biggest vacuum, and there is also one in vacuum flasks and food packaging.
wichtigste: A vacuum is a space without air and almost without particles.
A completely empty vacuum cannot be made on Earth.
Sound needs air, which is why you hear nothing in a vacuum.
Light and heat radiation also pass through a vacuum; this is how the warmth of the Sun reaches us.
A vacuum flask keeps drinks warm thanks to a vacuum between its walls.
In the 17th century Otto von Guericke showed the force of air pressure with the Magdeburg hemispheres.

abschnitte.text: The word **vacuum** comes from the Latin “vacuus” and means empty. It refers to a space in which the pressure is much lower than normal air pressure. But you can never make a space completely empty; a few particles always remain. That is why people speak of rough vacuum, high vacuum and **ultra-high vacuum**, depending on how few particles are still there.

For a long time scholars believed that nature hated emptiness. In 1643 the Italian Evangelista Torricelli made a vacuum with mercury in a glass tube and in this way invented the barometer. The mayor of Magdeburg, **Otto von Guericke**, built an air pump and pumped the air out of two hemispheres. Not even two teams of horses could pull them apart, so strongly did the air press from outside.

If you put a ringing bell under a glass bell jar and pump the air out, the ringing gets quieter and quieter. This is because sound needs particles to carry it. A slightly inflated balloon, on the other hand, gets bigger as the air is pumped out, because the pressure from outside falls. Light, however, passes unhindered through a vacuum, which is why the warmth of the Sun reaches us by **radiation**.

In a **vacuum flask** there is a vacuum between the double walls, through which hardly any heat can escape. Vacuum-packed food stays fresh for longer because hardly any oxygen gets to it. A vacuum cleaner produces **low pressure**, and air flows in together with dust. The glass bulb of a classic light bulb is empty of air or filled with a protective gas so that the filament does not burn up.

At **CERN** near Geneva particles in the LHC accelerator fly through tubes with an extremely good vacuum. It is emptier there than in space near the Earth. Electron microscopes, computer chips and solar cells are also made or operated in a vacuum. In space itself there is an almost perfect vacuum, which is why astronauts need a spacesuit.

begriffe.erklaerung: An almost empty space with very few particles.
The force with which air presses on everything around it.
A pressure that is lower than the air pressure all around.
A device that sucks air out of a container.

gewusst: In space there are on average only a few particles per cubic centimetre; in the air around us there are billions of billions.
An astronaut without a spacesuit would not burst in space, as is often shown in films, but could only stay conscious for a few seconds.
In a vacuum water boils even at room temperature.

teile.einleitung: The drum is one of humanity's oldest musical instruments. When you hit its stretched skin, the skin vibrates and makes a sound. In Switzerland it is especially famous through the Basel Carnival.
wichtigste: On a drum the stretched skin vibrates.
A big drum sounds lower than a small one.
It is usually played with beaters or sticks.
If the skin is stretched tighter, the note gets higher.
Someone who drums in a Swiss band is often called a Tambour.
The large kettledrum in the orchestra is called the timpani.
Basel is famous for its drumming at Carnival.

abschnitte.text: A drum usually consists of a hollow **shell** or frame and a **skin** stretched over it. In the past the skin was always made of animal hide; today it is often made of plastic. The shell can be made of wood, metal or plastic. The skin is tightened with screws or cords.

When you hit the skin, it starts to **vibrate** and makes the air vibrate. The shell strengthens the sound like a sound box. If you sprinkle grains of rice on the skin, you can see them jumping when you hit it. This shows that the skin is moving quickly up and down.

The bigger the drum, the lower its sound. A tighter skin vibrates faster and therefore sounds **higher**. The **timpani** in the orchestra are large copper kettles whose skin can be retuned quickly with a pedal. In this way a timpanist can play different pitches.

At the **Basel Carnival** groups called cliques parade through the old town with drums and piccolos. It begins with the Morgestraich at 4 o'clock in the morning on the Monday after Ash Wednesday. The drummers are called **Tambouren**. The Basel drumming technique is very demanding and is learned in special drumming schools.

Almost every culture has drums. Well known are the djembe from West Africa, the bongos from Cuba and the large taiko drums from Japan. In rock bands one person sits at the **drum kit** and plays several drums and cymbals at the same time. In the past drums were also used to send signals over long distances.

begriffe.erklaerung: The stretched hide or film that you hit.
A drummer, especially in Switzerland and in the army.
Large kettledrums in the orchestra that can be tuned.
A stick with a head that you use to hit the drum.
A hollow body that makes a sound louder.

gewusst: There is also an eardrum in your ear, which vibrates when there are sounds.
The Basel drum has an especially tall, narrow shape and sounds bright and crisp.
Japanese taiko drums can be bigger than a grown-up person.

teile.einleitung: In physics a vector is a quantity that has not only a value but also a direction. It is drawn as an arrow: its length shows how big something is, and its tip shows where it is going. Forces, velocities and accelerations are such vectors.
wichtigste: A vector has a magnitude and a direction.
Vectors are shown as arrows.
A force is a vector quantity because it has a magnitude and a direction.
Quantities without a direction, such as mass, time or temperature, are called scalars.
Vectors are added by joining the arrows together.
Two equal and opposite forces cancel each other out.
Velocity, acceleration and momentum are also vectors.

abschnitte.text: A **vector** is a quantity with **magnitude** and **direction**. If you only say “5 kilometres”, nobody knows where to go. If you say “5 kilometres north”, it is a vector. The word comes from the Latin “vehere”, and means something like “carrier” or “driver”.

Quantities that consist only of a number and a unit are called **scalars**. Examples are mass, time, temperature and energy. Vectors always include a direction, as with force, velocity and acceleration. That is why a force counts as a vector quantity: it matters how hard you push or pull and in which direction.

In drawings a vector is shown as an **arrow**. The longer the arrow, the greater the magnitude. The tip of the arrow shows the direction. In formulas vectors are often written with a small arrow above the letter, for example for the force F.

When several forces act at the same time, you can add them. To do this you join the arrows tip to tail; the arrow from the start to the end is the **resultant force**. If two teams in a tug of war pull equally hard in opposite directions, the forces cancel out and the rope stays still. If one team pulls harder, the rope moves in its direction.

An aeroplane flying into the wind makes slower progress, because its velocity and that of the wind combine. A swimmer crossing a river is carried off course by the current. A **satnav** also calculates with directions and distances, that is, with vectors. In football the direction of a shot decides whether the ball goes into the goal just as much as its strength.

In mathematics vectors are described with **coordinates**, for example how far they point to the right and upwards. Computer games and animated films use vectors to calculate how characters move. Engineers use them to calculate the forces in bridges and buildings. Vector calculus was developed in the 19th century by Hermann Grassmann and William Rowan Hamilton, among others.

begriffe.erklaerung: The size or length of a vector without its direction.
A quantity without a direction, for example mass or temperature.
The vector you get when you add several vectors.
Numbers that show how far a vector points in each direction.

gewusst: Velocity is a vector, but the speedometer only shows its magnitude.
If you ride a bike in a circle, your velocity vector keeps changing, even if your speed stays the same.
An object stays at rest when the sum of all the force vectors acting on it is zero.

teile.einleitung: Wave physics is the part of physics that deals with waves, that is, with vibrations that spread through space. They include water waves, sound, light and radio waves. If you understand waves, you can explain why a siren sounds lower as it passes or how headphones block out noise.
wichtigste: A wave is a vibration that spreads out and carries energy as it does so.
Important quantities are wavelength, frequency, amplitude and speed of propagation.
The rule is: speed equals wavelength times frequency.
Sound in air is a longitudinal wave.
When a sound wave passes from air into water, its frequency stays the same.
The Doppler effect makes an approaching siren sound higher.
From about 20 kHz upwards, it is called ultrasound.

abschnitte.text: A **wave** is a disturbance that spreads through a material or through space. Energy is carried along, but no material is taken over long distances. If you throw a stone into a lake, rings travel outwards, but a floating leaf only bobs up and down. There are waves in water, in air as sound and, as light, even in a vacuum.

The **wavelength** is the distance from one crest to the next. The **frequency** tells you how many vibrations happen each second and is measured in hertz. If you multiply the two, you get the speed of propagation. The concert pitch A of 440 Hz therefore has a wavelength in air of about 78 cm, at a speed of sound of 343 m/s.

In a **transverse wave**, the particles vibrate across the direction of travel, as with a shaken rope. In a **longitudinal wave**, they vibrate back and forth along the direction of travel. Sound in air is a longitudinal wave; the air is squeezed and stretched in turn. Light, by contrast, is a transverse wave.

When two waves meet, they overlap; this is called **interference**. When two crests meet, they strengthen each other. If two identical waves are out of step by half a wavelength, crest meets trough and they cancel each other out. Headphones with noise cancelling use exactly this trick.

When an ambulance drives towards you, its siren sounds higher; when it drives away, it sounds lower. This is because the waves are squashed together in front of the vehicle and stretched out behind it. This **Doppler effect** was described by the Austrian physicist Christian Doppler in 1842. The police use it for radar speed checks, and astronomers use it to measure how fast stars are moving.

People hear notes between about 20 Hz and 20 kHz. Above that, from about 20 kHz, it is called **ultrasound**, and below it infrasound. Bats and dolphins find their way with ultrasound, and doctors use it to make pictures of the inside of the body. When sound passes from air into water, the frequency stays the same, but it becomes more than four times faster and the wavelength correspondingly longer.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance between two crests of a wave.
The number of vibrations per second, measured in hertz.
The height of a wave, that is, how far it swings.
The pitch changes when the source of the sound is moving.
Sound with such a high frequency that people cannot hear it.

gewusst: In water, sound travels at about 1500 metres per second, in air only about 343.
There is no sound in space, because there is no air there that could vibrate.
The wavelengths of light are so small that about 2000 of them fit into a millimetre.

teile.einleitung: The second law of thermodynamics is one of the most important laws of nature in physics. It says that on its own, heat only ever flows from warm to cold and never the other way round. From this it follows that no machine can turn heat completely into work and that many processes in nature run in one direction only.
wichtigste: According to Rudolf Clausius, heat never flows by itself from a colder to a warmer body.
According to Lord Kelvin, no cyclically working machine can turn heat from only one reservoir completely into work.
A perpetual motion machine of the second kind is therefore impossible.
The efficiency of every heat engine is always less than 100 per cent.
In an isolated system, entropy never decreases.
A fridge does not break the law, because work in the form of electricity is supplied to it.
The second law sets a direction of time, the thermodynamic arrow of time.

abschnitte.text: If you put a warm and a cold object together, their temperatures even out. Hot tea cools down, the ice cube in the glass melts, and it never happens the other way round by itself. This is exactly what the **second law of thermodynamics** describes. In 1850 the German physicist **Rudolf Clausius** put it like this: heat never flows by itself from a colder to a warmer body. The first law says that energy is conserved; the second says in which direction it is converted.

To state the law more precisely, Clausius introduced the concept of **entropy** in 1865. Put simply, you can think of it as a measure of disorder or of the number of ways particles can be arranged. In an isolated system, entropy never decreases, and in real processes it increases. The Austrian **Ludwig Boltzmann** later explained why: disordered states are simply far more likely than ordered ones. For experts, the Clausius inequality applies to every cycle, according to which the closed integral of δQ/T is less than or equal to zero.

As early as 1824 the Frenchman **Sadi Carnot** studied how well steam engines can turn heat into motion. According to Carnot's theorem, no engine working between two heat reservoirs has a higher efficiency than an ideal, reversible engine. In 1851 **William Thomson**, later Lord Kelvin, stated that no cyclically working machine can turn heat from just one reservoir into work. Such a miracle machine is called a **perpetual motion machine of the second kind**. That is why in every engine part of the energy is lost as waste heat.

A **fridge** carries heat from the cold inside into the warmer kitchen, apparently against the second law. But this works only because work in the form of electric current is supplied to it. By itself, the heat would never flow that way. A **heat pump**, such as heats many Swiss houses, uses the same principle in reverse. It takes heat from the cold air or the ground and, with the help of electricity, brings it into the warm house.

abschnitte.titel: Arrow of time and heat death
