abschnitte.text: Many laws of physics would also work backwards in time, but the second law does not. A broken glass never puts itself back together on its own. This direction of time is called the **thermodynamic arrow of time**. Some researchers imagined that in the distant future the universe would reach a state without temperature differences, the **heat death**. In chemistry, the law helps to predict whether a reaction will happen by itself: at constant pressure and constant temperature, the Gibbs energy then decreases.

begriffe.erklaerung: The study of heat, a branch of physics dealing with heat, energy and temperature.
A measure of how spread out or disordered energy and particles are in a system.
The share of the energy put in that is turned into useful work.
An imaginary machine that would run for ever without any energy being supplied.
A large body that gives off or takes in heat without its temperature changing noticeably.

gewusst: Rudolf Clausius was a professor at the Polytechnic in Zurich, today's ETH, from 1855 to 1867, and introduced the concept of entropy during that time.
Ludwig Boltzmann's formula for entropy is engraved on his gravestone in Vienna.
Clausius formed the word entropy from the Greek word for transformation.

teile.einleitung: A spirit level shows whether something is exactly horizontal or vertical. Its heart is a small tube with liquid and an air bubble. Craftspeople need it every day, and it is handy for hanging a picture too.
wichtigste: With a spirit level you check whether something is straight.
In the tube you can see an air bubble.
If the level lies exactly horizontal, the bubble sits in the middle between the lines.
The bubble always moves upwards, because air is lighter than the liquid.
The tube with the bubble is called a vial.
The liquid often contains alcohol so that it does not freeze in winter.
A tube fitted crosswise shows whether something is vertical.

abschnitte.text: A **spirit level** is a straight bar made of aluminium, wood or plastic. Inside it are small, transparent tubes with liquid and an **air bubble**. You lay it on a surface or hold it against a wall. Then you look where the bubble is. Its German name “Wasserwaage” means “water scales”, but a spirit level weighs nothing; it only shows the position.

The tube is called a **vial**. It is curved very slightly upwards. Because air is lighter than the liquid, the bubble always rises to the highest point. If the level lies exactly **horizontal**, the middle of the tube is highest and the bubble sits between the two lines. If one side is higher, the bubble moves there.

The vial usually contains not pure water but a liquid with **alcohol**. It does not freeze in winter and moves easily, so the bubble reacts quickly. It is often coloured yellow or green so that you can see the bubble well. The tube is tightly sealed so that nothing evaporates. The first vial with an air bubble was described in France in the 17th century.

A spirit level usually has several vials. One lies lengthwise and checks whether something is horizontal. A tube fitted crosswise shows whether something is **vertical**, such as a door frame or a post. Some spirit levels also have a vial for 45 degrees. Small round **bullseye levels** check a surface in all directions at once, for example on cameras on tripods.

**Bricklayers** and **joiners** need the spirit level at work almost every day. With it, walls become straight, tiles flat and shelves not crooked. Tilers, carpenters and electricians use it too. Today there are also laser devices that project a straight line onto the wall. Many smartphones also have an app that works like a spirit level using built in sensors.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tube with liquid and an air bubble in a spirit level.
Exactly flat, like the still surface of a lake.
Exactly straight up, at a right angle to a horizontal surface.
A round vial that checks a surface in all directions.

gewusst: In German the vial is called “Libelle”, because the Latin word libella means a small balance.
With a water hose held upwards at both ends, you can mark equal heights even over long distances.

teile.einleitung: A wheel and axle is a simple machine made of a large wheel and a thin shaft that are firmly joined together and turn about the same axis. With its help you can lift or turn heavy loads with little force. Wheels and axles are found in cranks, steering wheels, door handles and even in screwdrivers.
wichtigste: A wheel and axle consists of a wheel and a shaft fixed on the same axis.
At the large wheel you need less force than at the small shaft.
In balance, the turning effect at the wheel and at the shaft is the same.
What you save in force, you have to make up for in extra distance.
A rope winch with a crank, as over old draw wells, is called a windlass.
A wheel and axle works like a lever that can keep on turning.
On a bicycle, the wheel and axle is used the other way round to gain speed.

abschnitte.titel: What is a wheel and axle?
abschnitte.text: The wheel and axle is one of the classic **simple machines**, like the lever, the pulley and the inclined plane. It consists of a wheel with a large radius and a **shaft** with a small radius. Both are firmly joined and turn together about one axis. Instead of a wheel it can also be a crank or a handle.

The same law applies to the wheel and axle as to the lever: force times radius is the same on both sides. This product is called the **torque**. If the wheel has a radius of 30 centimetres and the shaft 5 centimetres, the radius is six times bigger. So a load of 600 newtons on the shaft can be held with just 100 newtons at the wheel.

You get nothing completely for free: what you save in force, you have to make up for in distance. This is called the **golden rule of mechanics**. If a crank has a radius of 40 centimetres and the rope shaft 4 centimetres, the ratio is 10 to 1. So if you lift the load 1 metre, your hand has to move 10 metres round in a circle.

abschnitte.titel: Wheels and axles in everyday life
abschnitte.text: A **door handle** is easier to press if you hold it at the outer end, because there the lever arm to the axis is longer. A screwdriver has a thick handle, because the large radius increases the turning effect on the screw. Old lorries without power steering had huge steering wheels so that drivers could steer with less force. Taps, pepper mills and the cranks on window blinds also work on this principle.

Above old draw wells there is often a **windlass**, a rope winch with a crank. When you turn the crank, the rope winds round the thin shaft, and the full bucket comes up with little force. In the past such winches were also used on building sites, in mines and on ships to raise anchors or loads. In the Middle Ages, heavy loads were even lifted with **treadwheels**, in which people walked as if in a hamster wheel.

abschnitte.titel: The other way round on a bike
abschnitte.text: You can also use a wheel and axle the other way round. On a bicycle, a small cog, the **sprocket**, is fixed to the large back wheel. The chain pulls on the small sprocket, and the rim of the large wheel covers a much longer distance. In this way you gain speed, but you have to use more force for it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thick rod that turns and passes on force.
Force times distance from the axis of rotation; it tells you how strongly something turns.
A rope winch with a crank, for example over a well.
A simple aid such as a lever or pulley that changes forces.

gewusst: A steering wheel is a wheel and axle: the wheel is large and the steering column below it is thin.
With a long crank, a child can lift a load much heavier than themselves.
In ancient Greece, the wheel and axle was already counted among the basic machines.

teile.einleitung: Time dilation means that time does not pass equally fast everywhere. According to Albert Einstein's theory of relativity, clocks that move fast run more slowly than clocks at rest. In everyday life you notice nothing of this, but it can be measured with precise atomic clocks.
wichtigste: According to the special theory of relativity, moving clocks run more slowly.
Albert Einstein published this theory in 1905.
The time shown by a clock moving along with you is called proper time.
The formula is Δt = γ · Δt₀, where γ is the Lorentz factor.
At 0.99 times the speed of light, the Lorentz factor is about 7.
Time dilation happens at every speed, but in everyday life it is tiny.
In 1971 it was confirmed in the Hafele Keating experiment with atomic clocks on airliners.

abschnitte.text: People used to believe that time ran exactly the same for everyone everywhere. In 1905 **Albert Einstein** showed in his **special theory of relativity** that this is not true. If a clock moves relative to an observer, it runs more slowly for that observer. This “stretching” of time is called **time dilation**. Einstein developed the theory while he was working at the patent office in Bern.

A well known thought experiment is the **light clock**. A beam of light travels back and forth between two mirrors, and each trip is one tick. If the clock moves, an observer at rest sees the light travelling along a slanting, longer path. Because light is always equally fast for everyone, it takes longer to do so, so the moving clock ticks more slowly. The formula for time dilation can be derived from this idea.

The time on the clock moving along is called the **proper time** Δt₀. An observer at rest measures the longer time Δt = γ · Δt₀ for it. The **Lorentz factor** γ depends on the speed and is always at least 1. At everyday speeds γ is almost exactly 1, but at 0.99 times the speed of light it is about 7. Then about 7 seconds pass for the observer while the moving clock counts on by only one second.

If two spaceships fly past each other at a steady speed, each crew sees the other's clock running more slowly. That sounds like a contradiction, but it is not one, because each side may regard itself as being at rest. Only when one spaceship turns round and comes back can the clocks be compared directly. This thought experiment is called the **twin paradox**: the twin who travelled is younger on their return than the one who stayed at home.

In 1971 Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating flew round the Earth on airliners with **atomic clocks**. Afterwards the clocks showed tiny differences from clocks on the ground, as the theory predicted. **Muons**, short lived particles from cosmic rays, also reach the ground in large numbers only thanks to time dilation. Satellite navigation such as **GPS** has to take the effects of relativity into account. Without this correction, positions would be wrong by kilometres after just one day.

begriffe.erklaerung: Einstein's theory about space, time and motion.
The time shown by a clock that moves along with the observer.
A number that shows how much time is stretched at a given speed.
About 300,000 kilometres per second; nothing goes faster.
An extremely precise clock that counts the vibrations of atoms.

gewusst: Gravity slows time down too: a clock in the cellar runs very slightly slower than one on the roof.
Astronauts on the space station age by fractions of a second less in half a year than people on Earth.
Albert Einstein developed the special theory of relativity in Bern, where you can visit the flat he lived in at the time.

teile.einleitung: Displacement is a term from shipping and physics. A floating ship pushes water aside, and exactly this displaced water weighs as much as the whole ship. That is why the size of warships and many other ships is given as displacement in tonnes.
wichtigste: Displacement gives the mass of the displaced water and therefore the mass of the ship.
A ship with a mass of 500 tonnes displaces 500 cubic metres in fresh water.
If a rowing boat displaces 0.3 cubic metres, the boat and crew together weigh 300 kilograms.
If a cargo ship loads 200 tonnes, its displacement increases by 200 tonnes.
Gross tonnage, on the other hand, gives the total internal volume of a ship.
A ship that always sits in the water and pushes it aside is called a displacement hull.
If you throw a stone from a boat into the pond, the water level falls a little.

abschnitte.text: When you put a ship in the water, it sinks in and pushes water aside. According to **Archimedes' principle** the buoyant force is as big as the weight of the displaced water. A floating ship sinks in exactly as deep as it takes for the displaced water to weigh the same as the ship. The **displacement** in tonnes is therefore equal to the mass of the ship.

One cubic metre of fresh water has a mass of about one tonne. So a ship with a mass of 500 tonnes displaces about 500 cubic metres of water on a Swiss lake. A rowing boat that displaces 0.3 cubic metres weighs 300 kilograms with its crew. If a cargo ship loads 200 tonnes of cargo, it sinks deeper, and its displacement grows by exactly 200 tonnes.

Besides displacement there are other measures for ships. **Gross tonnage** does not describe the weight, but the total internal volume of a ship. It is used mainly for cargo ships and cruise ships, for example for harbour fees. For warships, on the other hand, the displacement is usually given.

A **displacement hull** always sits in the water and pushes it aside as it moves. This includes cargo ships, sailing boats and the paddle steamers on Swiss lakes. A **planing boat**, on the other hand, partly lifts itself out of the water at high speed and glides over the surface. That is why fast motorboats are usually planing boats.

Seawater contains salt and is therefore a little denser than fresh water. In the sea a ship has to displace less volume and therefore sits higher in the water. If it sails from the sea into a river, it sinks a little deeper. That is why cargo ships carry a **load line mark** on their side, with lines for different waters.

If a stone lies in a boat, the boat displaces as much water as the stone weighs. If you throw the stone into the water, it only displaces as much as its volume, and that is less, because stone is denser than water. That is why the water level of the pond falls a little. A floating ice cube, on the other hand, displaces exactly as much water as it produces when it melts, so the water level in the glass stays the same.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which water pushes a body upwards.
A ship that always sits in the water and pushes it aside.
A number for the total internal volume of a ship.
A marking on a ship that shows how deep it may be loaded.

gewusst: Even a huge ship made of steel floats, because with all its hollow spaces it displaces a lot of water.
A cubic metre of water weighs about a tonne, as much as a small car.
When floating sea ice melts, the sea level hardly rises because of it, but melting ice on land makes it rise.

teile.einleitung: Thermal expansion means that substances expand when heated and contract again when cooled. This applies to solid bodies such as metals, to liquids and especially strongly to gases. That is why bridges have gaps, and why the liquid in a thermometer rises.
wichtigste: Most substances expand when heated.
When cooled, they contract again.
The reason is that the particles move more when warm and need more space.
Gases expand much more than liquids and solids.
Bridges and rails have expansion joints so that they do not bend in the heat.
Water is an exception: it is densest at 4 °C.
Thermometers and bimetallic switches use thermal expansion.

abschnitte.text: When a substance is heated, its **particles** move faster and vibrate further back and forth. As a result they need more space, and the substance becomes a little bigger. When it cools down, the particles move closer together again. With solid bodies the change is so small that you usually cannot see it with the naked eye.

Most **metals** expand noticeably when heated. A steel rail 100 metres long becomes about 3 to 4 centimetres longer with a temperature difference of 30 degrees. Aluminium expands roughly twice as much as steel. A trick in the kitchen: a stuck metal lid on a jar is easier to open under warm water.

So that structures are not damaged in the heat, **expansion joints** are planned in. On large bridges you can see them as metal combs that fit into each other. Concrete slabs on roads and squares also have joints. Railway rails today are welded into long pieces and laid under tension so that they do not bend in summer.

**Liquids** expand more than solids; the liquid thermometer is based on this. **Gases** expand even more. A hot-air balloon rises because the heated air in the balloon expands and is therefore lighter than the cooler air outside. A blown-up balloon in a cold car, on the other hand, visibly shrinks.

Water behaves in a special way: it is densest at about 4 °C and expands again below that. That is why **ice** floats on water and lakes freeze from the top. At the bottom of a lake the water stays at about 4 °C in winter, so that fish survive. This special feature is called the **anomaly of water**.

A **bimetallic strip** consists of two different metals that are firmly joined together. Because the metals expand by different amounts, the strip bends when it gets warm. In this way irons, kettles and old thermostats switch off the electricity automatically. Thermal expansion is also used when shrinking metal rings onto wheels.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gap built in on purpose that leaves room for expansion.
Two joined metal strips that bend when warm.
The special feature that water is densest at 4 °C.
How much mass there is in a certain space.

gewusst: On hot summer days the Eiffel Tower in Paris is a few centimetres taller than in winter.
Freezing water expands so strongly that it can split rocks; this is called frost weathering.
High-voltage power lines sag lower in summer than in winter.

teile.einleitung: A cloud is a visible collection of tiny water droplets or ice crystals floating in the air. It forms when moist air rises and cools. Clouds bring rain, snow and thunderstorms and reveal a lot about the coming weather.
wichtigste: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals.
Rising air cools because it expands as the air pressure falls.
Dry rising air cools by about 1 degree for every 100 metres of height.
Water droplets need tiny particles as condensation nuclei.
Heap clouds are called cumulus, feathery clouds cirrus and layer clouds stratus.
Luke Howard introduced the Latin cloud names in 1802.
Tall towers of cloud in the afternoon can bring a thunderstorm.

abschnitte.text: Warm air can hold a lot of invisible **water vapour**. As it rises, the air pressure falls, the air expands and cools. Dry air cools by about 1 degree per 100 metres, so a parcel of air at 18 degrees is only about 10 degrees after 800 metres. When it gets cool enough, the vapour turns into small droplets on tiny particles of dust, salt or soot, the **condensation nuclei**.

In 1802 the English scientist **Luke Howard** introduced the Latin cloud names. **Cumulus** are white, round heap clouds that look like cotton wool balls and form on fine summer days. **Stratus** are layer clouds that cover the sky like a grey blanket. Cirrus are very high, thin and wispy feathery clouds made of ice crystals.

On hot days, heap clouds can grow into huge towers in the afternoon. These **cumulonimbus** clouds often reach more than 10 kilometres high and are flattened at the top like an anvil. Lightning, thunder, heavy rain and sometimes hail form inside them. If you see such towers of cloud, you should look for shelter in good time.

Thin clouds look white because the droplets scatter sunlight in all directions. Dense clouds look grey or dark from below, because little sunlight gets through them. **Fog** is really a cloud lying right on the ground. On the Swiss Plateau, in autumn and winter, a layer of **high fog** often forms, above which the sun shines on the mountains.

The **wind** moves the clouds across the sky, high up often much faster than at the ground. Behind high flying aircraft, white **contrails** form. They form because the water vapour from the engines freezes at once in the icy air. If the trails stay in the sky for a long time, the air up there is very moist, which often points to a change in the weather.

begriffe.erklaerung: The change from invisible water vapour to liquid droplets.
A tiny particle on which a droplet forms.
A white heap cloud on fine days.
A high, wispy feathery cloud made of ice crystals.
A blanket of cloud lying low over the land.

gewusst: A single medium sized heap cloud contains several hundred tonnes of water.
Clouds float because their droplets are so tiny that even weak upward air currents carry them.
There are clouds on other planets too; on Venus, for example, they are made of sulphuric acid.

teile.einleitung: Alternating current is electric current that changes direction regularly. Every socket in Switzerland supplies alternating current, which swings back and forth 50 times a second. It won out because its voltage can easily be changed with transformers.
wichtigste: Alternating current changes direction regularly; direct current always flows the same way.
In Europe and Switzerland the electricity grid has a frequency of 50 hertz.
Swiss sockets supply 230 volts of alternating voltage.
Alternating current is produced in generators, in which magnets and coils rotate.
With transformers, the voltage of alternating current can easily be changed.
Batteries, rechargeable batteries and solar cells, on the other hand, supply direct current.
SBB trains run on their own alternating current grid at 16.7 hertz.

abschnitte.text: With **direct current**, the electrons always flow in the same direction, like water in a stream. With **alternating current**, they keep changing direction, swinging back and forth. How often this happens each second is called the **frequency**, measured in hertz. If you draw a graph of it, you get an even wavy line, the sine curve.

In Switzerland and almost all of Europe, mains electricity has a frequency of **50 hertz** and a voltage of 230 volts. So it changes direction 100 times a second. In the USA and parts of Japan it is 60 hertz and about 120 volts. For cookers and washing machines there is also three phase current at 400 volts, which is made of three offset alternating currents.

Alternating current is produced in a **generator**. In it, a magnet turns inside a coil of wire, or a coil turns in a magnetic field. With every half turn, the direction of the voltage produced reverses. Generators are driven by water, steam or wind turbines.

The big advantage is that the voltage can easily be raised or lowered with a **transformer**. For transport over long distances it is raised to high voltage so that little energy is lost. Locally it is lowered back to 230 volts. In the past this was not possible with direct current.

At the end of the 19th century, two camps in the USA argued about the best electricity system. Thomas Edison backed direct current, while Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse backed alternating current. This dispute is called the **War of the Currents**. Alternating current won, partly in 1895 with the big power station at Niagara Falls.

Many devices such as mobile phones, laptops and LED lamps work with direct current inside. Their power supply therefore converts the alternating current; this is called **rectifying**. For very long lines, for example under the sea, high voltage direct current is used again today. SBB has its own grid with 15,000 volts and 16.7 hertz alternating current.

begriffe.erklaerung: How often something repeats each second, measured in hertz.
Current that always flows in the same direction, as from a battery.
A machine that turns movement into electric current.
A device that changes the voltage of alternating current.

gewusst: Old fluorescent tubes flicker unnoticeably 100 times a second, because the current changes direction that often.
The unit hertz is named after the German physicist Heinrich Hertz.
The European electricity grid is so closely connected that all generators from Portugal to Poland run in the same rhythm.

teile.einleitung: Angular velocity tells you how fast something is turning. It gives the angle that a rotating body sweeps through in a certain time. Whether a roundabout, a bicycle wheel or the whole Earth: everything that turns has an angular velocity.
wichtigste: The angular velocity ω is the angle swept through per unit of time.
It is measured in radians per second, rad/s for short.
One complete turn corresponds to the angle 2π, about 6.28 rad.
For all points on a rotating rigid disc, the angular velocity is the same.
The speed of a point along its path is calculated with v = ω · r.
The angular velocity vector points along the axis of rotation, at right angles to the plane of rotation.
The Earth turns about its axis at about 7.3 · 10⁻⁵ rad/s.

abschnitte.text: In a rotation, every point moves on a circle. The **angular velocity** ω (omega) tells you how big the angle is that a point sweeps through each second. It is calculated as angle divided by time. The angle is measured in **radians**. One full turn is 2π rad, which equals 360 degrees.

If a roundabout turns once in 4 seconds, ω = 2π / 4 s, about 1.57 rad/s. The second hand of a clock takes 60 seconds for one round and has about 0.105 rad/s. A motor turning at 3000 revolutions per minute makes 50 revolutions per second, which is about 314 rad/s. The general formula is ω = 2π / T, where T is the **period of rotation**. In this way quite different rotations can be compared.

On a rotating disc, all points have the same angular velocity. But their **speed along the path** is different: points at the edge cover a longer distance in the same time. The rule is v = ω · r, where r is the distance from the axis. If a point moves at 10 m/s on a circle with a radius of 0.5 m, then ω = 20 rad/s. That is why you feel faster on the outside of a roundabout than in the middle.

The Earth turns once about its axis in just under 24 hours. This gives an angular velocity of about 7.3 · 10⁻⁵ rad/s, which is very little. But because the Earth's radius is so large, at the **equator** you still move at about 1670 km/h. In Switzerland the distance from the Earth's axis is smaller, so you travel more slowly there, at about 1100 km/h. We notice nothing of this, because everything around us moves along evenly.

Physicists also describe angular velocity as a **vector**, that is, as an arrow. This arrow lies on the axis of rotation and is at right angles to the plane in which the body turns. Its direction is found with the **right hand rule**: the curled fingers show the direction of rotation, and the thumb shows the direction of the vector. In this way rotations in space can be described unambiguously, for example for spinning tops or satellites.

begriffe.erklaerung: A unit of angle; one full turn is 2π rad.
The time needed for one complete turn.
How fast a point moves along its circular path.
The number of turns per unit of time, for example per minute.

gewusst: The hour hand of a clock turns 12 times more slowly than the minute hand.
Figure skaters spin much faster when they pull their arms in to their body.
Because of the Earth's rotation, a point on the equator travels faster than an airliner.

teile.einleitung: The volt is the unit for electrical voltage. Voltage is like a pressure that drives the electric current through the wires. The unit is named after the Italian scientist Alessandro Volta, who built the first battery.
wichtigste: The volt is the unit of electrical voltage; its symbol is V.
The unit honours the Italian Alessandro Volta.
Around 1800 Volta built the voltaic pile, the first battery.
One kilovolt is 1000 volts, and 0.5 volts is 500 millivolts.
A car battery has 12 volts, a lithium-ion cell in a mobile phone about 3.7 volts.
Swiss sockets supply 230 volts.
The highest lines in the Swiss transmission grid work at 380 kilovolts.

abschnitte.text: The **volt** measures the **electrical voltage** between two points. You can compare it with the water pressure in a pipe. The higher the voltage, the more strongly the current is driven through a circuit. Voltage is measured with a voltmeter. In physics 1 volt equals 1 watt divided by 1 ampere.

**Alessandro Volta** lived from 1745 to 1827 and came from Como in Italy. Around 1800 he built the **voltaic pile**. It consisted of many discs of zinc and copper, separated by cloth or cardboard soaked in salt water. With it, electric current could be produced continuously for the first time. Napoleon was so impressed that he honoured Volta and made him a count.

For large and small voltages prefixes are used. One **kilovolt** is 1000 volts, one megavolt a million volts. A millivolt is a thousandth of a volt, so 0.5 volts is exactly 500 millivolts. The nerve cells in your body work with voltages of only about 70 millivolts. Lightning, on the other hand, can reach many millions of volts.

A normal AA battery supplies 1.5 volts, a flat battery 4.5 volts. The **starter battery** of an ordinary car has 12 volts. A single lithium-ion cell in a mobile phone supplies about 3.7 volts. USB ports usually give 5 volts. In Switzerland the sockets supply 230 volts, which is dangerous for people.

To carry electricity over long distances, **high voltage** is used. This means less energy is lost in the lines. The Swiss transmission grid run by Swissgrid works at 220 and 380 kilovolts. Large pylons carry these lines over valleys and passes. In substations the voltage is lowered step by step to 230 volts for households.

begriffe.erklaerung: The electrical push that drives the current through a circuit.
A store that turns chemical energy into electrical energy.
Very high electrical voltage used to carry electricity over long distances.
The first battery in the world, built from stacked metal discs.

gewusst: Electric eels can give electric shocks of several hundred volts.
Birds can sit on power lines because there is almost no voltage between their feet.

teile.einleitung: An inelastic collision is a crash in which part of the kinetic energy is lost and turned into deformation and heat. In a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies even stick together and move on together. Typical examples are car accidents or two balls of modelling clay that stick together.
wichtigste: In an inelastic collision part of the kinetic energy turns into deformation and heat.
In a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies then move on together.
Momentum is always conserved in a collision, but kinetic energy is not.
If a body collides perfectly inelastically with an equally heavy body at rest, half of the kinetic energy is lost.
With a ballistic pendulum you can measure the speed of bullets.
The coefficient of restitution shows how elastic a collision is: 1 is perfectly elastic, 0 is perfectly inelastic.

abschnitte.text: In a collision two bodies hit each other briefly and hard. If they bounce off each other like billiard balls without losing energy, the collision is **elastic**. If, on the other hand, they are deformed or heated, it is called an **inelastic collision**. If they stick together afterwards, the collision is perfectly inelastic.

Even in an inelastic collision the total **momentum**, that is mass times velocity, stays the same. If a car of 1500 kg at 20 m/s runs into a stationary car of 500 kg and the two get stuck together, the momentum is 30,000 kg·m/s. Shared over 2000 kg, this gives a common speed of 15 m/s. In this way many accidents can be worked out using the conservation of momentum.

The **kinetic energy** is smaller after the collision than before. The rest is in the deformation of the bodies and in heat, sometimes also in a loud bang. A body of 2 kg at 6 m/s has 36 J; if it collides perfectly inelastically with a body of 4 kg at rest, only 12 J are left and 24 J are converted. If two equally heavy balls of modelling clay fly towards each other at the same speed and stick together, no kinetic energy at all is left.

A **ballistic pendulum** is a heavy block of wood hanging on threads. A bullet gets stuck in it, and the block swings out. From the speed of the block you can work out the speed of the bullet. If a 10 g bullet gets stuck in a 990 g block and both move at 2 m/s, the bullet was travelling at 200 m/s.

Modern cars have a **crumple zone** at the front and the back. In an accident it deforms in a controlled way and so absorbs a lot of kinetic energy. This makes the impact less hard for the people inside. Helmets, crash barriers and run-off areas in ski races also use this effect.

Most collisions in everyday life lie between elastic and perfectly inelastic. A ball that falls from a height of 1 m and only bounces back 0.64 m high has a **coefficient of restitution** of 0.8, because the square root of 0.64 is 0.8. A bouncy ball has a high coefficient, a sack of sand almost zero. The smaller the coefficient, the more energy is lost.

begriffe.erklaerung: Mass times velocity, the force behind a movement.
The energy a body has because it is moving.
A part of a car that deforms in a crash and absorbs energy.
A number between 0 and 1 that shows how strongly a body bounces back.

gewusst: The ballistic pendulum was invented as early as the 18th century by the Englishman Benjamin Robins.
A meteorite that crashes onto the Earth makes an almost perfectly inelastic collision and produces enormous heat.
In crash tests engineers calculate with exactly these formulas.

teile.einleitung: Wave particle duality is an astonishing discovery of physics: light, and also tiny particles such as electrons, sometimes behave like waves and sometimes like particles. Which side you see depends on the experiment. This discovery was a cornerstone of quantum physics.
wichtigste: Light behaves both like a wave and like a particle.
The particles of light are called photons.
Electrons and other small particles also show wave properties.
The double slit experiment shows the wave nature through a pattern of stripes.
The photoelectric effect shows the particle nature of light.
Albert Einstein explained the photoelectric effect in 1905, while he was working in Bern.
Wave particle duality is a foundation of quantum physics.

abschnitte.text: “Duality” means that something has two sides. With light these are its **wave nature** and its **particle nature**. In some experiments light spreads out like waves on a pond; in others it arrives like individual little balls. Neither picture on its own describes light completely.

Around 1800 the Englishman Thomas Young sent light through two narrow slits. On the screen behind them a pattern of bright and dark stripes appeared. This can happen only if waves overlap and partly cancel each other out, which is called **interference**. For a long time this **double slit experiment** was seen as proof that light is a wave.

In the **photoelectric effect**, light knocks electrons out of a metal plate. It turned out that what matters is not the brightness but the colour of the light. Albert Einstein explained this in 1905: light consists of small packets of energy, the **photons**. At the time Einstein was working at the patent office in Bern, and in 1921 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics for this work.

In 1924 the Frenchman Louis de Broglie claimed that particles such as **electrons** must also be waves. Shortly afterwards, in 1927, experiments really did show interference patterns with electrons. Even whole molecules made of dozens of atoms produce such patterns. With large things such as a football, though, the wavelength is so tiny that you notice nothing of it.

Wave particle duality is a foundation of **quantum physics**, which describes the world of the smallest particles. Electron microscopes use the wave nature of electrons and can therefore show much finer details than light microscopes. Digital cameras, solar cells and light barriers are based on the photoelectric effect. Lasers and computer chips would also be unthinkable without this knowledge.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particle of light, that is, a tiny packet of light energy.
The overlapping of waves, in which they strengthen or cancel each other.
Light knocks electrons out of a material.
The part of physics that describes the smallest particles and their strange behaviour.

gewusst: If you send electrons one at a time through a double slit, a pattern of stripes still appears after many runs.
Isaac Newton thought light was a stream of particles, while his contemporary Christiaan Huygens thought it was a wave, and both were partly right.
Einstein received the Nobel Prize not for the theory of relativity but for explaining the photoelectric effect.

teile.einleitung: A prediction is a reasoned idea about what will happen in an experiment. You make it before you try something out. Scientists all over the world work in exactly this way.
wichtigste: You make a prediction before the experiment.
A good way to start the sentence is “I think that ...”.
A good prediction is based on what you already know.
With an experiment you test whether the prediction is right.
A prediction may also be wrong; that is quite normal.
If it is not right, you think of a new prediction.
In science a prediction is often called a hypothesis.

abschnitte.text: A **prediction** is a statement about what will probably happen. It is more than just guessing, because you think about reasons for it. A typical sentence is: “I think that the stone will sink in the water, because it is heavy.” In science such a prediction is called a **hypothesis**.

Research often follows fixed steps. First you observe something and ask a **question**. Then you make a prediction and plan an **experiment**. After that you observe closely, write down the results and compare them with the prediction.

You predict that a stone will sink in water and a cork will float. To test this, you put both into a basin of water. The stone sinks and the cork floats, so your prediction has been **confirmed**. Now you can ask further questions, for example whether a big piece of wood floats too.

Sometimes something quite different from what you expected happens in an experiment. That is not a mistake, but an important **finding**. You then think about why it turned out differently and make a new prediction. Many great discoveries came about in exactly this way, because scientists were surprised by a result.

If you make a prediction beforehand, you observe much more carefully. You remember better what you have learnt if you have thought it through yourself first. Predictions also help you to plan an experiment sensibly. In mathematics a statement that has not yet been proved is called a **conjecture**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical word for a scientific prediction.
A planned test to answer a question.
Looking closely and writing down what happens.
What comes out of an experiment.

gewusst: According to legend, Galileo Galilei dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa to test a prediction about falling.
Some mathematical conjectures remained unproved for more than 300 years.
Even a wrong prediction helps you, because afterwards you know more than before.

teile.einleitung: The long jump is an athletics event in which, after a run up, you jump as far as possible into a sandpit. Behind a good jump there is a lot of physics: speed, take off angle and gravity. In ancient Greece, athletes were already competing at jumping.
wichtigste: In the long jump you run up, take off and land in a sandpit.
You must take off at the take off board at the latest.
Anyone who steps over the board makes a foul, and the jump does not count.
At take off you swing your arms forwards and upwards.
After take off, gravity pulls the jumper back to the ground.
The measurement is taken to the mark in the sand that is closest to the board.
The men's world record is almost 9 metres.

abschnitte.text: First the jumper takes a fast **run up** along a track. Then they take off on one leg at the **take off board** and swing their arms forwards and upwards. In the air they bring their legs far forwards. Finally they land in the sandpit, which cushions the landing.

The take off must happen before the end of the board. If you step over it, it is a **foul**, and the jump does not count. The measurement is taken from the edge of the board to the mark in the sand that is closest to the board. So anyone who falls backwards or reaches behind with a hand loses valuable centimetres.

abschnitte.titel: The physics of the long jump
abschnitte.text: After take off, the body flies along a curved path, a **parabola**. **Gravity** constantly pulls it downwards. The distance depends above all on the run up speed, which is why good long jumpers are often fast sprinters too. The take off angle also plays a part; for top athletes it is usually about 20 degrees.

The men's world record is held by Mike Powell of the USA with 8.95 metres, from 1991. For women, Galina Chistyakova of what was then the Soviet Union jumped a full 7.52 metres in 1988. Bob Beamon's jump of 8.90 metres at the 1968 Olympic Games is also famous. At the time this jump was more than half a metre further than the old record.

The long jump was already part of the pentathlon at the ancient **Olympic Games** in Greece. Back then the athletes jumped holding small weights in their hands. The long jump has been included since the first modern Olympic Games in 1896. Today it is part of every big athletics competition; in Switzerland it is organised by the federation Swiss Athletics.

In Switzerland the long jump is part of many sports days and athletics competitions for children. There you often jump from a **take off zone** instead of a narrow board. This makes it easier, because you do not have to hit the board exactly. With practice at the run up and arm swing, the jumps soon get longer.

begriffe.erklaerung: A white board at the end of the run up track, from which you take off.
A jump that does not count because a rule was broken.
The force with which the Earth pulls everything down towards it.
The fast running before take off.

gewusst: The men's world record is longer than two cars one behind the other.
Bob Beamon's record jump from 1968 remained unbeaten for almost 23 years.
With a tailwind of more than 2 metres per second, a jump does not count as a record.

teile.einleitung: Honey flows slowly off a spoon, whereas water splashes away quickly. This thickness of a liquid or a gas is called viscosity. It describes how strongly a substance resists flowing.
wichtigste: Viscosity is a measure of how thick and sticky liquids and gases are.
Dynamic viscosity is measured in pascal seconds.
At 20 °C water has a viscosity of about 1 millipascal second.
Liquids become runnier when heated, whereas gases become more viscous.
Kinematic viscosity is dynamic viscosity divided by density.
Ketchup becomes runnier when shaken; this is called shear thinning.
A paste of cornflour and water becomes solid under quick pressure; it is dilatant.
A falling ball viscometer measures viscosity using a sinking ball.

abschnitte.text: **Viscosity** tells you how thick and sticky a substance is. In a flowing liquid the layers slide past each other and rub as they do so. The greater this internal friction, the more viscous the substance. Honey is thousands of times more viscous than water. As early as around 1687 Isaac Newton described how this friction depends on the speed of the layers.

**Dynamic viscosity** has the symbol η, pronounced eta, and the unit pascal second. According to Newton: shear stress equals viscosity times velocity gradient. If water at 0.001 Pa·s has a gradient of 100 per second, the shear stress is 0.1 pascal. If you divide dynamic viscosity by density, you get **kinematic viscosity**. It is given in square metres per second.

With liquids the viscosity falls when they are heated. That is why warm honey or warm oil flows much more easily. With gases it is the other way round: they become more viscous when heated. This is because the gas particles whizz around faster and collide more often. With engine oil it is important that it lubricates well both in cold winters and in a hot engine.

Some substances change their thickness when you stir or press them. **Ketchup** becomes runnier after being shaken hard; this property is called **shear thinning**. Wall paint is also made like this, so that it glides on when painted and does not drip afterwards. A paste of cornflour and water behaves in a **dilatant** way: if you hit it quickly, it becomes as hard as a solid. If you let your finger sink in slowly, it is liquid again.

With a **falling ball viscometer** a ball is allowed to sink in a liquid. The more slowly it sinks, the more viscous the liquid. Other devices measure how long a liquid takes to run through a thin tube. In factories chocolate, paints, shampoo and engine oil are tested in this way. In medicine the thickness of blood plays a part in circulation.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that can flow, that is, a liquid or a gas.
The unit of dynamic viscosity, written Pa·s.
A substance becomes runnier when it is stirred or shaken.
A substance becomes thicker or even solid when quick pressure is applied.

gewusst: In the famous pitch drop experiment in Australia, pitch has been dripping through a funnel since 1927, and only a few drops have fallen so far.
You can run across a pool of cornflour and water, but if you stand still, you sink in.

teile.einleitung: Efficiency tells you how well a machine or device uses energy. It describes the ratio of useful energy to the energy put in. The higher the efficiency, the less energy is lost along the way.
wichtigste: Efficiency is the ratio of useful energy to the energy put in.
It is usually given as a percentage.
No device has an efficiency of 100 per cent, because some energy is always lost.
The loss usually shows up as heat that nobody needs.
Electric motors have a very high efficiency, often more than 90 per cent.
An old light bulb turns only about 5 per cent of its energy into light.
High efficiency saves energy and money and protects the environment.

abschnitte.text: Every machine is given energy, for example electricity, petrol or food. Only part of it is used for what the machine is meant to do. **Efficiency** is the share of this **useful energy** in the energy put in. It is often written with the Greek letter eta (η).

You divide the useful energy by the energy put in. An example: a motor is given 100 joules of energy and gives out 80 joules as movement. Then the efficiency is 80 divided by 100, that is 0.8 or **80 per cent**. The remaining 20 joules are **losses**, usually in the form of heat from friction.

Energy never disappears; it is only changed into another form. This is called the **law of conservation of energy**. The lost energy turns mainly into heat, sometimes also into noise or vibrations. That is why a phone charger gets warm and a car engine gets hot.

A classic **light bulb** turns only about 5 per cent of the electricity into light; the rest becomes heat. An **LED lamp** is several times more efficient and needs only a fraction of the electricity for the same amount of light. A petrol engine in a car usually reaches only 25 to 40 per cent, whereas an electric motor reaches more than 90 per cent. Large hydroelectric power stations, of which Switzerland has many, even reach about 90 per cent.

The higher the efficiency, the less energy has to be produced. This saves money and raw materials and protects the climate. That is why the **energy label** on appliances such as fridges or washing machines shows how economical they are. The steam engine of the 18th century had an efficiency of only a few per cent, and engineers have been working ever since to make machines more and more efficient.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of the energy that is really used for the work you want done.
Energy that is lost without being used, usually as heat.
Energy is never lost; it is only changed from one form into another.
A word for how economically something uses energy.

gewusst: A perpetual motion machine, a machine that runs for ever without any energy being put in, is impossible according to the laws of physics.
Your body has an efficiency too: when cycling, only about a quarter of the energy from food becomes movement.
Heat pumps can give off more heat than the electricity they use, because they also take heat from the surroundings.

teile.einleitung: In everyday life speeds are usually given in kilometres per hour, but in physics often in metres per second. To convert, you only need one number: 3.6. If you divide km/h by 3.6 you get m/s, and if you multiply m/s by 3.6 you get km/h.
wichtigste: To go from km/h to m/s, you divide by 3.6.
To go from m/s to km/h, you multiply by 3.6.
The factor 3.6 comes from the fact that 1 hour has 3600 seconds and 1 kilometre has 1000 metres.
90 km/h is 25 m/s, 108 km/h is 30 m/s and 144 km/h is 40 m/s.
A gale blowing at 15 m/s blows at 54 km/h.
The 80 speed limit outside built-up areas in Switzerland is about 22 m/s.

abschnitte.text: **Kilometres per hour** (km/h) tells you how many kilometres you travel in one hour. This unit is on the speedometer and on road signs. **Metres per second** (m/s) tells you how many metres you cover in one second. It is the SI unit of speed and is used in physics and in weather forecasts.

An hour has 60 times 60, that is 3600 seconds. A kilometre has 1000 metres. If you travel at 1 km/h, you cover 1000 metres in 3600 seconds, so 1000 / 3600 = 1 / 3.6 metres per second. That is why the **conversion factor** is exactly 3.6.

90 km/h divided by 3.6 gives 25 m/s. A gale at 15 m/s blows at 15 · 3.6 = 54 km/h. An aeroplane at 250 m/s flies at 900 km/h. Which is faster, 20 m/s or 60 km/h? Since 20 m/s is exactly 72 km/h, the 20 m/s wins.

In Switzerland the limit is usually 50 in built-up areas, 80 outside them and 120 km/h on the motorway. At 50 km/h a car covers about 14 metres per second, at 80 km/h about 22 metres. So if you look at your mobile phone for one second, you drive many metres blind. That is why the **reaction distance** is so important for safety.

For a quick estimate you can divide km/h by 4 and add a little. The other way round, you multiply m/s by 4 and take a little off. A leisurely walk at 5 km/h is just under 1.4 m/s. **Sound** travels at about 340 m/s in air, which is over 1200 km/h.

begriffe.erklaerung: How far something moves in a certain time.
A number used to convert a value into another unit.
A display in a vehicle that shows the speed in km/h.
The distance you travel before you react to a danger.

gewusst: The fastest sprinters in the world briefly reach over 40 km/h, that is more than 11 m/s.
Sailors measure speeds in knots; one knot is about 1.85 km/h.
A cheetah manages over 25 metres per second when sprinting.

teile.einleitung: A voltmeter is a measuring device for electrical voltage. With it you can check, for example, whether a battery is still full or whether there is voltage across a lamp. It is important to connect it correctly, otherwise the measurement will be wrong.
wichtigste: A voltmeter measures electrical voltage in volts.
It is always connected in parallel with the component whose voltage you want to measure.
A voltmeter has a very high internal resistance, so that hardly any current flows through it.
Its circuit symbol is a circle with a V in it.
On a new flat battery it shows about 4.5 volts.
Across a closed switch you measure about 0 volts, across an open one almost the whole battery voltage.
Today the voltmeter is usually part of a multimeter.

abschnitte.text: A **voltmeter** shows how big the **voltage** between two points is. It has two test leads, usually a red one and a black one. You hold these to the two places between which you want to measure. In circuit diagrams it is drawn as a circle with a V in it. The ammeter looks similar; it measures current and has an A in the circle.

A voltmeter is always connected **in parallel** with the component. If you want to measure the voltage across a lamp, you connect the two test leads to the two terminals of the lamp. The measuring device has a very high **internal resistance**, often about 10 megohms in digital devices. As a result hardly any current flows through the voltmeter, and the circuit is hardly disturbed. If you wrongly connect it in series with the lamp, the lamp hardly lights up, because almost no current flows any more.

If you hold a voltmeter to a new **flat battery**, it shows about 4.5 volts. You can recognise a weak battery by a clearly smaller value. In a circuit with a battery, a switch and a lamp, the voltmeter shows about 0 volts across the closed switch. If the switch is open, you measure about the whole battery voltage there. In this way you can also track down faults such as a broken wire.

In the past voltmeters had a **needle** that was moved by a small coil in a magnetic field. Today most devices show the voltage as a number on a display. The voltmeter is often part of a **multimeter**. A multimeter can also measure current and resistance. With a rotary switch you choose what is measured and in which range.

With simple measuring devices at school you only measure small voltages from batteries or power supplies. The 230 volts from the socket are life-threatening. Only **electricians** with suitable devices may take measurements on the mains. Car batteries should also be handled carefully, because large currents flow in a short circuit. Before measuring, you always set the correct measuring range.

begriffe.erklaerung: The electrical push for the current, measured in volts.
Components are connected side by side to the same two points.
The resistance inside a device, very high in a voltmeter.
A measuring device that can measure voltage, current and resistance.

gewusst: A voltmeter can show a voltage even when no current is flowing at all, for example across an open switch.
If you hold the test leads to the battery the wrong way round, a digital voltmeter simply shows a minus sign.

teile.einleitung: A clockwork, or movement, is the inside of a clock or watch that moves the hands forward evenly. In mechanical watches tiny gear wheels, springs and a swinging little wheel fit together exactly. Switzerland, especially the Jura Arc, is world famous for such fine movements.
wichtigste: In a mechanical clock a movement with gear wheels drives the hands.
In a grandfather clock a pendulum swings back and forth.
In a wristwatch a small wheel swings, the balance wheel.
In a battery watch a small quartz crystal gives the exact beat.
An automatic watch winds itself through the movement of the arm.
In a cuckoo clock a bird calls at every full hour.
Watchmakers build and repair movements.
There are especially many watch factories in the Jura Arc.

abschnitte.titel: What is a movement made of?
abschnitte.text: Every mechanical movement has a **power source** that supplies energy, for example a wound spring or a heavy weight. A **gear train** of gear wheels passes the force on and transmits it to the hands. So that the spring does not run down all at once, the escapement releases the force only in small portions. A regulator makes sure these portions always come at the same speed.

In grandfather clocks and wall clocks the regulator is a **pendulum** that swings evenly back and forth. In 1656 Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock, which was much more accurate than earlier clocks. In pocket watches and wristwatches a pendulum would be impractical, so there the **balance wheel** swings, a small wheel with a fine hairspring. It swings several times a second and produces the typical ticking.

In a battery watch a tiny **quartz crystal** gives the beat. When electricity flows through it, it vibrates 32,768 times a second, and a chip counts these vibrations. An **automatic watch** is mechanical but has a small swinging weight, the rotor. When you move your arm, the rotor turns and winds the spring.

The **cuckoo clock** originally comes from the Black Forest and is also a popular souvenir in Switzerland. At every full hour a little door opens, a bird comes out and small bellows make the call. Many movements can do even more, such as show the date, strike the hours or work as a stopwatch. Experts call such extra functions **complications**.

In the **Jura Arc**, for example in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Le Locle, the Vallée de Joux, Biel and Grenchen, there are many watch factories. Watchmakers learn their trade in an apprenticeship lasting several years. They put together parts that are often smaller than a grain of rice, and work with a magnifying glass and tweezers to do so. Since 2020 watchmaking in the Jura Arc has been part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.

begriffe.erklaerung: Several gear wheels that pass on force and movement.
The part that releases the force of the spring in small, equal portions.
A swinging little wheel with a hairspring that gives the beat.
A crystal that vibrates very evenly when electricity flows through it.
An extra function in a watch, such as a date display.

gewusst: A mechanical wristwatch can consist of several hundred tiny parts.
The ticking of a clock comes from the escapement, which briefly stops a gear wheel at every step.
The number 32,768 was chosen for quartz watches because you can divide it down to exactly one second by halving it again and again.

teile.einleitung: Wolfgang Pauli was one of the most important physicists of the 20th century. Born in Vienna, he taught at ETH Zurich for more than 30 years and received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1945. His Pauli principle explains why atoms are built the way they are.
wichtigste: Wolfgang Pauli was born in Vienna in 1900 and died in Zurich in 1958.
He discovered the exclusion principle, also called the Pauli principle.
In 1945 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics.
In 1930 he predicted the neutrino, a tiny particle that is very hard to detect.
From 1928 he was a professor at ETH Zurich.
He was known for his sharp criticism, for example with the remark “That is not even wrong.”
He had a long correspondence with the Zurich psychiatrist Carl Gustav Jung.

abschnitte.text: Wolfgang Pauli was born on 25 April 1900 in **Vienna**. His godfather was the famous physicist Ernst Mach. Even as a schoolboy he was interested in the latest physics. In Munich he studied under **Arnold Sommerfeld** and gained his doctorate there. As a student of about 21, he wrote a long review article on the theory of relativity that even Albert Einstein praised highly.

In 1925 Pauli set out the **exclusion principle**. It says that in an atom no two electrons may have all their quantum numbers the same. You can picture it like this: each place in the electron shell may be taken by only one electron. That is why the electrons are spread over different shells. This explains the structure of the periodic table and why solid substances do not simply fall into one another.

In 1930 researchers faced a puzzle: in radioactive decay, energy seemed to go missing. In a letter, Pauli suggested that a tiny, electrically neutral particle carries off the missing energy. The Italian physicist **Enrico Fermi** later gave it the name **neutrino**, which means little neutral one. Only in 1956 could it actually be detected. Neutrinos fly almost unhindered through everything, even through the whole Earth.

In 1928 Pauli became professor of theoretical physics at **ETH Zurich**. During the Second World War he worked for some years in Princeton in the USA and then returned to Zurich. In 1949 he became a Swiss citizen. In 1940 he proved the **spin statistics theorem**, which divides particles into fermions and bosons. A weak form of magnetism in metals, Pauli paramagnetism, also bears his name.

Pauli was feared for his strict judgements and was nicknamed “the conscience of physics”. Of a bad theory he is said to have remarked that it was “not even wrong”. People joked about the **Pauli effect**: supposedly instruments broke or experiments failed as soon as Pauli was nearby. With Carl Gustav Jung he exchanged ideas about dreams and about the relationship between physics and the mind. Pauli died in Zurich on 15 December 1958.

begriffe.erklaerung: The rule that no two electrons in an atom have exactly the same properties.
A tiny, negatively charged particle in the shell of an atom.
A very light, neutral particle that flies through almost everything.
A number that describes a state of an electron in the atom.
A famous award for outstanding achievements in science and other fields.

gewusst: Every second, billions of neutrinos from the Sun fly through your thumbnail without you noticing anything.
At the CERN research centre near Geneva, Wolfgang Pauli's papers are kept in their own archive.
In 1930 Pauli sent his neutrino idea as a letter to a meeting in Tübingen, because he preferred to go to a ball in Zurich himself.

teile.einleitung: Tribology is the science of friction, wear and lubrication. It studies what happens when surfaces rub against each other, for example in engines, bearings or on skis. The name comes from the Greek word “tribein” for to rub.
wichtigste: Tribology deals with friction, wear and lubrication.
The term became known through the British Jost Report of 1966.
The Stribeck curve shows the friction in a lubricated plain bearing depending on the speed.
Friction is smallest when a film of lubricant separates the surfaces completely.
Abrasion and adhesive wear are important kinds of wear.
Graphite and the plastic PTFE have especially low friction.
Squeaking doors are caused by the stick-slip effect.

abschnitte.text: Wherever parts touch and move, **friction** and wear occur. Tribology studies these processes and looks for ways to reduce them or use them deliberately. The term was made known in 1966 by the British **Jost Report**, named after the engineer Peter Jost. It showed that poor lubrication causes industry enormous costs.

Lubricants such as oil or grease form a thin film between two surfaces. The **Stribeck curve**, named after the German engineer Richard Stribeck, shows how friction changes with sliding speed. With very slow movement the surfaces still touch, and the friction is high. It is smallest when a film of lubricant separates the surfaces completely.

Wear is the gradual loss of material from surfaces. In **abrasion** hard particles such as sand scratch a surface and remove material. In **adhesive wear** surfaces briefly weld together at tiny points of contact, and as they slide on, material is torn out. On top of this there is fatigue from repeated loading and chemical attack.

**Graphite**, the material in pencil leads, is a popular solid lubricant, because its layers slide easily over each other. The plastic PTFE, known as Teflon, has an especially low coefficient of friction and is used for pan coatings and bearings. Ball bearings replace sliding with rolling and so greatly reduce friction. Modern engines use special coatings to save fuel.

A squeaking door is caused by the **stick-slip effect**, a jerky switching between sticking and sliding. A drop of oil in the hinge usually stops the squeaking at once. When skiing, ski wax makes sure that the skis glide well over the snow. Brakes, shoe soles and car tyres are tribology too: here a lot of friction is wanted.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force that arises when surfaces touch and move against each other.
Slow removal of material by friction and loading.
Oil, grease or a solid substance that reduces friction and wear.
Jerking between sticking and sliding that causes squeaking or creaking.
A bearing in which a shaft turns on a film of lubricant.

gewusst: The bow of a violin also makes the string sound through the stick-slip effect.
More than 500 years ago Leonardo da Vinci was already studying the laws of friction.
In our joints a joint fluid acts as a natural lubricant.

teile.einleitung: Corrugated cardboard is a light but astonishingly strong material made of paper, from which most parcels and removal boxes are made. Its secret is inside: a wavy layer of paper between smooth layers. These waves make the cardboard firm, even though it consists mainly of paper and air.
wichtigste: Corrugated cardboard consists of smooth layers of paper with at least one wavy layer in between.
The waves inside make the cardboard particularly strong.
Corrugated cardboard is light, because there is a lot of air between the waves.
It is used above all for parcels, boxes and removal boxes.
The layers are usually glued together with starch glue.
Corrugated cardboard is easy to recycle and is often made from waste paper.
Wavy paper was first used in the 19th century as a lining for hats.

abschnitte.text: Corrugated cardboard is a **composite material** made of several layers of paper. On the outside are smooth papers called **liners**. Between them is a paper bent into waves, the so called **fluting**. If you cut a piece of cardboard open, you can clearly see the waves at the edge.

A single sheet of paper creases very easily. But if you bend it into waves, it can suddenly carry much more weight, rather like a corrugated iron roof. The waves act like many small **supports** and arches that spread the weight. Together with the smooth outer layers, this makes a stiff, light component. Engineers use the same principle when building bridges and aircraft.

There is **single wall** cardboard with one layer of fluting and **double wall** or triple wall cardboard for heavy loads. The waves can be fine or coarse and are labelled with letters such as B, C or E. Fine waves make thin cardboard for pizza boxes, coarse waves thick cardboard for furniture or machines. Triple wall corrugated cardboard is so strong that pallets and even furniture can be made from it.

In a big machine called a **corrugator**, the fluting paper is softened with steam and pressed into waves between hot, toothed rollers. Then glue made of **starch**, often from maize or potatoes, is put on the tips of the waves. Then the smooth liners are glued on. Finally the cardboard is cut to size, creased and printed.

Wavy paper was invented in England in the middle of the 19th century and was first used as a lining in tall **hats**. From the 1870s it was used in the USA to pack fragile things such as glass bottles. Soon afterwards, smooth papers were glued onto the waves, and so today's corrugated cardboard was born. With mail order and later online shopping, it became the most important packaging in the world.

Corrugated cardboard is made largely from **waste paper**. Used boxes are collected, dissolved in water and made into new paper. In Switzerland, municipalities collect cardboard separately, often apart from paper. Before throwing boxes away, you should fold them flat and remove sticky tape if possible.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smooth layer of paper on the outside of corrugated cardboard.
The wavy layer of paper inside corrugated cardboard.
A material made of several layers or substances that are stronger together.
Used paper that is collected and made into new paper.

gewusst: The first wavy papers were not in parcels but in hats.
From thick corrugated cardboard you can build chairs that hold an adult.
A corrugated cardboard box consists largely of air.

teile.einleitung: The triple point is a very special state of a substance in which solid, liquid and gas exist side by side at the same time. This only happens at exactly one temperature and exactly one pressure. For water it is at 273.16 kelvin, that is 0.01 °C, and about 611 pascals.
wichtigste: At the triple point three phases of a substance are in equilibrium at the same time.
The triple point of water is at 273.16 K (0.01 °C) and about 611 Pa.
According to Gibbs' phase rule, a pure substance has zero degrees of freedom at the triple point.
Triple point cells are used in the laboratory to calibrate thermometers.
Mercury also has a triple point, at about minus 38.8 °C, which serves as a fixed point of the temperature scale.
Since 2019 the kelvin has been defined by the Boltzmann constant.
Freeze-drying uses sublimation below the triple point.

abschnitte.text: A substance can be solid, liquid or gas; these are called three **phases**. Which phase it is in depends on temperature and pressure. At the **triple point** all three meet: ice, water and water vapour are in equilibrium at the same time. The word “triple” comes from the Latin “triplex” and means threefold.

A **phase diagram** shows at which pressure and which temperature a substance is solid, liquid or gas. Three boundary lines separate the areas and meet exactly at the triple point. According to Gibbs' **phase rule**, a pure substance has zero degrees of freedom there: you can change neither the pressure nor the temperature without one phase disappearing. That is why the triple point is an extremely precise reference point.

The triple point of water is at 273.16 kelvin, that is 0.01 °C, and about 611 pascals. That is not even a hundredth of normal air pressure. Until 2019 the **kelvin** was defined exactly by this point, and since then by the Boltzmann constant. In **triple point cells**, glass vessels with pure water, it is produced in the laboratory to calibrate thermometers.

On Mars the air pressure is so low that it is close to the triple point pressure of water. That is why liquid water can hardly last on the surface of Mars: ice there often turns straight into vapour. Carbon dioxide has its triple point at more than five times normal air pressure. That is why **dry ice** never melts here, but turns directly into gas.

Below the triple point pressure, ice turns directly into vapour; this is called **sublimation**. **Freeze-drying** uses this: food is deep-frozen and gently dried in a vacuum. This is how instant coffee, astronaut food and crunchy pieces of strawberry in muesli are made. Flavour and vitamins are well preserved in the process.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state of a substance, for example solid, liquid or gas.
The direct change from solid to gas without becoming liquid.
Unit of temperature that starts at absolute zero.
To compare a measuring device with a precise reference value and adjust it.

gewusst: Washing also dries on the line in winter when it is freezing, because the ice slowly sublimates.
Some substances such as water even have several triple points, because there are different kinds of ice.
At normal air pressure carbon dioxide cannot be made liquid at all.

teile.einleitung: A wind tunnel is a facility in which strong, even wind is produced in order to test how air flows around aircraft, cars, buildings or even athletes. Instead of letting an aircraft fly through the air, the air is simply blown past a model that stays still. In this way shapes can be improved before expensive prototypes are built.
wichtigste: In a wind tunnel the model stands still and the air flows past it.
For the flow, only the relative movement between air and body matters.
A nozzle in front of the test section speeds up the air and makes the flow even.
The forces on the model are measured with a wind tunnel balance.
Streamlines are often made visible with smoke.
In 1901 the Wright brothers tested wing shapes in a wind tunnel they had built themselves.
In Emmen in the canton of Lucerne, RUAG runs one of the largest wind tunnels in Europe.

abschnitte.text: A wind tunnel is a pipe or tunnel through which large **fans** blow air. In the middle is the **test section**, in which a model or a real vehicle stands. Because for the flow all that counts is how fast the air and the body move relative to each other, it does not matter whether the aircraft flies or the air flows. In the wind tunnel this is much easier to watch and to measure.

In front of the test section there is a strong narrowing, the **nozzle**. It speeds up the air and makes sure the wind blows equally strongly and smoothly everywhere. In an open tunnel the air is sucked in and blown out again. In the **Göttingen type**, the air circulates in a closed loop, which saves energy and creates more even conditions.

The model sits on a **wind tunnel balance**, which measures exactly how hard the air pushes it backwards or lifts it upwards. From this, drag and lift are calculated. With threads of smoke or fine mist, the **streamlines**, that is, the paths of the air, become visible. Sometimes small woollen threads are stuck onto the model, or lasers are used to detect swirls.

In the 19th century researchers were already building the first wind tunnels. The **Wright brothers** became famous; in 1901 they tested many wing shapes in a tunnel they had built themselves. With this knowledge they achieved the first controlled powered flight in 1903. In the 20th century ever larger facilities were built in Göttingen, in France and in the USA, and later tunnels for supersonic speeds too.

Car makers test their vehicles in the wind tunnel to reduce drag and so save fuel or electricity. A **moving belt** under the model car imitates the moving road. Ski racers, bobsleigh teams and professional cyclists practise their position in the wind tunnel and test suits and helmets. Bridges, tower blocks and stadiums are also tested so that they can withstand strong wind.

In **Emmen** in the canton of Lucerne, RUAG runs one of the largest wind tunnels in Europe. Models of aircraft are tested there, but also cars, lorries and sports equipment. The model must not be too big compared with the test section, otherwise the **tunnel walls** distort the flow. That is why scaled down models are usually tested and the results converted to the real size.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which the air slows down a moving body.
The force that raises an aircraft wing upwards.
An imaginary line that shows which way the air goes.
A scaled down, accurate copy of a vehicle or building.

gewusst: For skydivers there are vertical wind tunnels in which you can float in the air.
Bicycle helmets and ski suits are also tested in the wind tunnel, because even small improvements gain hundredths of a second.
The Wright brothers built their first wind tunnel from a simple wooden box and a fan.

teile.einleitung: A gearwheel is a wheel with teeth round its edge that meshes with another gearwheel and turns it. With gearwheels you can pass on rotation, make it faster or slower and change its direction. They are found in clocks, bicycles, cars, mixers and in Switzerland's rack railways.
wichtigste: The points round the edge of a gearwheel are called teeth.
Two meshing gearwheels turn in opposite directions.
The smaller gearwheel turns faster than the larger one.
If one wheel has 20 teeth and the other 10, the small one turns twice for each turn of the large one.
Gearwheels are usually made of metal or plastic.
On a bicycle, gearwheels and a chain drive the back wheel.
The large gearwheel at the front by the pedals is called the chainring.

abschnitte.text: A gearwheel is a round part with regular **teeth** round its edge. When two gearwheels mesh, each tooth pushes the next tooth of the other wheel along. In this way the rotation is passed on without anything slipping. Several gearwheels together are called a **gearbox** or gear train.

If one gearwheel turns clockwise, the other turns anticlockwise, so they run in **opposite directions**. A small gearwheel has to turn more often so that as many teeth go past as on the large one. The ratio of the teeth is called the **gear ratio**. With 20 and 10 teeth, the gear ratio is 2 to 1, and the small wheel turns twice as often.

If a small gearwheel drives a large one, the rotation becomes slower but stronger. If a large wheel drives a small one, it becomes faster but weaker. This is used in the **gears** on a bicycle: on a steep climb you change into a low gear so that you can pedal with little effort. On a flat road you choose a high gear to ride faster.

On a bicycle, the large **chainring** sits at the front by the pedals and the small sprockets at the back wheel, connected by the chain. In a hand whisk with a crank, gearwheels turn the beaters much faster than you turn the handle. In mechanical clocks, tiny gearwheels make sure that the second, minute and hour hands turn correctly. Cars, washing machines and drills also contain gears.

On a **rack railway**, a gearwheel on the locomotive meshes with a toothed rack between the rails. This lets the train go up and down very steep stretches without slipping. The Vitznau Rigi Railway of 1871 was the first rack railway in Europe. With a gradient of up to 48 per cent, the Pilatus Railway is considered the steepest rack railway in the world.

Gearwheels are very old; in ancient times they were already used in mills and waterwheels. The **Antikythera mechanism**, a Greek device more than 2000 years old with many bronze gearwheels, calculated the movements of the Sun and Moon. In the Middle Ages, gearwheels were built into tower clocks. Today gearwheels are made very precisely from steel or plastic, and some are smaller than a grain of rice.

begriffe.erklaerung: Several gearwheels together that change a movement.
The ratio of how often two connected wheels turn.
The large gearwheel at the front by the pedals of a bicycle.
A straight bar with teeth that a gearwheel can mesh with.

gewusst: A mechanical Swiss wristwatch can contain more than a hundred tiny parts, including many gearwheels.
With three gearwheels in a row, the first and the third turn in the same direction.
The Pilatus Railway uses two horizontal gearwheels that grip the rack from both sides.

teile.einleitung: A turbulent flow is a swirling, restless flow in which liquids or gases mix strongly. You can see it in a wild mountain stream, in the smoke above a candle or in churning thunderclouds. The opposite is calm, orderly laminar flow.
wichtigste: Turbulent flows have irregular eddies and mix strongly.
When candle smoke rises smoothly at first and then becomes tangled, you can see the change from laminar to turbulent.
According to the idea of the energy cascade, energy passes from large eddies to smaller and smaller ones.
In a rough pipe with fully turbulent flow, the pressure loss grows roughly with the square of the speed.
A golf ball with dimples flies further because the turbulent boundary layer breaks away later.
Behind a cylinder in a flow, the Kármán vortex street forms.
Clear-air turbulence occurs in a cloudless sky, often near jet streams.
In Reynolds averaging the velocity is split into an average value and a fluctuation.

abschnitte.text: In a **laminar flow** layers slide calmly past each other, like playing cards in a pack. In a **turbulent flow**, on the other hand, eddies of all sizes form and keep changing. The particles move in all directions and mix strongly. You can see the change clearly in candle smoke, which first rises as a smooth thread and then becomes tangled.

Around 1883 the British scientist Osborne Reynolds used coloured threads of water in glass tubes to study when a flow becomes turbulent. From this came the **Reynolds number**, which links the speed, size and thickness of the flow. If it is small, the flow stays laminar; if it is large, it becomes turbulent. In a smooth pipe the change usually happens at a Reynolds number of about 2300.

In a turbulent flow large eddies break up into smaller ones, and these into even smaller ones. This passing on of energy is called the **energy cascade**. In the very smallest eddies the kinetic energy is turned into heat by friction.
