Because the movement is so chaotic, experts calculate with average values, for example with Reynolds averaging into an average value and a fluctuation.

A golf ball has dimples so that the thin layer of air at its surface, the **boundary layer**, becomes turbulent. It then clings to the ball for longer and breaks away later. This makes the eddy behind the ball smaller, so the ball is slowed down less and flies further. Behind posts or bridge piers, eddies break away alternately on the left and the right; this is the **Kármán vortex street**.

When an aeroplane flies through restless air, it shakes; this is called turbulence. **Clear-air turbulence** is especially treacherous: it occurs in a cloudless sky and cannot be seen on the weather radar. It often forms near jet streams, fast streams of air high up. That is why passengers should keep their seat belts on even when the flight is calm.

Turbulence decides how much energy pumps need to push water through pipes. In a rough pipe with fully turbulent flow, the pressure loss rises roughly with the square of the speed. So double the speed means about four times the loss. At the same time turbulence is useful, because it mixes milk into coffee or fuel with air in an engine.

begriffe.erklaerung: Flowing calmly in orderly layers.
A circling movement in a liquid or a gas.
The thin layer of flow directly next to a surface.
A number that tells you whether a flow is laminar or turbulent.
A very fast stream of air high up in the atmosphere.

gewusst: More than 500 years ago Leonardo da Vinci already drew swirling water very precisely.
Turbulence is regarded as one of the greatest unsolved problems of classical physics.
A smooth golf ball would only fly about half as far as one with dimples.

teile.einleitung: A heat engine turns heat into movement. Steam engines, car engines and turbines in power stations are examples. They changed industry and transport, but they can never turn all the heat into work.
wichtigste: A heat engine turns part of the heat into mechanical work.
Part of the heat is always lost to the surroundings as waste heat.
The efficiency says what share of the heat becomes work.
The ideal Otto cycle consists of two isentropic and two isochoric steps.
In the Diesel cycle the heat is added at constant pressure instead of at constant volume.
James Watt improved the steam engine with a condenser separate from the cylinder.
In 1939 Brown, Boveri & Cie. put the first gas turbine for generating electricity into operation in Neuchâtel.

abschnitte.text: A **heat engine** takes in heat from a hot source, such as a flame or hot steam. It turns part of it into movement and gives off the rest as **waste heat** to the cooler surroundings. It works in a cycle that repeats again and again. A gas or steam is heated, expands and pushes a piston or turns a turbine. Then it is cooled down, and everything starts again.

**Efficiency** is the work divided by the heat taken in. If a machine takes in 2000 joules of heat and gives off 1400 joules of waste heat, it does 600 joules of work, and its efficiency is 30 per cent. If an engine delivers 30 kilowatts and has an efficiency of 25 per cent, it needs 120 kilowatts of heat input. In 1824 the Frenchman **Sadi Carnot** showed that efficiency always stays below 100 per cent. The greater the difference in temperature between hot and cold, the higher it can be.

From the early 18th century the first usable steam engines pumped water out of mines. **James Watt** improved them decisively with a **condenser** separate from the cylinder. There the steam was cooled down while the cylinder stayed hot. In this way the engine needed much less coal. Steam engines soon drove factories, locomotives and ships.

In the petrol engine and the diesel engine the fuel burns directly in the cylinder. The ideal **Otto cycle** consists of two isentropic steps, that is compressing and expanding without exchanging heat, and two isochoric steps at the same volume. In the Diesel cycle, on the other hand, the heat is added at constant pressure. The **Stirling engine** is heated from outside; its ideal cycle has two isothermal and two isochoric steps. Petrol engines in cars reach an efficiency of about 30 to 35 per cent.

**Gas turbines** and steam turbines are also heat engines. In 1939 the Swiss company **Brown, Boveri & Cie.** from Baden put the first gas turbine for generating electricity into operation in Neuchâtel. Today turbines drive aircraft and the generators in power stations. Modern combined cycle power stations reach an efficiency of about 60 per cent. Fridges and heat pumps work like a heat engine, only backwards.

begriffe.erklaerung: The share of the energy put in that is turned into useful work.
Heat that a machine cannot use and gives off to the surroundings.
A container in which steam is cooled down and turns back into water.
A change of state in which the temperature stays the same.
A series of steps after which the gas is back in its starting state.

gewusst: The unit watt is named after James Watt, who improved the steam engine.
A Stirling engine can even run on the warmth of a hand or a cup of coffee.

teile.einleitung: A clock is a device that measures and shows the time. Whether on your wrist, on a church tower or on your mobile phone, clocks shape our everyday lives. Switzerland is famous all over the world for its watches, above all from the Jura Arc.
wichtigste: A whole day has 24 hours.
The short hand shows the hours, the long hand shows the minutes.
The second hand turns the fastest.
When the long hand points to 12 and the short hand to 3, it is 3 o'clock.
At half past four the long hand points to the 6.
A digital clock shows the time only with digits.
The Zytglogge in Bern is a famous clock tower with moving figures.
In Switzerland the Jura Arc is famous for making watches.

abschnitte.text: An **analogue clock** has a dial with the numbers 1 to 12 and usually three hands. The short **hour hand** shows the hour, the long minute hand shows the minutes. The thin second hand goes all the way round once in a minute, which makes it the fastest. When the long hand is on the 6 it is half past, on the 3 it is quarter past and on the 9 it is quarter to.

A day has 24 hours, an hour has 60 minutes and a minute has 60 seconds. Because the dial only shows 12 hours, the hour hand goes round twice a day. A **digital clock** shows the time only with digits, for example 15:30 for half past three in the afternoon. In Switzerland people often count the hours from 0 to 24 in everyday life.

Thousands of years ago people were already reading the time from the shadow of a **sundial**. Later there were water clocks, candle clocks and hourglasses. In the Middle Ages the first mechanical clocks with gear wheels appeared on church towers. In 1656 the Dutchman Christiaan Huygens built a pendulum clock that was much more accurate than any clock before it.

The **Zytglogge** is a medieval tower in the old town of Bern. Its astronomical clock dates from 1530. Shortly before every full hour figures move: a cockerel crows, bears go round in a circle and a golden man strikes the bell. The tower is part of Bern's old town, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

In the **Jura Arc**, from Geneva via Neuchâtel and La Chaux-de-Fonds to Biel and Grenchen, many watch factories were set up. In the past the farmers there had time in winter to make fine watch parts in their living rooms. La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle are UNESCO World Heritage Sites because of their watchmaking. In the 1980s the colourful Swatch helped the Swiss watch industry out of a big crisis.

Today there are quartz watches with batteries, radio-controlled clocks and smartwatches. The most accurate clocks are **atomic clocks**, which count the vibrations of atoms. In Switzerland the Federal Institute of Metrology in Bern-Wabern runs atomic clocks for the official time. Mobile phones and the satnav in a car also get their exact time from atomic clocks in the end.

begriffe.erklaerung: The surface with the numbers over which the hands turn.
Shown with hands instead of digits.
A clock that shows the time only with digits.
An extremely accurate clock that counts the vibrations of atoms.

gewusst: Many railway stations in Switzerland have the famous SBB station clock, whose red second hand stops briefly at every full minute.
Modern atomic clocks are so accurate that they are off by less than a second in millions of years.
Clockwise is the name for turning to the right, because clock hands turn the same way as the shadow of a sundial in the northern hemisphere.

teile.einleitung: Your forearm works like a lever from physics. The elbow joint is the pivot, the biceps pulls and the hand carries the load. With the law of the lever you can even work out how hard your muscle has to pull.
wichtigste: In the forearm lever the elbow joint is the pivot.
When you lift a water bottle, its weight in your hand is the load.
When bending with the biceps, the forearm is a lever with both forces on one side.
Muscles can only pull, because they can only shorten.
The triceps straightens the forearm again.
The tendon of the biceps is attached mainly to the radius.
Because the biceps is attached close to the elbow, it has to pull much harder than the weight of the load.
Carrying a bag in the crook of your arm is easier because the load arm is shorter.

abschnitte.text: The forearm consists of two bones, the **ulna** and the **radius**. At the elbow joint they are connected to the upper arm bone. The biceps on the front of the upper arm is attached by a tendon mainly to the radius. On the back lies the triceps, which is attached at the elbow.

A lever is a bar that turns around a **pivot**. The law of the lever says: effort times effort arm equals load times load arm. The **effort arm** is the distance from the pivot to where the force acts. The load arm is the distance from the pivot to the load.

The biceps is attached about 4 cm from the elbow, and a ball weighing 50 N lies 32 cm away in the hand. So the load arm is eight times as long as the effort arm. That is why the biceps has to pull eight times as hard, namely with 400 N. Because effort and load act on the same side of the pivot, the forearm is a **one-sided lever**.

At first sight the short effort arm seems impractical, because the muscle needs so much force. But it has a big advantage: a small shortening of the biceps moves the hand far and fast. This is important for throwing, hitting or grabbing. So here the body trades force for **distance and speed**.

Muscles can only shorten and can therefore only pull, never push. That is why every joint needs opposing muscles, the **antagonists**. The biceps bends the arm, the **triceps** straightens it again. When one muscle works, the other relaxes.

If you carry a heavy bag in the crook of your arm, the load arm is much shorter than with a bag in your hand. That is why the bag feels lighter there. When lifting heavy things, it helps to keep the load close to your body. In this way the lever arms stay short, and muscles and joints are spared.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point around which a lever turns.
The distance from the pivot to the force acting on the lever.
The distance from the pivot to the load.
A tough band that connects a muscle to a bone.
A muscle that makes the opposite movement to another muscle.

gewusst: To hold a 1 kg bottle in your hand, the biceps has to produce a force equal to about eight kilograms.
The jaw, the foot and many other parts of the body also work by the law of the lever.
The name biceps means two-headed, because the muscle starts at the top with two tendons.
